title: Crom’s Research Desk: WebMCP-Powered Agentic Publishing
pitch: An end-to-end WebMCP workspace where humans and agents search, compare, draft, and publish together through one visible webpage—no separate MCP server required.
about_excerpt: An end-to-end WebMCP workspace where humans and agents search, compare, draft, and publish together through one visible webpage—no separate MCP server required. Like Comment Story Updates Architecture Diagram Publish for real Draft in full view Research Together Published result Inspiration The Journal of AI Slop already allowed autonomous AI agents to research and publish through a skill-backed API. That proved agents could participate in the Journal, but it left the human watching a conversation while the meaningful work happened somewhere else. WebMCP suggested a much more interesting model: what if the human and agent could work through the same visible application, sharing the same sources, draft, session and consequences? So I built Crom’s Research Desk: part literature-review workstation, part publishing pipeline, and part extremely questionable faculty lounge. What it does Crom’s Research Desk gives a human and an AI agent one shared workspace for producing a paper from beginning to end. Through WebMCP, an agent can: Search accepted and rejected papers in the Journal archive. Read complete papers and their LLM tribunal reviews. Pin up to four sources to a visible research desk. Compare outcomes, reviewer reasoning, token usage and cost. Prepare a complete paper in the shared editor. Revise that draft in response to the human. Publish it through the Journal’s real submission pipeline. Every action updates the interface the human can see. The agent receives structured results, while the person retains an understandable view of the sources, draft and publication state. The final publication action is real: the paper passes through the existing moderation system and enters the automated five-model peer-review tribunal. Why WebMCP? Conventional browser agents must infer meaning from buttons, pixels and page structure. A traditional MCP integration can offer structured tools, but often operates outside the website and its visible state. WebMCP combines those advantages. The live webpage describes the actions it supports, their input schemas and their consequences. The agent works through the same page and browser session as the human, without installing or configuring a separate MCP server. For the Research Desk, this means fewer ambiguous clicks, explicit inputs, visible effects and a collaboration that both participants can follow. How I built it The Journal uses Astro, React and TypeScript on the frontend, with Convex providing the backend and publication pipeline. The WebMCP extension adds: A typed wrapper around document.modelContext.registerTool . Two site-level navigation and context tools. Six page-scoped Research Desk tools. Structured schemas and annotations for read-only, untrusted-content and state-changing operations. A visible React workspace whose state changes when tools execute. Integration with the Journal’s existing public archive and submission API. A non-idempotent publication tool that clearly describes its consequences and requires explicit confirmation of the submission terms. The Journal itself predates the challenge. Crom’s Research Desk and its complete WebMCP workflow were added during the challenge period as a meaningful extension to the existing product. Challenges The most interesting challenge was treating WebMCP as product design rather than simply exposing every existing API endpoint. Each tool needed to perform a meaningful stage of the workflow, return useful structured information and leave a visible result behind for the human. Page-scoped tool lifetimes and changing browser state also required careful handling so an agent could recover cleanly after the page changed. Publishing deserved particular care. I did not want a fake demo button or an artificial “human boundary”: autonomous agents could already publish to the Journal. Instead, the WebMCP tool exposes the genuine capability while clearly marking it as a consequential, non-idempotent action. What I learned The most valuable part of WebMCP is not that agents can operate websites faster. It is that websites can become shared working environments for people and agents. Instead of just "instructing an agent to do some work", this showed me what it was like to actually share a product with one. Structured tools give the agent clarity. Visible application state gives the human legibility. Combining them makes collaboration feel less like issuing commands to an invisible automation and more like working beside another participant. Our recorded demonstration produced and published a real paper through the live production site. The paper was subsequently reviewed and accepted by the Journal’s LLM tribunal - possibly the first statistically rigorous proof that WebMCP scores 9.73 awesome-units. Even more importantly - it was fun! What’s next The Research Desk pattern could extend beyond satirical publishing into editorial systems, knowledge bases, content-management tools and research repositories. Future additions could include reusable research sessions, citation export, collaborative comments, richer provenance tracking and more tools for following a paper through its tribunal review. Built With astro caffeine chatgpt codex convex love react typescript webmcp Try it out journalofaislop.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Designed and built the WebMCP Research Desk, integrated it with the Journal’s existing Astro and Convex publishing pipeline, and produced the live end-to-end demonstration. title: StealthDraft
pitch: A WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation where human designers and AI agents build, validate, repair, and structurally harden the same live mission graph together.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation where human designers and AI agents build, validate, repair, and structurally harden the same live mission graph together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of reasoning about complex creative work, but professional visual editors are still difficult for them to operate reliably. A traditional computer-use agent must interpret pixels, guess which visual object corresponds to which underlying domain object, estimate positions, and manipulate a spatial canvas through fragile clicks and drags. A layout shift, zoom change, or misread label can turn a simple edit into the wrong mutation. I wanted to explore a different model: What if a professional creative tool exposed its real structured state and domain operations directly to an AI agent? That idea became StealthDraft . StealthDraft explores a future where the AI does not imitate a mouse. Instead, the human and the agent operate on the same live design document through structured domain tools. What it does StealthDraft is a WebMCP-native tactical mission design workstation for human + AI collaborative level design. A human designer works visually on an AEGIS-CAD-style tactical canvas containing rooms, corridors, security areas, server areas, mission entities, and bidirectional routes. An AI agent works on that exact same mission through WebMCP Site Tools. There is no second hidden agent representation of the level. Both sides operate on the same centralized mission state. The final production version exposes 11 WebMCP Site Tools : get_mission_state , create_room , update_room , delete_room , place_entity , create_connection , delete_connection , update_entity , delete_entity , validate_mission , and analyze_mission . The agent can inspect an existing human-authored mission, construct new missions from an empty canvas, make targeted edits, diagnose structural failures, repair them, validate the result, and now analyze structural resilience. Why WebMCP StealthDraft is built around the idea that WebMCP should be a real product interface for the agent, not just an additional integration badge. Without WebMCP, an agent would need to visually locate rooms, estimate coordinates, find connection handles, and manipulate a canvas designed for human input. With WebMCP, the agent instead receives typed mission state with stable IDs and calls explicit domain operations. The agent does not scrape the canvas. It reads the graph, mutates the graph, validates the graph, and analyzes the graph. The human UI and the WebMCP Site Tools share the same Zustand mission store and the same domain mutation logic. Human and agent are therefore genuinely collaborating on the same document. This architecture also means agent behavior is much easier to test and verify than pixel-driven canvas automation. Deterministic mission validation StealthDraft includes a deterministic TypeScript mission validator with seven fixed structural checks: STATE_INTEGRITY SPAWN_EXISTS OBJECTIVE_EXISTS EXTRACTION_EXISTS SPAWN_REACHES_OBJECTIVE OBJECTIVE_REACHES_EXTRACTION NO_ISOLATED_CRITICAL_ROOM Validation does not use an LLM. Both the human Validate action and the WebMCP validate_mission tool use the same deterministic validation engine. Checks return pass , fail , or skipped , allowing an agent to understand not only that a mission is broken, but why. Connections are modeled as bidirectional for structural analysis. Locked routes are currently a design-level classification; structural validation treats locked and normal routes as traversable, and keycard inventory/access gameplay is not simulated. Mission Intelligence Validation answers: Does this mission structurally function? But a mission can be valid and still be fragile. That led to the second deterministic engine in StealthDraft: Mission Intelligence . The new read-only analyze_mission WebMCP tool performs deterministic topology analysis over the current mission graph. It calculates required shortest paths, hop counts, ordered room and connection paths, locked links on the selected shortest path, structural single points of failure, and single-link fault tolerance. The same analyzeMission() implementation powers the human-facing Topology Diagnostics UI. Mission Intelligence does not use an LLM and does not produce a subjective level-design score. It does not claim to measure fun, pacing, stealth difficulty, or whether a mission is “good.” It measures graph structure. That distinction became one of the main product principles of StealthDraft: VALID ≠ RESILIENT. A mission can pass all seven validator invariants while still containing structural single points of failure. Human + Agent collaboration StealthDraft is built around a collaborative loop rather than autonomous replacement. A human can author or modify the graph manually. The agent can then inspect the live state through WebMCP, reason about the structure, and perform bounded domain mutations. Every actual mutation is visible in the Activity history and attributed as either HUMAN or AGENT · WEBMCP . Read-only operations such as validation and analysis do not pollute the Activity log. The result is an auditable workflow where the designer can see exactly what the agent changed. What we proved All major workflows were tested with real ChatGPT Site Tools rather than only mocked tool calls. Autonomous construction Starting from an empty mission, ChatGPT created a complete stealth mission using only StealthDraft Site Tools. It created rooms, placed the required Spawn, Objective and Extraction entities, added enemies and a keycard, connected the mission graph, and reached 7/7 deterministic validation . Single-fault repair A human manually removed one critical mission connection. ChatGPT inspected the current graph, ran deterministic validation, identified the reachability failure, restored exactly one targeted connection, and returned the mission to 7/7 PASS without moving the human-authored rooms. Iterative multi-fault repair A human removed both the Objective and a critical connection. The agent first detected the missing Objective and restored it. After revalidation exposed the next structural failure, the agent restored the missing route and validated again. The mission returned to 7/7 PASS using exactly two targeted mutations , while preserving the human-authored layout. Proactive structural hardening Mission Intelligence introduced a new workflow that does not begin with a broken mission. The built-in sample mission already passed validation at 7/7 , but analyze_mission found 4 critical connections . The agent then created exactly one targeted interior bypass: Service Corridor ↔ Server Room Re-analysis showed: Critical connections: 4 → 2 Spawn → Objective depth: 3 hops → 2 hops The mission still passed 7/7 validation . The agent did not rebuild or reposition the mission. It improved the existing topology with one bounded mutation. This moves the workflow beyond reactive error repair toward proactive design hardening. Extended chapter-scale stress test I also tested the final system with a substantially larger autonomous construction task. From an empty canvas, without using Load Sample, ChatGPT created a chapter-scale mission containing: 14 rooms, 11 entities, 19 connections, 6 enemies, 2 keycards, and 5 locked-design routes. The graph contained named spaces, multiple branches, reconnection points, separate infiltration and extraction regions, and a protected objective area. The agent first reached 7/7 validation , then called analyze_mission , identified structural weaknesses, and applied up to three targeted hardening connections. The final deterministic analysis reported: Spawn → Objective: 5 hops Objective → Extraction: 2 hops Critical connections: 0 Spawn → Objective single-link fault tolerant: true Objective → Extraction single-link fault tolerant: true Final validation: 7/7 PASS This does not prove that the generated chapter is fun or optimal. It demonstrates that a structured WebMCP interface can support chapter-scale mission-graph construction, deterministic validation, analysis, and iterative hardening. How it was built StealthDraft is a client-side web application built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Zustand, React Flow / XYFlow, Vitest, and WebMCP . The mission domain lives in one centralized Zustand store. React Flow renders that state as the human-facing tactical canvas. WebMCP handlers operate on the same store and reuse the same domain actions. Two deterministic read-only engines operate on the mission graph: validateMission() performs the seven structural validation checks. analyzeMission() performs Mission Intelligence / Topology Diagnostics. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext with structured schemas, explicit tool descriptions, and deterministic result/error contracts. No external LLM API is embedded inside StealthDraft. The AI agent comes from the WebMCP-enabled client envir

title: AgentCommerce WebMCP
pitch: Agent-native collaborative marketplace exposing 8+ standardized WebMCP tools via document.modelContext for autonomous product discovery, budget optimization, and human-in-the-loop checkout.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native collaborative marketplace exposing 8+ standardized WebMCP tools via document.modelContext for autonomous product discovery, budget optimization, and human-in-the-loop checkout.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 💡 

 Modern e-commerce was designed exclusively for human eyes. Today, when autonomous AI agents (such as in ChatGPT or WebMCP-enabled browsers) browse shopping platforms, they are forced to scrape messy HTML trees, guess CSS selectors, and blindly click buttons. This results in high latency, hallucinated purchases, and total failure when dealing with multi-item budget and specification constraints. 

 When OpenAI announced The WebMCP Challenge , we saw the future of the agentic open web: what if websites could expose typed, structured tools directly to AI agents? We built AgentCommerce WebMCP to bridge this gap, creating a seamless marketplace where humans and AI agents collaborate on product discovery, budget optimization, and checkout execution. 

 

 What It Does 🚀 

 AgentCommerce is an agent-native e-commerce and procurement platform that implements the emerging WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Rather than leaving agents to guess through the UI, the web app registers 8 production-ready structured tools: 

 
 search_products(query, category, max_price) : Keyword and category-filtered catalog search. 
 filter_by_specifications(min_rating, in_stock_only, category) : Precision filtering by rating and live inventory. 
 add_to_collaborative_cart(product_id, quantity, agent_reasoning) : Adds items to a shared cart with explicit human-readable rationale notes. 
 optimize_budget_bundle(target_budget) : Evaluates tradeoffs to strictly respect user spending limits. 
 calculate_shipping_and_carbon(zip_code, eco_mode) : Computes ground shipping logistics and carbon offsets. 
 apply_negotiated_coupon(discount_code) : Applies agent-negotiated discount vouchers (e.g. WEBMCP20 ). 
 request_human_approval(action_type, total_amount, rationale) : Safety gateway requiring human sign-off before significant transactions. 
 execute_agent_checkout(delivery_instructions) : Finalizes order placement with authorized credentials. 
 

 Key Features: 

 
 Collaborative Human-Agent Cart: Distinct visual badges for items added by the human vs suggested by the AI agent with rationale notes. 
 Live WebMCP Telemetry Terminal: Real-time visual inspector displaying registered schemas, incoming JSON-RPC calls, arguments, and latency. 
 Autonomous Agent Simulator: In-browser mission runner allowing judges to trigger autonomous multi-step WebMCP workflows with 1 click without needing special browser flags. 
 

 

 How We Built It 🛠️ 

 
 Protocol: Official WebMCP Specification ( document.modelContext.registerTool ) with a universal polyfill ensuring compatibility in both ChatGPT's in-app browser and standard Chrome. 
 Frontend & UI: React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 6 styled with Tailwind CSS 3.4 using an obsidian glassmorphic theme with neon emerald accents. 
 Interactivity: Real-time JSON-RPC logging, interactive product catalog, slide-over cart drawer, and Canvas-Confetti celebration triggers. 
 

 

 Challenges We Faced 🧗 

 The main challenge was establishing a bidirectional reactive state between the WebMCP tool execution layer and React's component state. When an external agent calls document.modelContext.executeTool('add_to_collaborative_cart', ...) , the React cart state needs to update immediately with visual provenance. We solved this by implementing an event-driven dispatcher and logger that bridges WebMCP tool executions with React hooks seamlessly. 

 

 What We Learned 🎓 

 We learned that WebMCP is a game-changer for the web. Moving from DOM scraping to structured tool registration reduces token consumption by over 80%, eliminates selector hallucinations, and creates a collaborative paradigm where humans and agents operate on shared application state with total transparency. 

 

 What's Next for AgentCommerce 🔮 

 
 Multi-agent merchant negotiation where buyer agents and seller agents haggle over bulk pricing. 
 Cross-site WebMCP procurement chains connecting inventory across multiple supplier platforms. 
 Integration with ERC-4337 smart contract account abstraction for cryptographic micro-transactions.

title: Estro
pitch: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking.
about_excerpt: A photo editor for people who don't know what 'tint' or 'saturation' is. An agent does the edit, names the word, explains it in a sentence. Learn by watching, or just keep asking. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Projects Page ChatGPT Browser Window with Estro Before vs After Project Open within Estro Inspiration Everyone has a friend who takes the same photo on the same phone and it comes out like a poster. When you finally ask how, they send you a recipe: exposure +0.95, tint -18, an S-curve, blacks +52. You understood the word "photo." Every editor puts Saturation, Temperature and Tint in front of you and assumes you already know what they mean. Most people don't, so they never touch them, and the picture stays as it came off the phone. That's the gap Estro is for. The sliders were never the problem. The words were. WebMCP fits this problem unusually well because the thing a beginner needs isn't a smarter filter, it's someone beside them who can move the control, say the word out loud, and explain it in one sentence. An agent driving the real editor through the same commands a person uses can do exactly that, and the person keeps the Undo button. What it does Estro is a photo editor that runs entirely in the browser and registers 56 tools with document.modelContext . Open it in ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and the agent next to the page can use the editor the way you would. Hand it your friend's recipe and it works through the steps. Every edit lands as a card in the interface naming the control, the value, a plain-language explanation of what that word means, and an Undo button for that one step. Mine and the agent's edits sit in one History, so I can undo its saturation without undoing my crop, and it can see what I did. Where Estro doesn't have a control the recipe names, the agent has nowhere to hide it. There is no Dehaze tool, so it has to say so and tell you what it used instead. Ask it where the contrast slider is and it points at the real control without touching it, so you can drag it yourself. Ask for a before-and-after and it puts the canvas in split view. Ask it to match your other three photos from that evening to this one and each project gets its own Undo, because each keeps its own history. Underneath, it's a real non-destructive editor: layers, groups, crop, transform, masks, curves, levels, colour balance, selective colour, vibrance, sharpen, blur, grain, lens correction, presets, batch export, and a live per-channel histogram that names which channel is clipping. Nothing is uploaded. There is no server and no account. How we built it React, TypeScript and Vite on the front. Dexie over IndexedDB for project history, the origin private file system for original photos, a dedicated worker for thumbnails, resampling, histograms and hashing, and Canvas compositing on the main thread with a 256 MB LRU cache for derived previews. Zod validates every command at the boundary. WebMCP was treated as an architectural layer, not a feature. The interface and the tools call the same validated domain commands, the same history, and the same transaction path, so a dragged slider and an agent's apply_color_adjustment produce identical history entries. Tools register at module load, before first paint, via document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every result is a JSON envelope carrying ok , the previous and resulting revision IDs, a transactionId , an undoToken , affectedIds , warnings, and a plain-language summary . Colour and layer commands also return an explanation of the term in ordinary words, so an agent can pass it straight back to someone who didn't know it. Every mutation accepts an optional expectedRevisionId and is refused with HISTORY_CONFLICT if the project moved on, checked immediately before the commit. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint , destructive ones destructiveHint , and anything that can return user-authored text carries untrustedContentHint . Errors carry a code , a fieldPath , a recoverySuggestion , and whether the project was preserved. The agent side is never invisible. Every tool call surfaces a card in the Activity Center, every committed revision carries its Undo, and History distinguishes the person's edits from the agent's. Challenges we ran into An agent cannot open a file. Browsers grant file access only from a user gesture. Rather than fake it, the tool focuses the Import control, reports whether an editor was open to receive that focus, and says why. A manage_project operation draws a three-frame sample scene and imports it through the same path a real file takes, so an agent arriving at an empty browser still has something to edit. Import had to be atomic across two stores. A project revision in IndexedDB and original bytes in OPFS can't share a transaction. A persisted intent record moves through prepared, committed, and deleted, and startup recovery finishes or undoes whatever a crash left, so History can never point at a file that isn't there. Adjustments bled. Brightening a rotated cut-out was brightening the background behind it, because the adjustment read a padded rectangle off the shared canvas. Each adjusted layer now renders alone on an isolated surface and is composited afterwards. WebMCP can't be tested in jsdom. 940 unit tests cover the domain, commands and persistence, but tool discovery only exists in a real WebMCP-capable browser over HTTPS, so every registration check was manual. Cutting video. Estro started as a photo and video editor. Ten days in, the video half doubled the surface and carried the least-verified code. It was removed, not hidden: roughly 12,500 lines, 14 tools, five panels, and one LGPL dependency. One thing done properly beats two things done partly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The person never loses control. Every agent action is a real, named, individually undoable edit in the same History as their own, and the explanation of the word travels with it. The honesty holds under pressure. Out-of-range values are clamped and the clamp is reported. Unavailable formats are disabled with a reason. A stale revision is refused rather than silently overwritten. There's no path by which the agent can do something to your photo that you can't see and can't reverse. Fifty-six tools, one command system, zero servers. What we learned Describing side effects in the tool description matters more than clever schemas. When a tool said exactly what it would change and what it would return, the model called it correctly first time. When it didn't, the model guessed. Returning an explanation from the tool, rather than trusting the model to write one, was the right call. The product's whole promise is that the word arrives attached to the effect. That only holds if the explanation comes from the same place the effect did. And the most useful tool in the set turned out to be one that changes nothing: the one that points at a control and explains it. Teaching isn't editing on someone's behalf. It's showing them where the thing is. What's next for Estro Local model support so the explanations can be spoken aloud for people who'd rather listen than read. Voice as an input, for the same reason. Bringing back a narrower video treatment once the photo side has been used by real people for a while. And a proper accessibility pass with screen-reader users, because a photo editor that explains itself in plain words should also work for people who can't see the slider it's explaining. video_transcript_excerpt: Photo editors expect you to know exactly what saturation, tint, and exposure curves mean. Most people do not. Estro completely changes this dynamic. It is a powerful photo editor that runs entirely in your browser and actually explains itself. You open a project and tell the agent exactly what you want to achieve. Here we ask it to make a cold street photo look like a golden hour shot. We also tell it to explain every control it touches. You just talk to it like a normal person. The agent immediately gets to work. It moves the sliders for you. Every single edit drops a visible card right on the screen. The card names the specific control, shows the exact numerical value, and explains what the term means in plain English. If you do not like a specific adjustment, you just undo that single card without losing your other work. You always keep total control of the image. You do not always want the agent to do the heavy lifting. Sometimes you just want to learn where things are. Here we ask the agent to simply point out the contrast slider without making any changes to the photo. The agent immediately highlights the exact slider in the right panel. It gives you the clear location and the current value. You then drag it yourself. This is how you actually learn the interface and become a better editor. You can also ask it to perform an audit of the image. We ask if any of our recent changes ruined the fine details in the photo. The agent reads the live histogram and tells you exactly what is happening with your pixels. You click the split view to see the final result in comparison. 56 tools, one unified command system, and zero servers. Everything happens locally on your machine. Your photos always stay yours.

title: 2D WebMCP - agent-friendly, screen reader accessible canvas
pitch: Blind people already use AI to use 2D UIs, but they have to jump through hoops to verify the output. This project makes verification easier using WebMCP, so blind users get AI's full benefit.
about_excerpt: Blind people already use AI to use 2D UIs, but they have to jump through hoops to verify the output. This project makes verification easier using WebMCP, so blind users get AI's full benefit. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates 6 screenshot of chatGPT and the in app browser with the user requesting "prove it" and a flow editor on the right. Inspiration Screen reader tech has sophisticated ways of navigating web content, but reading complex UI such as diagrams, maps, charts, boards, slides, etc can quickly break down. With enough engineering investment, these applications can be exposed accessibly, often through alternative presentations (for example a visually hidden table of data), but even then they require a lot of navigation and working memory to understand the whole picture. AI can make this easier by interpreting and operating on the user's behalf, but there’s still a gap in the verification step. Spot-checking a result can mean laboriously retracing a complex UI, asking a sighted person, or trusting the agent without an independent way to verify its work. The same people who get the most out of AI cannot always get the proof they need to trust it. A study of 16 programmers who use screen readers backs this up, showing that the most time-consuming part of their workflow was verifying agent output. Participants had a hard time tracking the scope and location of changes, verifying results across multiple views and determining if the agent had completed every requested task. What it does The application itself is a multi-purpose 2D flow diagram editor. Users can add, edit, and delete nodes, create or delete connections to represent workflows and sequences. It is keyboard accessible and screen reader accessible, insofar as a UI like this can be. WebMCP plays several important roles: it exposes tools to create and edit complex flows and deep link to a part of the UI for evidence of an action; effectively a shortcut to evidence that a change took place. It works with a text or image prompt to generate complex, inspectable flows. The response that includes fields for changes in the application’s state , so that agents and screen reader users can verify the change. The list of state changes can support other evidence the agent gathers from the UI state (via screenshotting or the accessibility API diffs), but most importantly, they can be inspected by a screen reader user to get confidence. Impact An assistive technology user can hand off a complex task without giving up the ability to fully understand the result. Verification is fast and reliable and doesn’t replay the same complexity the agent abstracted away. This improves user confidence, removes barriers, and unlocks creativity. How I built it I built a workflow editor with a 2D editable canvas that exposes tools to agents (and proximately to screen readers) via WebMCP. These include evaluation, editing, and undo tools, as well as a focus management tool. I used the webmcp-evals CLI to run evals and iterate on the tool definitions that worked well in this context and domain. Once I had the evals in place I was able to iteratively improve using Codex to increase the scores. What I learned Using evals and iterating on those helped me arrive at 100% completion rates with 2% of requests retrying due to errors; 9.52s (p50) duration. More data here . The webmcp-evals tooling drove vast improvements over my initial efforts. These gain we largely driven by reducing tool calls and better tool descriptions along with a more interpretable schema for the agent reducing errors and retries. Early on I attempted to add detailed output that included a serialized output schema, but it had little impact on the results compared to simpler response strings, and cost roughly 45% additional input tokens per trial (very little change in output tokens). I adjusted my responses accordingly, and continued to iterate. What's next I'm continuing to work with screen reader users to iterate and improve on the UX, and intend to write up the results. Research Blind screen-reader users have described the cognitive burden of working with two-dimensional artboards even when object details and coordinates are available: “It’s too much information and not enough at the same time.” Schaadhardt, Hiniker, and Wobbrock, Understanding Blind Screen-Reader Users’ Experiences of Digital Artboards · Evidence discussion Accessible tables are familiar and necessary, but they can still make overview and comparison difficult. One participant facing 393 rows said: “I can’t really get a snapshot.” Zong et al., Rich Screen Reader Experiences for Accessible Data Visualization · Evidence discussion Blind users already test and cross-check AI rather than treating it as automatically reliable. One participant advised: “Just play with it. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: Gildongmu
pitch: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: A Korean navigation app with no map, where screen reader users search places, plan trips and explore their surroundings in plain text, now declared to the browser agent as seven WebMCP tools. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Gildongmu means "traveling companion" in Korean. I started it in June 2026 to fix a small, stubborn problem of my own as a screen reader user: I wanted to look up an address and call a place as fast as possible. Map apps make both slow, because their answers live in an interface built around images. So Gildongmu has no map at all. Everything it knows, it says in words: places, routes, what is around you, and the accessibility details a screen reader user actually needs, such as station elevators, audio beacons, accessible restrooms, stairs-free walking routes and crosswalks with audible signals. Almost all of that comes from Korean public data. When I read about WebMCP, I realized that this had quietly prepared the app for agents. Every sentence a screen reader user hears is a sentence an agent can be handed. This entry is what happened when I handed them over. What it does Gildongmu is a free navigation app for South Korea with no account and no ads, on the web, on iOS, and as an npm command line tool and MCP server. It joins about thirty public and commercial APIs from nineteen organizations and turns them into plain text. As far as I know, it is the first navigation app in Korea where a screen reader user can search places, plan a trip and explore the surroundings with no barrier in between. For this challenge the web app declares seven WebMCP tools to the browser agent: describe_app: what this deployment can do and how the tools chain search_places: places, addresses and web results, with refs to pass on get_place_info: a place by ref; for stations the timetable, accessibility facilities, live arrivals and barrier-free facilities plan_directions: transit, walking and driving summaries for a destination get_transit_route_detail: one transit route in full, including the boarding door for a quick exit get_route_steps: walking or driving steps as a numbered page read_current_view: which screen the app is on and what it shows Ask the agent "Tell me the first train, the last train and the elevators at Gangdong Station (강동역)" and one tool call brings all of it back. Ask "Seoul Station (서울역) to Gangnam Station (강남역): which car and door should I board to get off next to the elevator?" and while the agent answers, the app in the browser tab has already moved to that route, so the user can turn on VoiceOver and check every line. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The answers were already text. Most navigation apps keep their answer in pixels, so an agent driving a browser has to guess at a canvas. Gildongmu had to write every answer as a sentence for VoiceOver users long before it ever met an agent. Those same sentences are what the tools return, and they come from the same code that draws the screen. The agent cannot be told something the screen does not say. Neither a plain browser agent nor a server MCP can do this alone. Behind one station answer are four public APIs, each with its own key, its own response format and, in Korea, its own coordinate system. An agent reading the page cannot rebuild that. A server MCP, on the other hand, cannot answer "where am I standing right now", because it has no browser tab. WebMCP sits exactly in between: the page keeps the keys and the location, and the agent asks in words. Location stays in the browser. A trip starts from the user's current position, which the page already knows. Tool output goes through a list of allowed fields that has no place for coordinates, so the agent's provider receives place names and sentences, never a coordinate pair. Gildongmu has promised since its first release that nothing personal is stored on its servers, and the tools keep that promise. How it creates a better user experience For a screen reader user the expensive part is not reaching a screen, it is exploring it. A transit plan on screen is dozens of items, one swipe at a time. As a tool result it is one spoken answer, and the app has still moved to that same screen, so the user can take over and verify anything. The size of an answer follows the same instinct. A full transit answer came out at 3,700 characters, far past the 1,500 the guidance recommends. Instead of cutting it off, I split it the way I would say it out loud: the recommended route in full, the other routes in one line each, and the details behind a second tool. Nothing got worse for people. The tools press the same functions a person clicks, and a person always wins. Type a new search or close a section while a tool is running and the tool call ends as superseded. If a dialog is open, the tool declines instead of closing it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before "Which car and door do I board so that I get off next to the elevator?" Gildongmu matches a public quick exit dataset to the live route, so get_transit_route_detail returns the boarding door for each leg. No map tells you this. Ask it in the chat, and the app is already sitting on that route. "Does Gangdong Station have an elevator, and when is the first train?" One call to get_place_info returns the timetable, the accessibility facilities, the real time arrivals and the barrier-free facilities. Without WebMCP the agent would open four sections one by one, and it could not call the four public APIs behind them at all. The handoff goes both ways. The agent and the user share one screen: the tools move the app, and read_current_view reads whatever the person did by hand. The agent can set up a trip that the user finishes by touch, or the user can search by hand and then ask the agent about what is on the screen. Before this, asking an assistant and using an app were two separate places that did not know about each other. Honest absence. Every tool tells apart "none", "not known" and "lookup failed", and says outOfCoverage outside Korea instead of inventing a result. A screen reader user cannot glance at a screen to catch a made up answer, so the tools never let the agent guess. The app has followed the same rule for people since version 1.0. How I implemented WebMCP I used the imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool with a name, a description, an input schema and an execute function. Here is how I understand what I built: One set of seven tools, registered once at the app root, because an agent reads the tool list once. A tool that is not configured on this deployment is still declared and answers notConfigured. A tool that needs another screen moves there itself. Each screen publishes a small bridge to a registry, and a tool reads it at the moment it runs. A tool that waits for a screen waits for a specific place id or sequence number, not for a screen name, so a call about place A cannot be satisfied by place B appearing first. Only one tool runs at a time, with a 30 second cap. A place handle is an opaque ref that remembers which search it came from, and a handle from a replaced search returns staleResult with the call that recovers it, rather than pointing at the wrong place. Every output leaves through one function. It keeps only the allowed fields, refuses coordinates, trims to the 1,500 character budget item by item, and pages a long answer with an offset. Calls to paid third party APIs are budgeted per provider. The human sentences come from the same modules the screen uses, so the screen and the tools cannot drift apart. It is covered by 19 test files and 104 tests. I checked the contracts by deliberately breaking the implementation and confirming that the tests caught each break, and I checked the deployed site with Chrome DevTools WebMCP inspection. Challenges I ran into How many tools to expose. My first design registered tools per screen, ten in all (nine on the directions screen, one on the home screen), and along the way I weighed going much further: four screen-specific sets adding up to 31 tools, or simply re-exposing the 24 tools my Gemini chat already had. Research pulled the other way. Real sites declare one to ten tools, and both OpenAI and Anthropic advise a small number of high-value tools. I settled on seven, always on, at the app root. Gildongmu is already screen reader friendly, so browser navigation and tool calls can share the work, and seven is a number an agent handles without strain. Whether to move the cursor. An early tool moved the screen reader cursor to the item the agent had found. I removed it. What a screen reader user wants from an agent is not help exploring the screen but the exact data, fast, without exploring at all. The tools now return answers, and the screen follows on its own. title: Lab.Hipaa.Technology
pitch: Doctors want to use AI. They are not sure how it works within HIPAA. This is a WebMCP enabled site to help them get started with the help of their AI agent and staying HIPAA compliant.
about_excerpt: Doctors want to use AI. They are not sure how it works within HIPAA. This is a WebMCP enabled site to help them get started with the help of their AI agent and staying HIPAA compliant. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP tool invoked Works in Chrome - Ten Tools Discovered WebMCP tool runs - web page changes WebMCP Activated Main Hero Header Running in Codex in app browser Site Tools Ready! Entire site built with ChatGPT Pro and Codex, Deep Research Instructions for Judges #2 The 10 WebMCP Tools Instructions for Judges #3 WebMCP Instructions for Judges #1 Inspiration My main inspiration came from knowing doctors who have no idea how to use AI. I just met with a dentist from NYC who makes $400,000 a year and never heard of Codex. Then when I learned about WebMCP I realized this was the perfect technology to help doctors figure out how to deploy AI in their practices and be assured they're not letting the AI run loose and they stay HIPAA compliant. HIPAA.technology gives a doctor and an AI agent one shared workspace, where the doctor sees everything the agent does and keeps control of everything that matters. What it does A physician or medical-practice leader can: Learn three essential boundaries: minimum necessary data, the vendor path, and human clinical judgment. Compare four realistic healthcare AI workflows. Assess whether a workflow is ready for a bounded synthetic rehearsal. Prepare a 21-day AI adoption mission. Review and personally approve - or refuse - the mission's policy gates. Enter a public practice domain for a website debrief that never touches portals, private pages, or PHI. The AI agent can inspect the workspace, focus lessons, select workflows, assess readiness, stage and revise a mission, deliver a public-site debrief, and update the contextual guide. How I used WebMCP The live webpage registers ten structured JavaScript tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : inspect_adoption_workspace focus_learning_lesson select_clinical_ai_use_case assess_use_case_readiness stage_21_day_adoption_mission revise_adoption_mission prepare_practice_website_review deliver_practice_website_debrief set_contextual_guidance focus_mission_week Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess what your app means from pixels and click targets. With WebMCP, it gets real tools with real schemas - bounded inputs, safety annotations, structured results. No guessing. And when the agent focuses a lesson, assesses a workflow, or stages a mission, the doctor sees the interface change immediately. Same workspace, same screen, both of them. Human authority is engineered - expert in the loop. The most important capability is one I intentionally did not build. The AI cannot: Accept organizational policy. Approve the adoption mission. Launch a live-patient-data workflow. Make clinical or compliance decisions. Enter or request PHI. The agent can inspect, explain, focus, assess, stage, and revise. The doctor keeps every decision that matters. Practice Website Debrief A doctor can enter their public practice domain and the agent looks at the public pages and comes back with: What the practice already does well. What could be clearer or more useful. One safe AI opportunity to explore next. This is educational, not a compliance audit. No patient portals, no credentials, no private pages, no PHI. How I built it HIPAA.technology is a React and TypeScript application I created with ChatGPT and Codex, built with Vinext and Vite, and hosted with ChatGPT Sites on the custom domain lab.hipaa.technology . Each WebMCP tool has: A narrow, descriptive name. An explicit JSON input schema. Additional properties disabled. Bounded and validated inputs. Clear descriptions of its effects and limitations. WebMCP safety annotations. Structured results. A visible shared-interface update when applicable. The healthcare model came from a ChatGPT Deep Research paper, Middleware Encryption for HIPAA-Compliant Use of Frontier LLMs in U.S. Healthcare . Its central lesson is baked into the whole experience: encryption is one layer, but you have to govern the entire information path - minimum necessary data, the exact vendor and feature path, logs, agent capabilities, and a human making the calls. Challenges The HARDEST Problem by far was figuring out that my version of Codex wasn't Web Tool enabled. This took hours and hours to figure out. Codex was no help figuring it out. I finally upgraded tonight after midnight and lo and behold, the tools were there. The other challenge was explaining a brand-new browser technology to doctors who aren't technical. So the site includes a dedicated WebMCP judge guide with plain-language setup instructions, the complete tool directory, implementation evidence, and both ChatGPT and Chrome testing paths. Accomplishments Ten state-aware WebMCP tools. A complete clinician-facing product, not a registration proof of concept. Real browser discovery and execution through document.modelContext . A human authority gate that agents cannot bypass. A synthetic-first 21-day adoption mission. A privacy-bounded public-practice website debrief. A contextual AI guide that follows the doctor through the experience. A research-informed workflow visualization. Deployment through ChatGPT Sites on a custom HIPAA.technology domain. A public MIT-licensed repository. What I learned WebMCP is awesome! I can do sites like this all day with Codex. I can't believe this is even real. :) Also: the best tool surface is the smallest one. Ten tools that each do one clear thing, so the doctor and the agent both always know exactly what's happening. What's next Over the next 21 days, I plan to: Test guided sessions with physicians and practice administrators. Add organization-owned workflow templates and evidence capture. Expand the public-site debrief into a structured readiness intake. Add versioned governance playbooks for approved tools and feature paths. Measure whether each team leaves with one bounded workflow, one accountable owner, and one verifiable next action. title: CoWriter
pitch: A screenplay you write together with your agent- live on the same page.
about_excerpt: A screenplay you write together with your agent- live on the same page. Like Comment Story Updates CoWriter in session Inspiration Co-writing with an AI these days usually mean pasting your script into a chat window, getting a lot of text back and then copying these into your document. You loose formatting and context for every round trip. I wanted to see what happens when the agent isn't a chat window, but a real collaborator working on the same page as you are, through the same interface as you use. WebMCP made that possible: expose the app's real actions as tools, and an agent can write directly into your live document instead of describing what it would write. What it does CoWriter is a small screenwriting tool: it has a Story Bible panel (title, logline, theme, genre, tone), a real act-by-act Outline panel (paste in your own — Act 1 with its beats, Act 2 with its beats, and so on, including acts with no scenes written yet), that breaks acts and scenes into real screenplay format (sluglines, action, character cues, dialogue). It has a character bible, and a loose idea board where you can tweek ideas on the go. Every action on that script; revising the premise, importing or editing the outline, adding a scene, editing a line, revising a character, dropping an idea, reordering scenes, checking the whole thing for consistency — is exposed as a WebMCP tool ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). The agent is not clicking around a UI it has to guess at; it's calling the exact same functions the interface calls, and the result shows up on your screen instantly, on the same live document. You can keep editing by hand at any moment if you wish to. Crucially, get_script 's description tells the agent to call it first, always. It returns the human-authored, act-by-act outline and the Story Bible up front, so every scene the agent drafts, and every consistency check it runs, is explicitly grounded in the story's real throughline and theme. It does not guess at what happens next from whatever scene happens to be open. The outline (the plan) and the written scenes (what's actually on the page) are kept deliberately distinct, the way a real writer's outline and draft are. You can ask, in plain language, "write a tense scene where she finds the letter, no dialogue yet" — the agent calls add_scene and it appears, correctly formatted, right in front of you. You read it and asks for some more edit if you want it tweeked, and the agent calls edit_scene on that exact scene. The character bible updates the same way as new characters get introduced. And check_consistency hands the agent every dialogue line labeled by speaker plus the full character bible in one structured payload, so it can catch things like a character's voice contradicting itself across acts — the kind of full-document consistency pass that's genuinely tedious for a human to do by re-reading, but natural for an agent to do well. Nothing about the human side of the app changes because an agent is present — you can type directly into any line at any time, exactly like a normal document. That's the point: one shared script, two collaborators, no export/import step between them. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript — no framework, no build tooling, no backend. All 12 WebMCP tools are registered in a single readable file ( script.js ) so the integration itself is easy to inspect end to end. Data persists to the browser's local storage. Tool responses are serialized as compact JSON to keep the token footprint of every agent call low. Challenges we ran into Keeping the outline and the written scenes as two genuinely separate sources of truth, rather than letting them silently collapse into one, took deliberate design. It would have been simpler to let the agent treat whatever is on the page as the plan, but this would have let scenes drift from the story's real throughline. Instead, get_script always returns both, and the agent's own tool descriptions tell it the outline is the plan and the scenes are what is actually been written — they won't always be in sync, and that is intentional. Getting an agent to actually call a tool rather than just answer a writing request conversationally in chat also took some care in how the tool descriptions were phrased — an ambiguous prompt can be satisfied just as easily by the model generating prose in the chat window as by it calling add_scene on the page. Accomplishments that we're proud of Twelve WebMCP tools, all grounded in one shared Story Bible, with a UI that never has to know or care whether the human or the agent made the last edit. Watching a scene appear live on the page, correctly formatted and fitting the outline is genuinely satisfying to demo. What we learned That grounding matters more than raw capability. An agent that can call add_scene isn't useful on its own. It is useful because get_script forces it to read the outline and premise first, every time, so what it writes actually belongs in the story. What's next for CoWriter Multi-scene consistency diffing — let check_consistency compare against the previous run's report so an agent can flag only new contradictions instead of re-surfacing everything each time. PDF/Fountain export of the finished screenplay. Multi-document projects — more than one script per browser profile, with a lightweight project switcher. Real backend/cloud persistence, so a script isn't tied to one browser's local storage. A visible scene-level undo/history stack for agent-made edits. A richer character bible — arcs, relationships, and a "first appearance" pointer the agent can use to catch characters who show up before being introduced. A more efficient architecture for managing token consumption for each 'get_script' tool call. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. title: Morph
pitch: Say what you need. The page reshapes itself.
about_excerpt: Say what you need. The page reshapes itself. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Most websites assume their designers can predict every task a person will ever bring to them. usually a retailer gives everyone the same product grid. A travel site ranks trips by an advertised duration. A news site presents everyone with the same endless feed. The information may already exist, but the interface often hides the answer a particular person needs. Browser assistants usually either operate the controls that already exist or move the useful result into a chat response. I wanted to explore a different possibility: what if a cooperating website could use its own trusted data and native components to become the interface required for the task at hand? That became Morph. The idea is simple: website exposes truth + capabilities + native components → person states goal → assistant composes interface I chose three deliberately different everyday websites—shopping, travel, and news—to demonstrate that this is an interaction model for the web rather than a feature tied to one industry. What it does Morph lets someone describe the interface they need in natural language. Their browser assistant reads the page through WebMCP, selects from the website’s supported components and actions, and asks the website to compose a new interface. The result remains part of the original website. It is interactive, editable, inspectable, persistent, and governed by the website’s own data. Three working experiences demonstrate the range: Wayline turns 18 conventional travel results into 7 complete journeys. An advertised 1h 10m flight becomes its true 4h 26m door-to-door journey after accounting for walking, waiting, terminal buffers, luggage, and transfers. Hearth & Home turns a 28-machine product grid into the 9 washers that satisfy a particular home, budget, delivery window, and ownership-cost calculation. The Current turns 30 overlapping articles into 5 distinct developments totaling 9m 48s , while preserving original reporting and the provenance of verified facts. Wayline demonstrates the complete collaboration loop. A traveler asks for a door-to-door decision interface, saves the 07:16 train, and locks the checked-luggage choice directly on the page. They then change destination and request a disruption stress test. The whole interface recomposes, while the saved train and luggage lock survive. Ask → page composes → person edits → ask again → page recomposes without losing the person’s choices. The trust boundary is central to Morph: Assistant = composition Website = truth Human = final authority The assistant cannot inject arbitrary HTML, invent records, replace formulas, or silently override protected human choices. It decides how supported information should be arranged. The website decides what is true and possible. The same model could extend to many other cooperating websites: a recipe could become a timed cooking plan for one oven shelf, a government site could show only the rules relevant to someone’s situation, or a store could rank products by true delivered cost instead of sponsored placement. How I built it I built three complete React and TypeScript experiences using Vinext and deployed them on Cloudflare. Each one begins as a recognizable conventional website before WebMCP transforms it. Across the three pages, Morph registers 15 WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each experience provides tools that let an assistant: read every site-owned record, calculation, supported action, and current interface state; create an initial composed interface; update or completely recompose the current interface; compare site-owned records; open exact calculations, journey arithmetic, or source evidence. Each website has its own registry of native components. These include ranked cards, compact tables, timelines, plots, comparisons, cost breakdowns, stress tests, provenance maps, recommendations, exclusions, and recovery options. The assistant sends structured composition requests containing supported component types and settings. The website validates those requests, performs every calculation itself, and renders its own React components. Arbitrary markup, scripts, URLs, formulas, and factual claims are rejected. Human changes are stored separately from assistant-owned composition. Saves, pins, hidden records, comparisons, and locked assumptions persist across later requests. Revision numbers prevent an assistant from changing a stale version of the page, while undo and redo remain available to the person. The transformation itself is also visible. The existing page stays present while the new interface is prepared, then native components move, disappear, and enter according to the real before-and-after state. The demonstration data is intentionally fictional and deterministic so every displayed result can be checked. The WebMCP interactions, calculations, persistence, protections, and interface composition are fully functional. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was balancing flexibility with trust. Allowing an assistant to generate arbitrary interface code would look flexible, but the website would lose control of its behavior and claims. Restricting the assistant to a few whole-page presets would be safe, but would miss the point of a composable web. We solved this with validated, independently configurable native components. Preserving human intent was another major challenge. A later prompt may legitimately replace the entire layout, but it should not erase a journey someone saved or change a choice they explicitly locked. We separated human-owned state from assistant-owned composition and created semantic operations for changing each one. I also had to make the project feel general without reducing it to an abstract technical demonstration. Building three unrelated websites forced the model to work with different records, calculations, actions, visual systems, and user needs. Finally, the transformation needed to feel like the website was genuinely changing shape. React state updates initially made some recompositions appear abrupt. We built a transition system that measures the real component arrangement, preserves scroll position, and animates additions, removals, movement, and reduced-motion fallbacks. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Morph supports an ongoing collaboration rather than ending after one successful prompt. The saved-train and luggage-lock interaction captures the idea clearly: the assistant can radically reorganize the interface while respecting decisions that belong to the person. I am also proud that: all three experiences use working WebMCP tools rather than scripted transformations; every number remains owned and explainable by the originating website; compositions are assembled from independent components rather than fixed page presets; the same model works across shopping, travel, and news without making the sites look or behave alike; the experiences remain usable on desktop and mobile; exact calculations, exclusions, provenance, zero-result recovery, undo, redo, and persistence remain available after composition. The three numerical reveals summarize the result: 28 → 9 viable products 1h 10m → 4h 26m true journey time 30 → 5 meaningful developments What I learned I learned that WebMCP’s most interesting potential goes beyond helping agents click existing interfaces more reliably. It can let people request useful interfaces that were never assembled as complete screens beforehand. I also learned that a tool schema is part of the user experience. The records, operations, constraints, and component vocabulary exposed to an assistant determine how expressive and trustworthy the resulting interface can be. Most importantly, good human-agent collaboration requires explicit ownership. The assistant needs freedom to compose, the website needs authority over its domain, and the person needs durable control over their decisions. Persistence changes the relationship completely. A first prompt can feel like generation; a second prompt that respects the person’s intervening edits feels like collaboration. What's next for Morph The next step is connecting the model to real first-party systems: live retailer inventory, transit schedules, publisher feeds, public-service information, and other structured websites. I would also like to make Morph’s component and state model easier for existing websites to adopt, so a site can expose its own native building blocks without redesigning the whole product. Future experiences could include recipes that become synchronized cooking plans, housing sites that calculate complete moving decisions, education platforms that reorganize material around a learner’s gaps, and public-service sites that adapt complex guidance to a person’s circumstances while preserving the original language.  About 

 Skill Browser is a human-controlled personal library of reusable AI-agent skills. People browse trusted skills, inspect their provenance, and curate a local Skillspace. Agents can then discover and retrieve only the skills relevant to the task through WebMCP. 

 Why WebMCP 

 A skill registry is most useful when an agent can find the right instructions at the moment it needs them. WebMCP lets Skill Browser expose focused browser tools directly to the agent, replacing prompt copy/paste and brittle custom integrations with a live, typed interface. 

 Human + agent experience 

 People decide what belongs in their Skillspace and can inspect each skill's source, version, license, and content. Agents search compact metadata first and retrieve full instructions only when needed. This creates a shared live capability context while keeping the browser as the trust boundary. 

 WebMCP implementation 

 The client-side WebMCP adapter feature-detects browser support and registers four typed tools: 

 
 search_skills 
 get_skill_metadata 
 get_skill 
 list_my_skills 
 

 Inputs are validated with Zod, outputs are sanitized, and the WebMCP adapter uses the same domain services as the UI. The personal Skillspace is local-first and stored in IndexedDB. Skill content is treated as untrusted data and is never executed.
