title: ShopCanvas
pitch: ShopCanvas turns agent requests into visible, live changes on an adaptive bento storefront, making WebMCP feel like a conversation with the website itself.
about_excerpt: ShopCanvas turns agent requests into visible, live changes on an adaptive bento storefront, making WebMCP feel like a conversation with the website itself. Like Comment Story Updates ShopCanvas: a visual WebMCP storefront. compare_products presents key tradeoffs side by side. inspect_product expands product details within stable bento cells. show_reviews filters critical low-light feedback. search_products reshapes the catalog around the request. Inspiration Shopping online often means repeatedly leaving the product you are considering. Specifications live in one section, reviews farther down the page, comparisons somewhere else, and the cart on another route. That visual travel creates cognitive travel: shoppers must remember their original question while the interface continuously changes context. At the same time, browser agents can feel disconnected from the websites they operate. Actions happen in the background, and users only see the final response in a chat. ShopCanvas began with a question: what if using an agent felt like having a conversation directly with the website? We wanted every request to produce an immediate, understandable visual response on one shared surface. What it does ShopCanvas is a fictional camera store presented as an adaptive bento-grid workspace. Users can ask a browser agent to: Search and sort products Focus on a specific camera Compare multiple cameras Filter product reviews Update a local mock cart ShopCanvas exposes these capabilities through five imperative WebMCP tools: search_products , inspect_product , compare_products , show_reviews , and set_cart_quantity . Every tool call visibly affects the page. The relevant cells expand smoothly, receive a temporary highlight, and display an acknowledgement naming the agent’s action. An accessible live region also announces what changed. All seven cells remain mounted in permanent grid positions. They expand or contract without teleporting, reordering, or appearing from nowhere. Dense content scrolls inside its cell while the overall page remains fitted to the viewport. Manual controls and agent actions use the same state transitions, so the user and agent always share one source of truth. A Back control restores previous canvas states, while session data persists locally between reloads. How we built it ShopCanvas is a static React and TypeScript application built with Vinext, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Zustand, Motion, and AJV. The mock catalog, reviews, product names, and imagery are bundled locally. There is no authentication, backend database, payment processing, or checkout flow. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level document using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool includes: A bounded JSON Schema Runtime AJV validation Rejection of unknown properties Cancellation support Concise, JSON-serializable results A visible UI acknowledgement A result returned only after the interface commits the change Both manual interactions and WebMCP calls dispatch the same semantic store actions. Session state is versioned and persisted in localStorage . Agent mutations are serialized, and cancelled operations use guarded rollback logic to avoid corrupting later changes. Because reviews represent user-generated content, review results are explicitly marked with untrustedContentHint: true . We used Playwright to validate the interface across desktop, tablet, mobile, and short-laptop viewports. Tests cover all five tools, persistence, malformed input, cancellation, concurrent calls, keyboard navigation, internal scrolling, fixed panel identity, responsive geometry, and visual regressions. A separate native-browser test discovers and executes the tools through the browser’s real document.modelContext implementation. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was preserving spatial continuity. Our early layouts replaced and reordered cells whenever the user entered a new state. Although functional, the result felt abrupt and contradicted the core idea of a stable workspace. We redesigned the grid so every cell has a permanent named slot. State changes now animate only the grid-track dimensions, allowing panels to expand and contract without being removed or moved. Fitting seven useful panels inside one viewport was another significant challenge. We avoided shrinking text until it became unreadable. Instead, each cell received a carefully bounded layout and its own keyboard-accessible scrolling region. We also had to coordinate asynchronous tool execution with visible feedback. Updating application state was not enough: the tool result needed to wait until the user could actually see the committed interface. Cancellation, overlapping calls, local persistence, and manual actions all had to remain consistent. Finally, WebMCP is still an evolving draft. We needed to accommodate differences between the current specification and native browser implementations while keeping the public tool surface small, predictable, and testable. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that ShopCanvas makes agent activity visible without turning the interface into a debug console. Every successful tool call has a clear visual consequence: The action is named The affected cells are highlighted The content changes on screen The grid resizes smoothly The tool waits for the visible commit The user can reverse the state with Back We also maintained the identity and position of all seven panels across every state transition. The same interface works from a 320-pixel mobile viewport through desktop layouts without introducing page-level scrolling. The complete application uses fictional data and original visual assets, requires no account, and remains fully usable through manual controls when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned We learned that good agentic UX is not only about exposing capable tools. Users need to understand what the agent changed, where it changed, and whether the action completed. Tool schemas are also part of the user experience. Small, bounded tools produced more predictable behavior than one large tool with many ambiguous responsibilities. Another important lesson was that a state update and a visible UI update are not the same event. Waiting for the interface to commit made the interaction feel significantly more trustworthy. Most importantly, spatial stability matters. When panels retain their location, users can build a mental map of the interface even while its proportions change. What's next for ShopCanvas Next, we would like to explore: Additional fictional product categories and workspace compositions Optional adapters for real product data Agent explanations showing why an item matched a request User-defined layout constraints beyond cart pinning Saved comparison workspaces Collaborative sessions across devices Richer accessibility preferences for motion, contrast, and density More advanced multi-step shopping workflows We also want to continue refining ShopCanvas alongside the evolving WebMCP specification. The long-term goal is broader than e-commerce: to explore websites as adaptive, shared canvases where people and agents collaborate visibly instead of exchanging commands with hidden background processes. title: Nodebook
pitch: A visual workspace where people and AI agents turn ideas into connected plans and maps using WebMCP, without losing important context in chat.
about_excerpt: A visual workspace where people and AI agents turn ideas into connected plans and maps using WebMCP, without losing important context in chat. Like Comment Story Updates A product roadmap where scope, progress, evidence, and agent-created relationships stay visible on one connected canvas. Nodebook exposes 15 WebMCP tools for reading context, creating maps, updating plans, adding evidence, and focusing important paths. The inspector makes agent work reviewable with linked maps, named comments, evidence, delivery status, and human-controlled locks. A learning map connects concepts, evidence, exercises, and an interactive quiz so people and AI can build understanding together. Inspiration AI assistants can help plan a product, research an idea, or explain a difficult concept. But their best work often ends up buried inside a chat. The person then has to copy the result into a document, rebuild the relationships, and explain the same context again in the next conversation. I built Nodebook to give people and AI assistants a shared visual workspace. The person chooses the direction, while the assistant helps organize the work directly on the canvas. What Nodebook does Nodebook is an infinite visual canvas for planning, tracing, and learning. A workspace can contain three kinds of connected maps: Build maps for features, scope, progress, risks, and evidence Trace maps for user journeys, system flows, and failure paths Learn maps for concepts, examples, exercises, and quizzes People can create and edit nodes, decide what is in scope, track delivery, attach evidence, leave comments, and lock important decisions. An AI assistant can read the same workspace through WebMCP. It can understand which node the person selected, create connected maps, update plans, add evidence and comments, and highlight important paths. For example, a person can select “Crash-safe recovery,” click “Trace,” and ask the assistant to map the recovery process. The assistant can read that selection, create the complete flow, connect it to the original feature, highlight the riskiest path, and leave an explanation, all without the person copying the project into the prompt. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Nodebook is useful because the person and the assistant work with the same information. Without WebMCP, an assistant would need to interpret screenshots, click through the interface, or ask the person to repeatedly copy information into a chat. Those approaches are slow and can lose important details. With WebMCP, Nodebook gives the assistant clear actions for reading and changing the workspace. The assistant receives the exact nodes, relationships, comments, evidence, and selected task. Its changes then appear immediately on the canvas, where the person can inspect and edit them. This creates a better experience than an embedded chatbot. The conversation is not the final product. The shared, lasting workspace is. How I implemented WebMCP Nodebook registers 15 browser tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools allow an assistant to: Read the workspace, maps, nodes, comments, and human selection Search across titles, descriptions, tags, evidence, and comments Create linked Build, Trace, and Learn maps Add or update nodes and connections Make scope and delivery updates Attach evidence and attributed comments Focus nodes and highlight important paths Every request is checked before it changes the workspace. Invalid links, missing nodes, duplicate IDs, unsafe source URLs, oversized requests, and broken connections are rejected. Each successful assistant action is applied as one undoable change. Locked nodes are skipped, and assistants are not given a tool that permanently deletes nodes. This keeps important decisions under human control. How it was built Nodebook is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and React Flow. Dagre arranges assistant-created maps into a predictable layout. Zustand manages the workspace, while Zod checks tool requests and imported files. The workspace is saved in the browser using IndexedDB. There are no accounts, API routes, analytics, cloud database, or Nodebook storage server. People can export the complete workspace as JSON and import it again later. The included demo contains a product roadmap, user journeys, a learning map, release checks, evidence, comments, locked decisions, and a research parking lot. Challenges The hardest part was making assistant actions feel like real product actions instead of hidden changes. I needed to make sure that a large graph update either succeeded completely or changed nothing. I also had to keep the visible canvas, undo history, browser storage, and WebMCP responses in agreement. Another challenge was balancing useful assistant access with human control. Nodebook solves this with strict validation, visible activity, attributed comments, undo support, locked nodes, and human-only deletion. Accomplishments I am proud that Nodebook is a complete working application rather than only a WebMCP experiment. It includes: 15 working WebMCP tools A detailed, editable demo workspace Linked maps with breadcrumbs Evidence and human-assistant comments Scope, progress, and learning states Path highlighting and automatic layout Undo and redo for assistant changes Local browser persistence Safe JSON import and export Automated unit and browser tests What I learned I learned that good human-AI collaboration needs more than a prompt box. The assistant needs clear actions and reliable context. The person needs to see what changed, understand why it changed, and remain able to edit, lock, or undo the result. WebMCP makes that possible using the website’s real data and actions. What’s next Next, I would improve keyboard navigation, test larger workspaces, add more starter templates, and make recovery guidance even clearer. I would also explore shareable, read-only workspace snapshots while keeping Nodebook’s main promise: the person owns the workspace and stays in control. title: Talli
pitch: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human.
about_excerpt: A conversational credit ledger that helps small businesses and their AI agents manage customer debt together, without taking financial control away from the human. Like Comment Story Updates Talli helps small businesses and informal traders record and manage customer credit using ordinary speech, text, or Telegram. Instead of filling out accounting forms, a merchant can simply say, “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay on Friday,” or “She paid $10 today.” Talli turns those conversations into structured customer balances and transaction histories. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can securely read the same live ledger, answer questions, identify overdue debts, and prepare proposed financial updates. However, the agent cannot finalize those changes. The merchant reviews and confirms every consequential update inside Talli’s visible interface. The Problem Millions of small businesses and informal traders sell goods on credit every day. A customer may take food, clothing, supplies, or other goods and promise to pay later. The business owner needs to remember: who took the goods how much they owe when they promised to pay whether they made a partial payment how much remains outstanding which customers are overdue Many business owners manage this information using paper notebooks, memory, calculator notes, chat messages, or a mixture of all four. This creates serious problems. Records can be lost, payments may not be reflected correctly, and business owners can struggle to explain how a customer’s balance was calculated. When several customers have similar names, it is also easy to update the wrong person’s record. Traditional accounting applications can help, but they are often designed around forms, tables, categories, and bookkeeping terminology. For someone who is busy serving customers and may not consider themselves an accountant, recording a simple credit transaction can feel like administrative work. The real challenge is not that these business owners do not understand their businesses. The challenge is that most financial software does not work the way they naturally communicate. The Solution Talli is a conversational credit ledger built around the way small businesses already talk about customer debt. Instead of completing a long form, a merchant can speak or type naturally: “Adele took goods worth $40 and will pay next Friday.” Talli converts that statement into a structured financial record containing the customer, amount, currency, transaction type, and relevant date. Later, the merchant can say: “Adele paid $10.” Talli records the partial payment, updates Adele’s outstanding balance, and preserves the history of how that balance changed. The merchant can also ask questions such as: “How much does Adele still owe?” “Who owes me money?” “Which payments are overdue?” “Show me Adele’s transaction history.” “How much have my customers paid?” “Mark this debt as settled.” Talli supports voice, typed conversations, a web interface, and Telegram. The same underlying ledger can therefore remain useful while the merchant moves between the channels they already use. Talli also understands that financial records require caution. If a request is unclear, Talli does not silently guess. It asks for clarification before allowing the wrong customer or obligation to be changed. The WebMCP Extension For the WebMCP Challenge, I extended Talli so that the live website can expose its financial capabilities directly to browser-based AI agents. Without WebMCP, an agent trying to assist a Talli user would have to inspect the page, interpret text on the screen, locate buttons, fill forms, and simulate clicks. That approach is fragile and can be especially dangerous when the website contains financial information. With WebMCP, Talli explicitly tells the agent what it can do, what information each operation requires, and which operations are read-only. The agent can discover structured tools for searching customers, checking balances, reviewing histories, finding overdue debts, and preparing ledger changes. It receives structured results from the same live ledger the person is viewing. This creates a shared workspace between the merchant, the browser agent, and Talli. A Typical Human-Agent Workflow Imagine that a merchant asks their browser agent: “Check Talli and tell me how much my customers owe me.” The agent calls Talli’s get_ledger_summary tool and receives a structured summary from the current ledger. The merchant then says: “Adele paid $10. Update her balance.” The agent calls prepare_ledger_mutation , but Talli discovers that several customers match the name “Adele.” Instead of choosing one, Talli returns clarification_required with a short list of matching customers and their balances. The ledger remains unchanged. The agent can then ask: “I found more than one Adele. Which customer made the payment?” After the merchant identifies the correct customer, the agent prepares the payment again. Talli validates the request and displays a visible review card containing the exact proposed change. The merchant reviews the amount and customer, then clicks Confirm inside Talli. Only at that point does the ledger change. This workflow demonstrates more than an agent operating a website. The agent helps with interpretation and preparation, Talli enforces financial safety, and the human retains final authority. Why Talli Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Talli is a strong WebMCP use case because customer credit management combines repetitive work with consequential financial decisions. An AI agent is well suited to: searching records summarizing balances finding overdue obligations reviewing transaction histories translating a natural-language request into a structured proposal However, an agent should not silently make an irreversible or incorrect financial change. WebMCP provides the structured boundary Talli needs. It allows the agent to interact with the application through clearly defined tools instead of guessing its way through the interface. Talli builds on that boundary with three important rules: Read operations can happen directly. Financial mutations must first become proposals. Only the human can confirm a proposal in Talli’s visible interface. The most important behavior is not simply that Talli knows how to act. It also knows when not to act. If two customers match a name, an obligation cannot be safely identified, or the ledger has changed since a proposal was prepared, Talli pauses the operation instead of guessing. This makes WebMCP part of the product’s safety model, not just another way to call backend functions. How Talli Creates a Better User Experience Talli reduces the amount of effort required to maintain accurate credit records. The merchant does not need to learn database fields, accounting terminology, or a complicated menu system. They can continue communicating naturally while Talli and their agent handle the structured work underneath. WebMCP improves this experience in several ways: The agent can access reliable structured data instead of trying to read values from the visual interface. The merchant can ask broader questions without manually searching through individual customer records. The agent can prepare a transaction while the merchant remains focused on running the business. Ambiguous requests produce clarification instead of silent errors. Proposed financial changes are shown in a visible, understandable review card. The merchant keeps control over the final decision. The agent and the person work from the same current ledger rather than separate or outdated copies of the data. Talli remains usable in browsers that do not support WebMCP. WebMCP is added as a progressive enhancement, so the normal voice, text, web, and Telegram experiences continue to work. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before the WebMCP extension, Talli could already understand conversations and maintain the ledger. However, an external browser agent did not have a dependable, structured way to use those capabilities. Now a person and their agent can work together to: inspect the business’s total outstanding credit search for a customer without manually navigating the interface explain how a customer’s current balance was calculated identify overdue obligations prepare new credit, payment, or settlement entries detect ambiguous customer references ask the human to resolve uncertainty present the exact financial change for review prevent an agent from confirming its own proposal keep a record unchanged until the human explicitly approves it For example, the agent can do the time-consuming work of finding the correct records and preparing an update, while the business owner makes the final judgment. That division of responsibility was difficult to achieve reliably through ordinary browser automation. WebMCP makes it possible to define the collaboration explicitly. title: Ratiflow
pitch: Capability grants for agents on a live page: the human picks the access, WebMCP exposes only that tool catalog, and every edit lands as a reversible, attributed revision.
about_excerpt: Capability grants for agents on a live page: the human picks the access, WebMCP exposes only that tool catalog, and every edit lands as a reversible, attributed revision. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Tagging a bot Document editor WebMCP flow Revision history Ratiflow Tagline Capability grants for page agents: the human chooses access → WebMCP registers only that catalog → every edit lands as reversible, attributed proof. Try it out Live: https://ratiflow-webmcp.vercel.app/ Repo: https://github.com/anthonyisaa/webMCP_Hackathon Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5KixpBV92v8 Inspiration Incident reports and launch docs already mix people and AI. The finished paragraph usually survives. The request, tools, sources, authorship, and rationale usually do not. The next teammate sees prose—not why it changed. Another agent often repeats the same work. Most “AI in docs” products add chat beside a document. Ratiflow answers a different WebMCP question: what is this agent allowed to do on this page, right now? The human chooses an access profile for the assignment. The live page registers only that tool catalog. The agent works inside that grant. The document records an immutable revision with prompt, sources, authorship, and diff. WebMCP fits because the website —not a side chat—owns the capability surface for the current task. What it does Ratiflow is a shared Markdown workspace focused on two high-stakes templates: an incident postmortem and a product launch decision. Select a passage Assign @Code , @Data , or @General (expertise label) Separately choose assignment access: Repository , Metrics , or Editorial Ratiflow maps that choice to a capability grant and registers the matching WebMCP catalog The agent updates only the selection; Flight Recorder + History keep the proof Product rule: bot name is not permission. The same @Code identity gets different tools when access switches from Repository → Editorial. During a managed run, the page withdraws the idle BYO-agent catalog and restores it after. Demo sources are deterministic fixtures so judges can replay the same path. Server authority (range, lease, revision, evidence) is the security boundary; the visible catalog only guides the agent. 90-second demo Open completed INC-482 postmortem doc at the live URL Assign @Code + Repository scoped edit Watch Flight Recorder: catalog → tool calls → commit Keep @Code , switch to Editorial scoped edit → different catalog Open History → inspect diff / Restore How we built it Next.js · React · TypeScript · Supabase/Postgres · Vercel Dynamic document.modelContext registration with generation-scoped catalogs Two mutually exclusive surfaces: idle BYO-agent tools vs managed-assignment tools Application-owned Luna ↔ WebMCP relay (Responses API tool search → browser getTools / executeTool ); credentials stay server-side Server enforcement of identity, access, document range, and source revision Full Markdown snapshots with digests, diffs, and Restore Challenges we ran into Connecting a server-side model to live browser WebMCP tools (discovery, execute, cancel, retry, stale descriptors). WebMCP has no pub/sub, so mentions wake the open page; long unattended runs are out of scope by design. Catalog visibility is guidance only—permissions are enforced on the server. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Live, judge-runnable WebMCP workspace with coach + Flight Recorder Capability grants as product: same agent identity, different access → different registered tool catalog Application-owned Luna↔WebMCP relay with fail-closed stale-tool handling Immutable revisions with prompt, sources, authorship, diff, and Restore Narrow scope: two document types, deterministic fixtures, reproducible demo Open-sourced under MIT What we learned WebMCP is not “MCP in the browser” and not a fixed API. The valuable unit is a live, task-scoped tool surface . Designing the handoff—human chooses grant → page registers tools → agent acts → human reviews proof—mattered more than adding more tools. Treat the catalog as UX and the server as authority. What’s next for Ratiflow Polish editor UX, add ChatGPT in-app browser smoke notes for judges, and expand fixture-backed evals around catalog switching and stale-tool rejection. Stay narrow: capability grants + reversible proof for high-stakes docs—not a general collab suite. title: Knoww
pitch: Knoww is the prediction market layer for the internet. It turns research and live market odds into a shared human-agent workspace for taking trades and preparing decisions with people in final control
about_excerpt: Knoww is the prediction market layer for the internet. It turns research and live market odds into a shared human-agent workspace for taking trades and preparing decisions with people in final control Like Comment Story Updates What Knoww does Knoww turns live prediction markets into a shared research workspace where people and agents can explore market information together. A person can ask an agent to find relevant events, narrow the visible market list, open a valid result, compare related markets, inspect the selected order book, change the chart range, and prepare the trade interface for review. Every step happens on the same page the person is viewing. The result remains visible, understandable, and easy to correct. Knoww gives the agent structured access to market discovery and analysis without giving it control of a wallet, a signature, or trade submission. The problem Prediction market research involves more than opening a result page. A single event may contain several related markets, outcomes, probabilities, charts, and order books. The useful context also depends on the filters, selected market, and chart range currently visible on the page. A browser agent can attempt to reconstruct this workflow through page inspection and clicks, but it must infer the meaning of interface elements and continuously track changing page state. That process can be fragile. WebMCP lets Knoww expose the meaning behind the interface directly. Instead of guessing which card, control, or outcome represents the user's intent, the agent receives narrow and typed operations connected to the current page. Why WebMCP is the right fit A separate market data integration could return probabilities and market information, but it would not naturally share the interface state the person is currently inspecting. WebMCP allows the person and the agent to work with the same filters, selected market, order book, and chart range. When the agent changes something, the person sees the result immediately through the normal Knoww interface. This creates one continuous research workflow. The agent can discover relevant events, narrow the market list, open a valid result, compare related markets, inspect the selected order book, adjust the chart range, and prepare the trade interface for review. Every action remains visible on the page. The person can verify the result, correct the agent, or stop the workflow at any point. What I built I added 12 WebMCP tools across the market discovery page and individual event pages. On /markets , get_markets_page_context reads the current page state. search_events searches public events. set_market_filters changes only supported visible filters. load_more_markets advances the visible results. open_event can open only an event already returned by Knoww. On an event page, get_current_event_context reads the active event and current selection. find_markets_on_page finds relevant markets within the event. compare_markets returns a focused comparison. get_selected_order_book reads the currently selected order book. select_market_view changes the visible market. set_chart_range changes the visible chart period. prepare_trade prepares the trade interface for the person to review. The available tools change with the page context. The market discovery page exposes discovery and navigation capabilities. An event page exposes comparison, order book, chart, and trade preparation capabilities. This keeps the tool set focused while supporting a complete workflow from market discovery to decision preparation. Example experience A person can ask: "Find Bitcoin related prediction markets, narrow the list, open the most relevant event, compare its markets, inspect the selected order book, and prepare the trade view for my review." The agent can complete this workflow through structured WebMCP tools while the person watches the same page change and remains free to correct any step. This is more reliable than asking the agent to infer the entire workflow from buttons, cards, and page layout. Human control and safety The WebMCP tools cannot connect a wallet, sign a transaction, or submit a trade. prepare_trade only prepares the visible trade interface. The person must inspect the values and complete any action with financial consequences. Every tool uses a typed and bounded input schema. Search limits, filter values, pagination, and navigation targets are constrained. open_event accepts only events already returned by Knoww. Tool results are marked as untrusted public content. These boundaries give the agent enough capability to provide meaningful assistance while preserving human control. Technical implementation Knoww uses Next.js, React, and TypeScript, and is deployed with Cloudflare Workers. It reads public Polymarket market data. I connected the WebMCP handlers to Knoww's existing React state and page actions instead of recreating the market logic in a separate integration. This means the person and the agent work with the same filters, selected market, order book, and chart range. When a tool changes the page state, the normal Knoww interface reflects that change. Tool registration runs through top level page JavaScript so the tools can be discovered by ChatGPT's in app browser. I also added registration cleanup so a normal React unmount does not incorrectly report a registration failure. Testing I tested the production /markets page in ChatGPT's in app browser. ChatGPT discovered all five tools registered on that page. I successfully executed get_markets_page_context and used search_events to find Bitcoin related events on the live production site. The remaining seven tools are registered only on event pages, where their event specific context is available. Challenges and lessons The difficult part was not exposing more control. It was deciding exactly which control the agent should receive. The WebMCP tools had to stay synchronized with React state while maintaining clear boundaries. Search limits, filter values, pagination, navigation targets, and available page actions all needed to be constrained. The page lifecycle also required careful handling so route changes and normal React cleanup did not appear as tool registration failures. The most important lesson was that WebMCP is strongest when it reveals the semantics of an existing interface without bypassing that interface or its permission model. Knoww now gives an agent enough structure to help someone reason about live prediction markets, while stopping exactly where financial authority should remain with the person.  What's next for Co-Desk — Human + Agent Support Operations 

 The idea 

 Co-Desk is a human + agent support desk : a single live ticket queue that a person and an AI agent operate together , in real time, over WebMCP. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Before WebMCP, an agent helping with a real web workflow could only navigate the page and click — slow, brittle, and hard to verify. Co-Desk inverts this: instead of the agent guessing at our UI, the site declares its own operations as structured tools the agent can call. A person opens the app and works; an agent discovers those tools and acts inside the real workflow. 

 What people and agents can do together now 

 A support team can hand the agent the whole routine workload — opening requests, adding notes, routing to teams, escalating, resolving the mechanical cases — while the human watches the same screen update live and owns the judgment calls. One shared queue, two operators, with the human always in the loop. That is the collaboration WebMCP makes possible. 

 How we built it 

 
 10 WebMCP tools ( listOpenTickets , getTicket , createTicket , addNote , updateStatus , assignToTeam , escalateTicket , resolveTicket , searchTickets , summarizeQueue ), each with a JSON Schema and real effects on a shared store. 
 Every action — human or agent — is written to one localStorage store and rendered live, so the queue and an activity feed update on screen. 
 Plain HTML/CSS/JS, no build step — trivially deployable. 
 

 Registration is done against document.modelContext : 
 await document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "resolveTicket" , 
 description : "Resolve a ticket with a short resolution summary." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 ticketId : { type : "string" } , 
 resolution : { type : "string" } , 
 } , 
 required : [ "ticketId" , "resolution" ] , 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* real action on the shared queue */ } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 Challenges 

 The hardest part was keeping one source of truth. Tools and the human UI both mutate the same queue, so we made them share one store and one change-notification path. That guarantees an agent's action and a human click are never out of sync. 

 Try it 

 Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, then ask the agent: "Summarize the queue, then handle the password-reset ticket — add a note, route it to account, and show me before resolving."

title: AutoLab by AutoMoto
pitch: Agent-native WebMCP tools for configuring, understanding, and building the car you share with an AI.
about_excerpt: Agent-native WebMCP tools for configuring, understanding, and building the car you share with an AI. Like Comment Story Updates AutoLab unifies an AI-operable vehicle configurator, a synchronized Garage digital twin, a visual Owner's Guide, and the code-native 3D Creation Engine behind them. Across five page contexts it defines 49 WebMCP tool registrations: 3 landing tools, 17 configurator tools, 14 embedded Garage tools, 13 standalone Owner's Guide tools, and 2 Creation Engine tools. Agents can safely inspect and revise a build, calculate pricing and ownership outcomes, direct a shared 3D vehicle, reveal and measure 42 named components, and inspect the measurement-driven workflow used to build the model. Human input interrupts active agent transactions, mutations are revision-gated and undoable, and results state their source or measurement basis. title: PlateWeave — Reliable 96-Well Designs, Avoid Costly Mistakes
pitch: A scientist and an AI agent co-design a validated 96-well plate: the human fixes precious samples and approves the exact export while WebMCP gives the agent precise, state-aware spatial operations.
about_excerpt: A scientist and an AI agent co-design a validated 96-well plate: the human fixes precious samples and approves the exact export while WebMCP gives the agent precise, state-aware spatial operations. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Problem Microplate layouts combine sample identity, fixed controls, replicate separation, row/column balance, edge effects, and pipetting order across 96 nearly identical wells. Scientists understand that visual canvas, but a screen-driving agent has to infer semantics from cells and coordinates. One mistaken click can duplicate a sample, move a control, or reuse a plan after the human changed the plate. Solution PlateWeave is a synthetic design studio with one shared, versioned state. The person can use the familiar 96-well interface, set or lock samples, compare candidates, and inspect the CSV. The agent uses nine imperative WebMCP tools to read exact identities, generate deterministic alternatives, compare page-computed metrics, apply a reversible layout, recover from stale human edits, validate, and prepare export. The page—not the model—enforces every constraint. Why This Matters Laboratory staff spend attention on repetitive spatial allocation where small clerical errors are expensive. This demonstrator shows a credible division of labor: scientists retain experimental judgment and approval, while an agent handles precise batch operations and explains measurable trade-offs. It makes no medical claim and controls no instrument. Why WebMCP Fits The plate is exactly the kind of dense visual surface where coordinate automation is weakest. WebMCP turns “click many similar cells correctly” into stable operations over sample IDs, well IDs, strategies, and state versions. The agent and human work on the same live plate and can see each other's changes immediately. Without WebMCP, preserving a human D6 lock while regenerating the remaining 23 samples is a fragile browser task; with it, that is one validated semantic operation. How We Used AI Codex planned and implemented the static app, deterministic domain model, WebMCP contracts, tests, and submission artifacts. How We Used Codex Codex converted the scenario into a narrow executable state machine, split the domain engine from browser registration, implemented nine schemas and lifecycle cleanup, and built regression tests for stale state, approval, idempotency, and cancellation. On 2026-09-02, Codex's desktop in-app Browser discovered all nine tools from the public deployment and successfully invoked the experiment read plus both candidate-generation strategies. Key Features Complete interactive 8×12 plate with 24 synthetic samples and four fixed controls. Architecture The project is dependency-free HTML, CSS, and JavaScript served by a small Node static server. src/domain.js owns normalized state and all business rules. src/app.js renders the plate and sends human actions through that domain, including a complete prepare/approve/export path without an agent. src/webmcp.js wraps the same methods as top-level imperative tools using document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext , awaited registration in try / catch , strict JSON schemas backed by runtime validation, AbortController cleanup, conservative read-only annotations, and per-call cancellation. Testing Instructions Run npm start with Node 20+ and open http://127.0.0.1:4173 . Known Limitations Synthetic single-plate demonstrator; no LIMS, robot, persistence, authentication, uploads, or patient data. title: VT
pitch: A human-approved coding workspace where agents inspect code, propose reversible patches, and verify changes through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A human-approved coding workspace where agents inspect code, propose reversible patches, and verify changes through WebMCP. Like 2 Comment Story Updates VT Code (coding agent) connecting to WebMCP app What it is VT is a browser coding workspace for safe human-and-agent collaboration. A visitor can explore a small in-memory project without credentials, open files in CodeMirror, edit a draft, inspect a unified diff, and use the browser's native WebMCP surface to ask an agent to perform the same structured actions. An optional authenticated VT Code bridge connects the editor to a running VT Code session and a real workspace. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Browser agents often have to infer editor state from pixels, DOM labels, and keyboard shortcuts. VT exposes the editor's meaningful operations as typed, discoverable tools through document.modelContext.registerTool. An agent can receive a bounded file listing, search result, file digest, or diff, then use that structured result as the next tool input. The person remains in the editor and reviews the exact proposed change before anything can reach the terminal. This makes a previously awkward workflow—find the right file, make a precise change, inspect the diff, and hand it to a coding session—legible to both the human and the agent without granting the browser direct filesystem write access. What people and agents do together A person opens the public editor and can use it normally even when WebMCP is unavailable. An agent lists project files, searches for a symbol or phrase, and opens the relevant file using returned paths. An agent reads the current file and its sha256: digest, then stages one exact replacement only when the draft is clean and the digest still matches. The person reviews the generated diff in the CHANGES panel and decides whether to approve it. In an active VT Code session, the person can attach the reviewed diff to a prompt and let VT Code apply its normal terminal/full-auto policy. The browser tool surface cannot approve, apply, or revert a filesystem change. Browser draft edits remain in page memory; VT Code and its terminal approval policy remain authoritative for connected changes. WebMCP implementation The browser registers eight bounded tools for file listing, search, reading, editor state, file opening, exact draft edits, diff review, and panel navigation. Each tool has a concise description, JSON Schema validation, a display title, abort-aware execution, annotations for read-only and untrusted content, and a 1,500-character result budget. File, diff, and collection responses include truncation metadata. The app listens for WebMCP toolchange events and unregisters tools through an AbortSignal. The stage_text_edit tool is intentionally narrow: it requires a current digest, rejects stale or dirty drafts, requires exactly one matching text span, and returns the base and draft digests. It never approves a patch, writes a local file, or bypasses the authenticated VT Code bridge. The Rust vtcode-webmcp bridge adds authenticated loopback WebSocket pairing, exact origin checks, bounded workspace operations, digest validation, event replay, reconnect support, and fail-closed handling for unsafe paths and stale changes. It is shipped as a first-class VT Code integration, and the maintained Vite WebMCP app lives in apps/webmcp/ . Why the workflow is safe The browser never writes directly to the filesystem. Workspace access is rooted, bounded, digest-checked, and protected against traversal, symlink/hard-link escapes, sensitive paths, and unsafe check execution. Real mutations remain subject to terminal approval or the existing explicit full-auto policy. The public page includes a deterministic in-memory fallback so judges can evaluate the product without credentials or a local backend. title: GomiMCP
pitch: Municipal waste rules that AI agents can understand and act on—without guessing, while humans retain control of final decisions.
about_excerpt: Municipal waste rules that AI agents can understand and act on—without guessing, while humans retain control of final decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Japan has highly organized waste-disposal systems, but the rules differ between municipalities. The same object may be classified differently depending on the city, quantity, size, material, or safety risk. People also rarely use exact official category names. They say things like: “I have ten of those transparent things sold at convenience stores for rainy days, something I put on the floor to sleep on, and a portable battery for charging my phone.” An AI agent can understand what the user probably means, but it should not invent municipal rules or automatically complete a potentially unsafe action. GomiMCP separates those responsibilities: The municipality declares the rules. The agent interprets the user’s language. The human makes the final decision. What it does GomiMCP is a static WebMCP-powered interface that exposes structured municipal waste rules directly from a webpage. The page registers three WebMCP tools: resolve_item converts ordinary or indirect wording into a canonical waste item. get_disposal_rule returns the municipality’s declared rule for that item. prepare_bulky_pickup prepares an eligible bulky-waste request without finalizing it. In the demo, the agent interprets one indirect Japanese request as ten umbrellas, one futon, and one mobile power bank. It makes eight real WebMCP calls: resolve_item ×3 get_disposal_rule ×3 prepare_bulky_pickup ×2 Under Aoba City’s fictional test rules, ten umbrellas and the futon are classified as bulky waste. GomiMCP prepares both requests and displays a Human Confirmation Gate totaling 800 yen. The mobile power bank is classified as high-risk. Automated preparation is refused, and the result is marked manual_review_required . The agent can prepare eligible requests, but it cannot press the final confirmation button. Nothing is booked until a human explicitly confirms it. How we built it GomiMCP is a static JavaScript application deployed with GitHub Pages. Its tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool provides a name, natural-language description, JSON input schema, execution logic, and safety annotations. The implementation separates: Item aliases and canonical identifiers Municipality-specific classifications Conditional rules such as quantity thresholds Fees and reservation requirements Risk levels and automation permissions Human-confirmation requirements Rule provenance and version information The LIVE WEBMCP TRACE displays only actual tool calls made through the page, making the interaction visible and auditable. No backend, database, authentication system, payment integration, or real municipality booking is used. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was deciding where language interpretation should end and authoritative decision-making should begin. Natural language is flexible, while municipal rules must be precise. Allowing a language model to invent a disposal category would be unsafe. Passing an entire ambiguous sentence directly into a rule engine would also be unreliable. We solved this with a staged flow: The agent interprets each description as one ordinary item concept. GomiMCP resolves that concept to a canonical item. The page applies the selected municipality’s declared rules. Risk policies determine whether automation must stop. Consequential actions stop at a visible Human Confirmation Gate. Another challenge was proving that the tools were actually called. The LIVE WEBMCP TRACE records real page-level tool activity rather than displaying a simulated agent response. Accomplishments that we're proud of We successfully demonstrated: Semantic interpretation of indirect Japanese descriptions Eight real WebMCP tool calls Deterministic results based on municipality and quantity Automatic refusal for a high-risk mobile battery Preparation of two eligible bulky-waste requests A mandatory human-confirmation boundary A visible and auditable trace of every tool call A complete product experience running as a static website We are especially proud that the demo shows a useful division of responsibility: the agent understands the user, the page owns the rules, and the human retains control of the final action. What we learned AI does not need to own every decision to be useful. The model is best used for understanding human intent. The authoritative source should still own the rule, the safety constraint, and the final action boundary. WebMCP makes this division practical. It allows an ordinary webpage to expose structured capabilities to an agent while preserving the page’s existing logic, state, and user interface. We also learned that observability matters. Showing the real tool-call trace makes the system easier to test, explain, and trust. What's next for GomiMCP The current version uses fictional municipalities and test rules derived from official municipal open-data structures. It must not be used as real-world disposal advice. Future work includes: Importing and validating real municipality-maintained rules Expanding rule provenance and version tracking Supporting more item conditions, such as dimensions and remaining contents Adding multilingual municipality-maintained descriptions Providing reusable schemas for additional municipalities Exploring Remote MCP and SDK integrations Testing the same contracts across more WebMCP-aware agents and browsers Our longer-term goal is simple: municipalities should be able to declare their rules once and make them safely usable by people, websites, and AI agents. title: Deshi digest
pitch: Deshi Digest is an AI-powered nutrition platform for Bangladeshi food, now enhanced with WebMCP so AI agents can search, compare, analyze, and help plan healthier local meals.
about_excerpt:
Deshi Digest is an AI-powered nutrition platform for Bangladeshi food, now enhanced with WebMCP so AI agents can search, compare, analyze, and help plan healthier local meals.

 Story

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Deshi Digest started from a problem in my own life. 

 Over time, I gained much more weight than I was comfortable with. I wanted to control my eating habits and understand what I was actually consuming every day. 

 So naturally, I tried looking for nutrition apps. 

 But I noticed a problem. 

 Most of them understood foods like pizza, pasta, cereal, sandwiches, or packaged Western products very well, but they were much less useful when my plate contained things like rice, dal, bhorta, khichuri, kacchi biryani, fish curry, paratha, pitha, or several Bangladeshi dishes together . 

 And even when I could find nutritional information, the experience still felt generic. 

 I did not just want an app that told me: 

 "You ate 700 calories." 

 I wanted something that actually understood me, my food, my habits, my goals, and the way people around me eat. 

 That was the beginning of Deshi Digest . 

 My initial thought was simple: 

 What if I could create a personalized AI food companion built around Bangladeshi food? 

 But as I continued building it, that idea became much bigger. 

 

 What Deshi Digest does 

 Deshi Digest is an AI-powered personalized food, nutrition, and lifestyle companion centered around Bangladeshi cuisine . 

 It is designed to follow the complete journey around food: 

 Understand what you eat → track it → get personalized guidance → decide what to cook → find the ingredients → and actually get the food. 

 Personalized food and nutrition 

 Deshi Digest helps users understand Bangladeshi meals instead of forcing them into a food database designed for another culture. 

 The system can help users explore foods, analyze meals, understand nutrition, track their food-related activity, and receive recommendations based on their own situation. 

 I have also been working on fine-tuning AI around Bangladeshi food , so the intelligence behind Deshi Digest can better understand local dishes, ingredients, terminology, and eating habits. 

 AI is therefore not simply a chatbot added on top of the website. 

 It is intended to become the intelligence connecting the entire experience. 

 

 Care Companion 

 Food is only one part of taking care of yourself. 

 That led me to build the Care Companion concept into Deshi Digest. 

 Instead of only showing numbers, the Care Companion is designed to stay alongside the user and help them understand their daily food decisions in a more personal and conversational way. 

 For example, instead of simply warning: 

 "You consumed too many calories today." 

 the companion should understand the context and help the user decide what to do next. 

 A user might say: 

 "I already had kacchi for lunch. What should I eat tonight?" 

 The Care Companion can help adjust the rest of the day's choices rather than treating one meal as a failure. 

 The goal is to make Deshi Digest feel less like a calculator and more like a personal food companion that understands your journey over time. 

 

 Built for students and bachelors too 

 While working on the project, I realized another everyday problem. 

 Students and bachelors often see amazing food online or at restaurants but think: 

 "I can't cook that." 

 or: 

 "That will cost too much." 

 But good-looking and enjoyable food does not always need expensive ingredients. 

 Deshi Digest is designed to help someone say: 

 "I have eggs, potatoes, rice, onions and 200 taka. What can I make?" 

 and receive practical ideas based on what they already have and what they can afford. 

 It can help turn ordinary ingredients into attractive meals while keeping the recipe realistic for someone living alone or on a limited budget. 

 So Deshi Digest is not just about telling people to eat less. 

 It should also help people enjoy food more intelligently. 

 

 From recipe to grocery 

 Then I thought about another problem. 

 Suppose Deshi Digest recommends a meal. 

 The user still has to: 

 
 figure out the ingredients, 
 find a grocery shop, 
 determine where it is, 
 travel there, 
 and then buy everything. 
 

 Why should the experience stop at the recipe? 

 That led to the grocery discovery and route experience . 

 Deshi Digest can help users discover grocery options and find a suitable route to get the ingredients they need. 

 The vision is that after choosing a meal, the experience can continue naturally: 

 Choose meal → see required ingredients → find grocery options → get the route → buy the food or ingredients. 

 And where purchasing is available through the platform, users can continue from discovery directly toward buying what they need. 

 This makes the platform useful not only for deciding what to eat , but also for answering: 

 "How do I actually get it?" 

 

 A complete food journey 

 This is the experience I want Deshi Digest to create. 

 Imagine saying: 

 "I want to cook something special tonight, but I only have 300 taka." 

 Deshi Digest could help: 

 
 understand your preferences 
 consider your recent meals 
 suggest suitable Bangladeshi dishes 
 show affordable alternatives 
 generate a practical recipe 
 identify missing ingredients 
 help locate grocery options 
 guide you to the shop 
 and help you obtain what you need 
 

 Or you could say: 

 "I already ate biryani for lunch. I still want something tasty tonight." 

 Your Care Companion could understand the context and help balance the rest of your day without simply telling you not to eat. 

 For me, this is what personalization should actually mean. 

 

 Why WebMCP? 

 While building all of these capabilities, I realized something else. 

 Why should Deshi Digest only work when someone manually opens the website and clicks through every feature? 

 An AI agent should also be able to understand what Deshi Digest can do. 

 That is why WebMCP fits naturally into the project. 

 With WebMCP, Deshi Digest can expose its useful capabilities directly to AI agents in a structured way. 

 Instead of an agent trying to visually understand buttons and pages, Deshi Digest can effectively tell the agent: 

 "These are the things I can help you with." 

 An agent could potentially use Deshi Digest to: 

 
 search Bangladeshi foods 
 understand local dishes 
 retrieve food and nutrition information 
 compare meals 
 analyze someone's food choices 
 work with the Care Companion 
 generate practical meal ideas 
 plan meals around a user's budget 
 find required ingredients 
 discover grocery options 
 help find routes to grocery shops 
 and assist with the journey from deciding what to eat to actually obtaining the food 
 

 

 Human + AI Agent + Deshi Digest 

 This creates an experience I find especially exciting. 

 Instead of: 

 Human → Website → Click → Click → Search → Result 

 we can move toward: 

 Human → AI Agent → WebMCP → Deshi Digest 

 For example, someone could simply tell their AI agent: 

 "Use Deshi Digest. I ate kacchi today, I don't want to spend more than 250 taka tonight, and I want something easy to cook. Find something suitable and tell me where I can get the ingredients." 

 The agent could use Deshi Digest's specialized capabilities to help complete that entire task. 

 The user does not need to know which page contains which feature. 

 They simply express an intention. 

 That is what makes WebMCP particularly interesting to me. 

 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges has been understanding Bangladeshi food itself. 

 Our food is incredibly diverse. 

 The same dish can have very different nutritional values depending on: 

 
 ingredients 
 portion sizes 
 cooking oil 
 preparation method 
 restaurant 
 household 
 and region 
 

 A Bangladeshi plate may also contain rice, meat, dal, vegetables, bhorta, curry, and several other items together. 

 Teaching AI to understand that is much more

title: RigBuilder - the AI assisted PC Builder
pitch: RigBuilder is a PC part picker where your agent is the interface: the page solves compatibility, constraint and budget - ChatGPT or Chrome drives it through WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: RigBuilder is a PC part picker where your agent is the interface: the page solves compatibility, constraint and budget - ChatGPT or Chrome drives it through WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Andreas: For the past year I have been interested in one particular question - what does an application look like when its primary user is an agent? And how can humans and agents collaborate? Since the start of last year, I have explored the MCP spec at depth and how it can be used by agents, and chronicled my adventures at my blog ( https://nullpointer.se ). I've been especially interested in "agentic UI", and what the future of applications and UI will look like, as we enter the agentic era. I have spent a lot of time exploring protocols such as AG-UI, A2UI and MCP Apps to try to understand what lies in the future for agentic applications and user interfaces. I am a strong believer in the paradigm of "generative UI", and the agent dynamically presenting just the information and the functionality the user needs - when he or she needs it. My main realization from the last year of experimentation with MCP and adjacant tech is that agentic user interfaces are not only more efficient, they are also more fun to use. In July 2025 I read about MCP-B on Hacker News and the idea that web apps could expose MCP tools directly to an agent running in the browser. Since I was deep into MCP at that time, I was really excited by this and started exploring the spec. Being in the Microsoft space, I did experiments with MCP-B tools running inside a Power App , and when MCP-B was accompanied by the WebMCP proposal and Chrome shipped its first preview, I tried that too in various demos - for example here . When I heard about the WebMCP hackathon I got really stoked, since I had been wanting to try WebMCP more. I also already had a good demo scenario - at the conference AgentCon Stockholm earlier this year I gave a talk on agentic applications and used a PC part picker to demonstrate how to use AG-UI to share state between an agent and an app (still live here ). It was a good example of an agentic application, but the website had to ship the AI-assistant and foot the inference bill. WebMCP inverts that, which is an interesting idea. The user brings the agent, and the site hands it tools. So we (Andreas Adner and my friends Rafsan Huseynov (in the US) and David Lorenze (in Spain)) expanded upon this idea and built RigBuilder, a PC Builder where an agent can help you out, using WebMCP. What it does RigBuilder is an agent-native PC part picker. It is also a compatibility and constraint solver , making sure that all parts fit together and are within your budget. Your agent (ChatGPT's desktop browser, or Chrome 149+ with an agent) drives the build through 14 WebMCP tools and the agent gets access to validation and a gets a state revision back on every call. For example, ask for "a quiet, compact 1440p gaming PC under $1500" and the agent helps you assemble it. Swap the case by hand and say "fix whatever broke" and the agent reads your change from the shared state. Ask to get under $1400 and the page's optimizer computes the swap plan for the agent to present, and so on and so forth. Ask to see it, and render_build tool produces a brand-free impression of your parts using an OpenAI imagegen model (expect mixed results, it's AI after all ;-) There is a also a second user group - admins. An admin can curate the part catalogue in an WebMCP-enabled admin experience, where he for example can get help from his agent to research a newly launched part on the web and add it to the catalogue with the help of the agent. And RigBuilder is also a complete manual part picker, if you don't have an agent. :-) How we built it React/Vite/TypeScript with Zustand, and a single Cloudflare Worker: D1 for the catalog, R2 for renders and part cards, KV for share links, a Durable Object for the daily render quota, a Rate-Limiting binding for bursts, Turnstile for the render gate, Cloudflare Access to gate access to the admin side. The WebMCP surface was the priority, so it got the most design effort. Every tool returns the same envelope: validated build, conflicts, revision, so the agent never has to guess what changed. Shared state is versioned: a write based on stale knowledge is rejected even if the agent never learned about revisions, because the guard defaults to the revision the agent last saw. Tool descriptions carry untrustedContentHint where web-sourced text enters. The render_build tool sends only part ids and enums; the Worker rebuilds the prompt and cache hash itself and never trusts a client prompt or image. The catalog is 448 hand-authored parts, 82 verified against manufacturer spec pages with recorded sources; every tool result says which is which. Challenges The main challenge was deciding what the WebMCP tools should actually do. We did not want to expose a simple "remote-control" layer that simply mapped tools to normal user interactions - buttons and clicks. The tools needed to give the agent capabilities beyond what a user could accomplish: validating an entire build, identifying conflicts, optimizing against a budget, and returning a complete, structured view of the resulting state. Finding the right level of abstraction was a challenge. Each tool had to be powerful enough to add real value, but focused enough for an agent to understand when and how to use it. Shared state created another WebMCP-specific problem: both the human and the agent can modify the build. The agent might plan its next action from a state that the user has already changed manually. We solved this with versioned state and revision guards that reject stale writes, while still allowing agents to use the tools without explicitly managing revision numbers on every call. From my experiments with AG-UI I have realized that shared state between agent and app is a major unlock when it comes to agentic applications - and WebMCP is really good fit here. Finally, we had to treat the agent as capable but not inherently trusted. Tool inputs are validated by the application, web-sourced catalog text is marked as untrusted, and sensitive operations are reconstructed and checked on the server. WebMCP makes an application dramatically more accessible to agents, but it comes with some new and specific challenges when it comes to security. What we learned WebMCP changes who and what you design for. When the agent becomes the interface, tool descriptions form the foundation of the interaction model. Designing a good agent experience requires the same care as designing a visual one; that care simply moves into the tools, their contracts, and the state they share with the page. This is a pretty interesting shift. It's also an interesting challenge that we can't really make that many assumptions with regard to the agent that is consuming the WebMCP tools. We also learned that the entire “add an AI assistant” architecture can disappear/morph. RigBuilder has no embedded model, inference bill, or chat widget. The user brings the agent, while the application contributes its tools, domain knowledge, and interface. There is no assistant bolted onto the side anymore - also a major shift. What's next Lots of stuff to do. More verified parts, exact cards for the whole catalog, live pricing, and the part I care most about - bringing the same pattern back to the business applications I work with in my day job. title: Home Gym Creator
pitch: Design a home gym with an AI agent. Edit one shared room through WebMCP while the app checks space, access, training goals, and budget.
about_excerpt: Design a home gym with an AI agent. Edit one shared room through WebMCP while the app checks space, access, training goals, and budget. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I first tried Codex Modeling Studio and was fascinated by the idea of designing something together with an AI agent in a shared visual workspace. It made me want to explore the same kind of human-agent collaboration in a domain I care about personally. Strength training is my hobby, so I started wondering whether the same approach could help design a home gym around real spatial, training, and budget constraints. That question became Home Gym Creator. What it does Home Gym Creator helps people design a home gym that fits their actual room, training goals, and budget. Users can model the room in 2D or 3D, add furniture, doors, windows, and unavailable areas, then choose equipment from a catalog of 24 fictional products. An AI agent can read and modify the same project through WebMCP. It can configure the room, search the catalog, add and arrange equipment, react to manual changes, and validate the finished layout. Every agent action is immediately visible in the editor and uses the same undo and redo history as manual edits. The application validates the layout by checking collisions, room boundaries, exercise clearance, access paths, ceiling height, wall mounting, training-goal coverage, and total cost. The agent respects these validation results and uses them to improve the design together with the user. How I built it I built Home Gym Creator with Next.js, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, and React Three Fiber. Manual actions and WebMCP tools use the same project commands, state, validation, and undo history. I used Codex and Cursor throughout development for planning, implementation, debugging, and testing. The app runs entirely in the browser and is deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into At first, the agent placed equipment too close to furniture or blocked paths from the door to the wardrobe and bed. I introduced collision detection, equipment and furniture use zones, and access-path validation to model these practical constraints. I did not want placement tools to contain rigid rules that removed the agent’s freedom. Instead, I added a tool that suggests suitable positions before placement and another that validates the complete layout afterward. Modeling realistic combinations was also challenging: for example, a wall-mounted pull-up bar can remain usable above a low object, and people can still walk underneath it. Representing these height-aware rules required careful iteration. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that the agent can use deterministic tools to check its own work and respect the user's room, budget, and training requirements. Selecting equipment often requires combining several products: for example, a strength setup for squats and bench press may need a rack, bench, barbell, and weight plates. The agent can choose that combination within the available budget, arrange it inside the room, and verify that it fits without collisions or blocked access paths. Making this complete workflow work reliably was one of my biggest accomplishments in the project. What I learned I learned about the current limitations of AI-generated 3D assets. My first attempt was to generate 50 equipment models at once, but it did not produce usable results. Generating one model at a time and improving it iteratively worked much better. I also learned how to guide an agent without adding rigid instructions to every tool. Instead, I gave it dedicated suggestion and validation tools, allowing it to explore solutions, check its own work, and improve the layout based on deterministic feedback. What's next for Home Gym Creator If I continue developing Home Gym Creator, I would add protective floor-mat planning, wall and floor customization, and more equipment options with additional 3D models. I would also expand the concept beyond home gyms toward commercial facilities, supporting multiple rooms and floors, changing rooms, and more complex equipment layouts. title: Cleanroom
pitch: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero.
about_excerpt: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero. Like Comment Story Updates Cleanroom What it does Cleanroom is a data-cleaning workbench for messy CSVs. You drop a file on the page and an agent in your browser profiles it, finds the concrete problems, queries and charts it, and proposes the fixes — without the file ever being uploaded anywhere. The design rule is one sentence: reads are free, writes are proposals. No tool mutates your table. When the agent wants to change something it computes the exact before/after diff, puts a card in front of you with its reasoning, and stops. You click Approve or Reject. undo is deliberately not exposed as a tool — the ability to walk a change back belongs to the person, not the model. The problem it solves Every analyst has the same bad afternoon. A CSV arrives and before you can answer one question you have to fix it: regions spelled five ways, amounts stored as ¥39,545 , four date formats in one column, duplicate rows silently doubling your revenue. An LLM is excellent at spotting exactly these problems. But letting one help has meant either uploading your data to a server or code interpreter — a non-starter the moment the file has customer names, salaries or anything your compliance team has an opinion about — or pasting a sample and hand-applying the suggestions yourself, which is the automation you wanted, gone. Cleanroom is the third option: the agent gets tools, not your data. Why this is WebMCP and could not be a server MCP This is not a remote MCP server with a web page bolted on. It structurally could not be one. The agent and the human operate on literally the same JavaScript object . One store is the single source of truth; the UI renders it and the tools operate on it. When the agent proposes a change the approval card appears in the human's rail in the same tick — no sync, no polling, no second copy that can drift. A remote agent cannot have that property, because a remote agent needs a copy. And everything a server MCP would need — upload, storage, auth, per-seat infrastructure — is simply absent. It's already your browser and already your session. The whole app is a static file. The privacy receipt The claim is "your data never leaves this tab," and a claim is worth nothing, so the page proves it. Before any other module loads, Cleanroom instruments fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon and WebSocket and counts every outbound request. The count is in the header, and the agent can read it too, via a get_privacy_receipt tool — so when you ask "did my data go anywhere?" it answers with a verifiable number instead of a promise. It reads zero because there is nothing to send it to: no analytics, no CDN, no webfont, no charting library. Even the sample dataset is inlined as a string rather than fetched, specifically so the ledger stays honest. The deployed site also ships connect-src 'none' in its CSP, so the browser enforces it independently of our own code. Being straight about the limit: this counts requests the page makes. It cannot police the browser itself or a malicious extension, and it isn't a substitute for a security review. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no runtime dependencies — a dependency that phones home would undermine the entire premise. Roughly 1,800 lines across eleven modules: a RFC-4180-tolerant CSV parser, type inference and column profiling, an issue detector, fifteen pure transform operations with a diff builder, the store that holds the undo stack, the WebMCP tool layer, the UI, and hand-rolled inline SVG charts. 14 tools are registered — eight read-only, six human-gated. Three implementation details did the most for how well an agent actually performs here: Every detected issue carries a suggested_fix — a ready-to-use propose_transform payload. The agent goes from "what's wrong?" to a queued, reviewable fix in one hop instead of guessing at an API shape. This cut the model's flailing more than anything else I tried. Errors are instructions. Every failure names the valid inputs — Column "reigon" does not exist. Available columns: order_id, order_date, region, … — and is returned as text rather than thrown, so the agent reads the recovery path instead of hitting an opaque host error. Results are context-window shaped. Profiles and aggregates are summaries by construction; raw rows are returned only on request and hard-capped at 200. A 100,000-row file is fully workable without a single row entering the model's context. Challenges WebMCP's API moved while it was being standardised — some hosts expose navigator.modelContext , the current spec draft uses document.modelContext , and earlier builds took a batch provideContext({tools}) instead of per-tool registerTool . Rather than bet on one, the registration shim feature-detects all of them and reports which it found, so the header tells the user the truth about their browser instead of failing silently. Tool results are returned in three shapes at once — MCP-style content , structuredContent , and a bare data object — so the same tool behaves identically across hosts. The harder problem was designing the pause . An agent that has to stop and wait is easy to build badly: it either blocks forever or barrels ahead assuming approval. propose_transform returns pending_human_approval with an explicit next_step , and a separate await_decision tool blocks on the human with a timeout and tells the agent what to say if it expires. Getting the agent to reliably not assume its change landed was most of the prompt-shaped work. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is interface design, and the same thing that makes an API pleasant for a junior engineer — good names, errors that say what to do next, results scoped to what you actually need — is what makes a model competent instead of erratic. The suggested_fix field was the clearest demonstration: same model, same data, dramatically better behaviour, purely from shaping the return value. The second thing: an approval gate makes an agent more useful, not less. Once a change is reviewable before it lands, you stop hedging your prompts and start letting it try things. What's next Multi-table joins under the same proposal model — the agent proposes the key and shows you the match rate before committing. Recipe export — the change log is already ordered and structured; emit it as a runnable script so a one-off clean becomes a repeatable pipeline. Approval policies — "auto-approve whitespace fixes, always ask about dropped rows." The gate exists; this is a rule layer on top of it. Try it In ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, open the page and ask: "What's wrong with this data? Don't change anything yet — just tell me what you'd fix and why." "Clean it up. Propose each fix separately so I can review them, and ask me before you touch anything that's a judgement call." In any other browser the built-in Agent Console calls the same registered tool objects a host calls — an inspector, not a mock — so you can see exactly what the agent sees.
