 Inspiration 

 Fraud is becoming more sophisticated as digital payments and online commerce continue to grow across Africa. 

 We noticed that many fraud systems focus heavily on the transaction itself: the amount, device, location, IP address, transaction history, and velocity. But a legitimate-looking transaction can still be fraudulent when a user has been manipulated through social engineering. 

 A person may receive a message from someone impersonating a bank, business, friend, or payment provider and voluntarily initiate what appears to be a completely normal transaction. 

 That led us to a simple question: 

 What if fraud detection could understand the context around a transaction, not just the transaction itself? 

 That question inspired Ayib FraudGuard by Markfisher Consulting, an AI-powered fraud intelligence and social-engineering protection platform designed to help identify suspicious activity before it becomes a financial loss. 

 Our vision is simple: Ayib provides the payment infrastructure, while Ayib FraudGuard provides the security intelligence protecting it. 

 What it does 

 Ayib FraudGuard analyzes transaction and contextual signals to identify suspicious behavior and generate a risk assessment. 

 It is designed to help fintechs, banks, payment platforms, marketplaces, and developers detect potential fraud through an API-driven security layer. 

 Key capabilities include: 

 AI-assisted anomaly detection
Real-time transaction risk analysis
Behavioral pattern analysis
Social-engineering risk detection
Risk scoring
API-based fraud intelligence
Security-focused automation
Developer-friendly integration 

 Instead of simply asking whether a transaction looks unusual, FraudGuard aims to help answer: 

 "Does the overall context suggest that this transaction may be fraudulent?" 

 The resulting intelligence can be incorporated into an application's workflow to support decisions such as allowing, challenging, reviewing, or blocking a transaction. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we are also exploring how fraud intelligence can become more accessible to web applications and AI-powered developer experiences through machine-consumable interfaces and workflows. 

 How we built it 

 We built Ayib FraudGuard as a cloud-native, API-first security platform. 

 The architecture combines a transaction-processing layer with AI-assisted risk analysis and security controls. 

 At a high level, the system: 

 Receives transaction and contextual signals.
Processes and normalizes the available data.
Evaluates behavioral and transactional patterns.
Uses AI-assisted analysis to identify anomalies and potential social-engineering indicators.
Produces a risk assessment.
Makes that intelligence available to the consuming application through an API. 

 We designed the platform to be modular so that additional fraud signals, detection models, security services, and developer interfaces can be added without rebuilding the entire system. 

 Our broader stack and experience includes TypeScript/Node.js, APIs, cloud infrastructure, AI/LLMs, CI/CD, observability, and security engineering. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Ayib FraudGuard was not born from a hypothetical problem. It was born from our experience building and launching Ayib. 

 When we first launched Ayib, we experienced multiple security breaches and incidents that exposed weaknesses in how we were protecting our payment infrastructure. These experiences made it clear that traditional security controls alone were not enough. We needed a security layer that could continuously analyze activity, identify unusual behavior, and help us detect potential threats before they became financial losses. 

 That experience became one of the key inspirations behind Ayib FraudGuard. 

 As we began building FraudGuard, one of our biggest challenges was determining how to combine AI-driven flexibility with the predictability and reliability required by financial systems. 

 AI can identify patterns that traditional rules may miss, but we could not simply allow an AI model to make financial security decisions without appropriate controls and safeguards. We therefore designed FraudGuard so that AI works as part of a broader security architecture rather than acting as the sole decision-maker. 

 We also had to solve several practical challenges: 

 Detecting suspicious activity with low latency.
Balancing false positives and false negatives.
Maintaining consistent AI model behavior.
Ensuring API reliability and availability.
Establishing appropriate security boundaries.
Designing for future scalability.
Providing sufficient observability into security decisions.
Making risk assessments understandable and actionable.
Integrating fraud intelligence into existing payment workflows. 

 Another major challenge was shifting our thinking from simply responding to security incidents to building infrastructure capable of anticipating and preventing them. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Our biggest accomplishment is turning lessons from Ayib's early security incidents into a working AI-powered fraud intelligence platform. 

 Instead of treating our security challenges as isolated incidents, we used them as an opportunity to build a reusable security layer that can potentially protect not only Ayib, but other fintechs, payment platforms, and digital businesses. 

 We are particularly proud of: 

 Turning real-world security incidents into a product opportunity.
Building an AI-assisted fraud detection pipeline.
Designing FraudGuard as an API-first platform.
Combining transaction data with behavioral and contextual risk signals.
Building an architecture that can evolve as fraud techniques change.
Exploring how AI and emerging web technologies can make security intelligence more accessible to developers.
Creating a foundation that can integrate with existing financial infrastructure. 

 Most importantly, we are proud that FraudGuard represents a shift from reactive security to proactive fraud prevention. 

 Our experience with Ayib taught us that discovering a security problem after it happens can be extremely costly. FraudGuard is designed around the idea that suspicious activity should be identified as early as possible. 

 What we learned 

 Building Ayib and subsequently Ayib FraudGuard taught us that security cannot be an afterthought, especially when building financial infrastructure. 

 We initially approached security largely from the perspective of protecting the application and infrastructure. Our experiences after launching Ayib showed us that financial security requires a much broader approach that considers transactions, users, behavior, context, infrastructure, and continuously evolving attack patterns. 

 We learned that fraud detection is not simply a machine-learning problem. 

 It requires a combination of security engineering, data, infrastructure, AI, user experience, and developer experience. 

 We also learned that accuracy alone is not enough. A fraud system needs to be fast enough for real-time transactions, reliable enough for production environments, and understandable enough for both humans and applications to act on its recommendations. 

 Most importantly, we learned that context matters. 

 A transaction can look completely legitimate when viewed on its own, but become highly suspicious when combined with behavioral, transactional, or contextual signals. 

 That lesson from building and securing Ayib continues to shape the architecture of FraudGuard today. 

 What's next for ayib fraudguard by markfisher consulting 

 Our next goal is to evolve FraudGuard from a fraud detection API into a broader fraud intelligence infrastructure for digital financial services.

title: OmniFlow Studio
pitch: A visual cloud studio where humans and AI agents design, stress-test, and synthesize production infrastructure together in real-time through 31 in-browser WebMCP tools.\n
about_excerpt:
A visual cloud studio where humans and AI agents design, stress-test, and synthesize production infrastructure together in real-time through 31 in-browser WebMCP tools.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 💡 Inspiration: Breaking Free from the Chatbox 

 Every software architect and cloud engineer has had this frustrating experience: you ask ChatGPT or Claude to "design an enterprise AI cluster" , and it spits out three pages of markdown text with ASCII diagrams. 

 You can't click on it. You can't simulate 50,000 requests per second to see where it chokes. You can't calculate real-time AWS or NVIDIA GPU costs without opening three separate pricing calculators. And you certainly can't turn it into production Terraform code without hours of manual transcription. 

 AI coding assistants were spatially blind —trapped inside narrow text boxes while real engineering happens visually on canvases, whiteboards, and topology graphs. 

 When I discovered the W3C Web Model Context Protocol (WebMCP) , everything clicked. WebMCP allows the browser tab itself to become the AI agent's interactive workspace. I asked myself: What if an AI agent didn't just write text, but lived inside the canvas with you—wiring components, stress-testing bottlenecks, debating trade-offs, and compiling infrastructure code in real-time? 

 That vision became OmniFlow Studio . 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 OmniFlow Studio is a collaborative visual systems architecture studio where humans and AI agent swarms co-create, stress-test, and synthesize cloud infrastructure live in the browser through 31 WebMCP tools : 

 
 Interactive 60 FPS Canvas : Drag, drop, and wire microservices, NVIDIA H100 GPU clusters, Redis semantic caches, and vector databases with interactive port wiring and adaptive bezier curves. 
 Live Multi-Agent Swarm Consensus : A human architect can trigger an automated debate between 4 specialized AI roles ( Lead Architect, SecOps Auditor, FinOps Advisor, and Chaos Daemon ). The swarm deliberates live, reaches consensus, and refactors the architecture. 
 Real-Time Traffic & Particle Physics : Simulate traffic spikes up to 50,000 RPS. The canvas visualizes dataflow bottlenecks using glowing packet particles and node heatmaps. 
 Chaos Engineering & Auto-Pilot : Inject chaos faults (Chaos Monkey node termination, DDoS floods, and GPU OOMs). An autonomous Auto-Pilot loop actively detects degraded nodes and self-heals the cluster. 
 Instant Code Synthesis : Compiles visual topologies directly into production Terraform (HCL) , Kubernetes Helm values , AWS CloudFormation , Docker Compose , and executive Markdown manifestos with live Mermaid diagrams. 
 

 

 🧮 Engineering Math & FinOps Foundations 

 To make the studio truly enterprise-grade, I implemented mathematical models directly into the client-side engines: 

 1. Frontier LLM KV-Cache & VRAM Sizing 

 When provisioning an NVIDIA H100 inference cluster, the memory sizing engine calculates continuous batching requirements using: 

 Memory KV = 2 × L × H × D × B × S × P 

 Where: 

 
 L = Number of transformer layers (e.g., 80 for 70B models) 
 H = Key-Value attention heads (e.g., 8 for GQA) 
 D = Head dimension (e.g., 128) 
 B = Concurrency batch size 
 S = Context sequence length (tokens) 
 P = Precision bytes ( 2 for FP16, 1 for FP8) 
 

 2. FinOps Egress & Real-Time TCO Formula 

 Monthly total cost of ownership accounts for compute instances, replicas, and network egress bandwidth dynamically: 

 $$\text{TCO} {\text{monthly}} = \sum {i=1}^{N} \left( C_{\text{base}, i} \times r_i \right) + \left( \frac{\text{RPS} \times 3600 \times 730 \times S_{\text{payload}}}{10^9} \times R_{\text{egress}} \right)$$ 

 Where C base , i is the hourly node rate, r i is horizontal replica count, and R egress is cloud egress cost per gigabyte. 

 

 🛠️ How I Built It 

 OmniFlow Studio was engineered from scratch with a zero-backend, client-side Edge architecture : 

 
 Core & Bundler : Built with HTML5 semantic elements, modern ES Modules, and bundled with Vite . 
 Design System : Handcrafted glassmorphic dark-mode CSS with cyber-glow telemetry accents, 100% responsive without heavy third-party UI bloat. 
 Canvas Engine : Custom HTML5 Canvas renderer running at a locked 60 FPS, featuring world-to-screen coordinate transformation, adaptive port attachment, and undo/redo history stacks. 
 WebMCP Architecture :

 
 29 Imperative Tools registered directly on window.document.modelContext.registerTool() . 
 2 Declarative HTML Forms using <form toolname="..."> and <input toolparamdescription="..."> for native DOM-level tool exposure. 
 Machine Discovery : Pre-configured /.well-known/webmcp.json and /llms.txt with CORS enabled for instant agent crawling. 
 
 Edge Deployment : Hosted globally on Vercel's Anycast Edge CDN with 0ms cold-start latency (no server sleep, no timeouts). 
 

 

 🧗 Challenges I Faced 

 
 Bidirectional State Sync : The hardest part was allowing humans to drag nodes with the mouse while AI agents simultaneously executed mutations (like batch_build_architecture or kill_random_node ) without UI race conditions or dropped frames. I designed an event-driven decoupled EventBus that synchronizes canvas coordinates instantly. 
 Preventing Awkward Wire Loops : Early prototypes suffered from overlapping connections when nodes shared columns. I wrote an adaptive port calculation algorithm and a topological DAG layering auto-layout engine ( applyAutoLayout ) that guarantees clean Left-to-Right dataflow with zero wire crossings. 
 Pure Client-Side WebMCP Execution : Ensuring that all 31 tools—including Terraform compilation and FinOps math—execute locally in under 5 milliseconds inside the browser without requiring a bulky backend server. 
 

 

 🧠 What I Learned 

 Building OmniFlow Studio convinced me that WebMCP is the future of human-AI collaboration on the web . 

 Text boxes force humans to translate their thoughts into prompts, and then translate the AI's response back into tools. With WebMCP, the human and the AI share the exact same canvas, the exact same state, and the exact same visual vocabulary . It feels less like asking a chatbot for help and more like pairing with a senior systems architect sitting right beside you. 

 

 🔮 What's Next for OmniFlow Studio 

 
 Live Cloud Deployment Hook : One-click pushing generated Terraform directly to AWS and GCP via ephemeral GitHub Actions runners. 
 Cost Anomaly Watchdogs : WebMCP agents listening to live Datadog/CloudWatch metrics to auto-tune replica counts dynamically. 
 Collaborative Multi-User Rooms : Enabling multiple humans and multiple agent swarms to co-design in the same canvas via WebRTC.

title: GENESIS WebMCP: Zero-Install AI Education OS on Chrome
pitch: Zero-Install WebAI OS on Chrome. Empowering any PC/Chromebook with 0.00005s offline learning, quiz generation, and knowledge synthesis via WebGPU, OPFS, and WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Zero-Install WebAI OS on Chrome. Empowering any PC/Chromebook with 0.00005s offline learning, quiz generation, and knowledge synthesis via WebGPU, OPFS, and WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 💡 Inspiration 

 Modern generative AI holds immense potential for education, yet schools and students face critical barriers: heavy local environment setups, expensive GPU hardware, unstable internet connections, and strict student privacy regulations. Furthermore, conventional AI agents struggle to interact reliably with web applications due to fragile DOM scraping. 

 We built GENESIS WebMCP to solve all these challenges at once. By pioneering the synergy of WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) , WebGPU , OPFS (Origin Private File System) , and on-device Gemma , we turn any standard Google Chrome browser on a low-spec PC or Chromebook into an ultra-fast, zero-install, 100% offline-capable AI learning and knowledge OS. 

 

 ⚡ What It Does 

 
 Zero-Install Instant Activation : No Python, CUDA, or local software installation required. Simply open Chrome and your private AI Brain boots up in milliseconds. 
 WebMCP Structured Agent Interoperability : Exposes web-native tools ( searchKnowledgeBank , generateInstantQuiz , renderA4Markdown ) directly to AI agents via navigator.modelContext , eliminating DOM scraping errors. 
 1.2ms On-Device WebGPU Inference : Runs optimized lightweight Gemma models directly on device VRAM/NPU with zero-copy DMA, achieving 100% private and offline operations. 
 0.00005s Reflexive Knowledge Index (OPFS) : Direct DMA connection to the local SSD allows instant search and retrieval across 10,787 structured knowledge nodes. 
 Antigravity A4 Studio : Renders complex interactive Mermaid architectural diagrams and produces publication-ready A4 documentation instantaneously. 
 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 
 WebMCP Integration : Declared structured tools and schema in navigator.modelContext so that AI agents (such as ChatGPT Desktop or browser-native agents) can invoke search, quiz generation, and documentation workflows seamlessly. 
 WebGPU Compute Pipeline : Direct hardware acceleration via WGSL shaders for on-device inference without server round-trips. 
 Origin Private File System (OPFS) : High-throughput, sandboxed local SSD storage for instant vector caching. 
 Marked.js & Mermaid v9 Engine : Embedded vector diagram synthesizer with automatic syntax sanitization and A4 print stylesheet. 
 

 

 🧗 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 Zero-Latency In-Memory Bridging : Designing an asynchronous event pipeline that ensures instant state updates without locking the browser UI during heavy LLM execution. 
 Multi-Device Hardware Auto-Adaptation : Automatically detecting device capabilities ( navigator.gpu ) to seamlessly switch between WebGPU direct DMA, WebAssembly SIMD, and Cloud TPU offloading. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 100% Zero-Local Dependency : Successfully running a full-scale AI education suite in pure Chrome without a single external package installation. 
 Battle-Tested in Real Exams : Successfully tested across hundreds of real-time university quizzes and exams with sub-second accurate responses. 
 Privacy-First Architecture : 100% of student personal data and test inputs remain securely inside the browser's local sandbox. 
 

 

 📚 What We Learned 

 WebMCP is a true paradigm shift for web development. Moving away from brittle screenshot-and-click automation toward declarative, machine-readable tool exposure enables AI agents to collaborate with web applications with 100% deterministic reliability. 

 

 🚀 What's Next for GENESIS WebMCP 

 
 Google Cloud TPU Integration (CCP) : Offloading massive batch learning synthesis to Cloud TPU v5p clusters for 120x accelerated deep learning. 
 Classroom-Scale Dynamic Live Twin : Enabling real-time peer synchronization between teachers' desktop hubs and students' Chromebooks via Service Workers.

 As the solo architect and developer, I designed and implemented the entire GENESIS WebMCP system, including the WebMCP protocol integration (navigator.modelContext), WebGPU compute pipeline, OPFS local storage architecture, and Antigravity A4 markdown studio.

title: Curbcut
pitch: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together.
about_excerpt: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Scanned Workspace Mechanical Repair Preview Verified Mechanical Repair Blocked Agent Action Contextual Proposal Responsive Workspace Inspiration Accessibility scanners are good at finding problems, but finding them is only the beginning. A developer still has to find the correct source code, understand the evidence, choose the correct repair, preview its effect, and check the result. We built Curbcut around the question: What if the developer and an external browser agent could work together on the same live accessibility workspace? The agent could handle repetitive technical work, while the developer maintained authority over changes that require meaning, context, or design judgment. What it does Curbcut is a browser-native accessibility repair workbench for static HTML and CSS. The workspace keeps everything together: Editable source A securely isolated live preview Real axe-core accessibility findings Exact source mapping and rendered-element highlighting Proposed code diffs A rendered preview of each proposed repair Human approval for semantic changes Fresh verification scans Exact Undo and clean source export A shared timeline of human and agent actions axe-core scans the actual rendered preview, and the results aren't hard-coded. Selecting an issue focuses its exact source range and highlights the corresponding element in the preview. Every repair begins as a non-mutating proposal. Curbcut shows the exact source diff and proposed visual result before changing the working source. Technical repairs, such as removing a positive tabindex, can be applied and verified in the code directly. Contextual repairs, including form labels, image alternatives, button names, and document text, remain blocked until the developer reviews and approves the exact proposal. If the browser agent attempts to apply a contextual proposal early, Curbcut returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED, visibly records the blocked action, and leaves the source unchanged. Curbcut exposes ten focused WebMCP tools covering the real workflow: workspace inspection, scanning, listing and inspecting issues, previewing, applying, rejecting, undoing, summarizing, and exporting. These tools operate on the same React store and preview used by the visible interface. There is no arbitrary JavaScript tool, arbitrary DOM mutation, or whole-document AI rewrite. How we built it Curbcut is a browser-only React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed as a static site on Vercel. It requires no account, backend, or database, and the developer’s source stays local to the browser. We use parse5 8.0.1 to parse canonical HTML with source locations and assign revision-bound internal node IDs. Mapping metadata is added only to generated preview markup, so it never contaminates the working or exported source. Repairs use validated raw-offset patches that preserve unrelated source text. Imported HTML is treated as untrusted. DOMPurify sanitizes it before it enters an iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and no same-origin permission. A nonce-based Content Security Policy blocks network requests, navigation, forms, embeds, and untrusted scripts. axe-core 4.13.0 runs inside that opaque preview realm. A validated postMessage bridge connects scanning and highlighting to the React workspace while checking the channel, request ID, message shape, and source revision. The top-level page registers exactly ten WebMCP tools through document.modelContext. Inputs are runtime-validated, imported source and accessibility snippets are marked as untrusted content, stale revisions are rejected, and read-only tools use the appropriate annotations. Most importantly, the agent cannot manufacture human approval. Contextual approval tokens are created only when the developer approves the exact visible proposal through the interface. Challenges we ran into The first major challenge was executing axe inside an opaque sandbox while safely returning useful results to the parent application. We needed enough communication for rendering, scanning, and highlighting without granting the preview same-origin access. The second was reliable source mapping. Existing HTML IDs were not sufficient because imported documents can have missing or duplicate IDs. We instead built parser-backed mappings using exact source ranges and preview-only internal metadata. The third was keeping proposals bound to the correct source revision. Rendering, scanning, agent calls, and human actions are asynchronous, so Curbcut rejects stale issue and proposal IDs and requires the exact proposed preview to report ready before Apply becomes valid. Finally, we had to make the human-agent boundary technically enforceable. A prompt asking the agent to wait was not enough. The application itself had to reject unauthorized contextual changes and preserve the proposal and source unchanged. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real end-to-end WebMCP workflow where external browser-agent actions visibly update the same workspace the developer is reviewing Real axe scans against an isolated live preview rather than stored or fixture-specific results Exact mapping from rendered axe nodes to editable source without relying on user-provided IDs Small deterministic patches instead of whole-document model rewrites A visible, enforceable human-approval boundary for semantic changes Fresh rescan verification, exact Undo, and clean export Five bounded repair families, with color contrast intentionally kept as evidence rather than guessed automatically An unrelated imported profile-form test proving that the scanner and mapping system are not hard-coded to the checkout demo 88 passing unit and integration tests and 30 passing browser tests A 72-trajectory WebMCP evaluation with 69 operationally correct workflows, zero approval-boundary violations, and zero infrastructure failures A production deployment exercised through browser-agent tooling with all ten tools discoverable and no WebMCP console errors Curbcut does not claim automated WCAG compliance. A cleared automated finding proves only that the targeted automated check disappeared after a fresh scan. Manual review, assistive-technology testing, and disabled-user expertise remain essential. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful product actions rather than generic browser control. The browser agent does not replace the application; it gains a structured way to participate in the application’s existing workflow. We also learned that accessibility repair is as much an authority problem as a code-generation problem. Some changes are mechanical. Others require someone to decide what an image, label, or control means. A useful agent should understand and respect that distinction. Finally, source mapping and safe execution boundaries were more challenging than generating the patches themselves. Making every action visible, reversible, revision-bound, and verifiable is what turned the idea into a coherent product. What's next for Curbcut Next, we would test Curbcut with more accessibility practitioners and frontend developers, improve the editing and diff experience, and carefully add more deterministic repair families where automation is defensible. Longer term, the same shared-workspace model could support reviewed accessibility contributions across larger projects. The principle would remain the same: let the agent handle mechanics while the human retains authority over meaning. title: Samu
pitch: Prove it's yours — without revealing the secrets that prove it. An agent-ready lost & found built on WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Prove it's yours — without revealing the secrets that prove it. An agent-ready lost & found built on WebMCP. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration In Niamey, lost items live in WhatsApp groups. Someone finds a wallet, posts a photo, and then faces an impossible choice: if they publish the details that identify it, anyone can copy the post and claim it; if they don't, the real owner can never prove it's theirs. There is no verification — just trust and luck. We wanted to solve that specific tension: how do you let someone prove they own something without anyone — not even the platform, not even an AI agent — ever seeing the private details that prove it? What it does Samu (Hausa for "to find" ) is a lost-and-found where an AI agent runs the ownership interview without ever learning the answers . Whoever finds an item enters a few distinctive private details by hand. The owner describes their loss; Samu searches and opens the matching item. On the item page, the claimant answers verification questions. The server compares the answers and returns one thing : verified or not verified . Never a score, never which answers were right, never the secrets. Why WebMCP is a strong fit WebMCP tools belong to the page — an agent must be on a page to use its tools. We turned that into the whole UX: as the agent moves from search to a specific item, its toolset changes under its feet. And because verification is fundamentally a conversation ("what was inside the zipped pocket?"), an agent is a genuinely better interface than a form — while the humans and the agent share the exact same capabilities. What people and agents can now do together that was hard before: an agent can prove something about private data to a stranger's listing without either side leaking that data. How we built it Next.js (App Router) deployed on Netlify , with Netlify Functions as the backend. A deterministic verification engine : salted SHA-256 for exact/choice answers, semantic similarity (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small , with a local trigram fallback) for free-text answers, and weighted scoring: $$\text{score} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \cdot m_i}{\sum_i w_i}\times 100$$ Passing requires clearing a threshold and getting at least one decisive (weight-3) detail right, so guessing a few easy facts is never enough. Postgres via Neon in production; a zero-dependency node:sqlite store in development, seeded with real Niamey neighborhoods. How we used WebMCP Every page declares its tools from a single spec ( lib/spec.ts ) and a runtime turns each entry into a live tool, registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . The tools are torn down by aborting the signal — so they truly die with the page. The verification page exposes get_item_summary , list_verification_questions , answer_question , finalize_claim , and request_contact ; the search page exposes search_matches and open_item . Crucially, our own chat UI drives the same tools an external agent uses — so the agentic surface is real, not a demo. Security: the proof never leaves the server The verification engine runs entirely server-side; secrets never appear in the bundle, an API response, or a data- attribute (we grep the client build to prove it). The verdict is a boolean , and answer_question never reveals correctness — so it can't become a brute-force oracle. A budget of 5 answers, rate limiting keyed on the platform-provided client IP (not a forgeable header), claim expiry, and constant-time hash comparison. Challenges we ran into The API's lifecycle. WebMCP has no unregisterTool() ; cleanup is AbortSignal-only. Getting this wrong gave us a maddening "Duplicate tool name" under React Strict Mode until we switched to { signal } . A bleeding-edge stack. On Node 26, ORMs fought us, so we leaned on the built-in node:sqlite — and learned the hard way never to delete the dev database file out from under a running server. Keeping the agent out of the trust boundary. The hardest design rule was also the most important: security never rests on the agent. A manipulated agent can ask "give me a hint?" — and get nothing, because the server, not the agent, decides. What we learned That the most interesting property of WebMCP isn't automation — it's that a site can hand an agent a narrow, honest surface of actions while keeping its secrets and its decisions to itself. Prove it without revealing it. What's next Assisted returns (scheduling, contact), match alerts, and a fully agent-driven end-to-end journey from "I lost my bag" to "return arranged." title: Agent-Ready Palm Desert
pitch: AICV is building the Agent Ready City layer. A structured, searchable map that AI agents can use to answer real questions about visiting and relocating. This is the WebMCP City of Palm Desert MVP.
about_excerpt: AICV is building the Agent Ready City layer. A structured, searchable map that AI agents can use to answer real questions about visiting and relocating. This is the WebMCP City of Palm Desert MVP. Like Comment Story Updates Home page Agent cards Agent itinerary Inspiration Most relocations do not begin with a moving truck. They begin with a visit. A founder starts wondering whether life—and perhaps part of the company—might work somewhere else. The founding team comes for a retreat. They tour a few workspaces, meet local people, try to understand the talent base, and pay attention to what an ordinary Tuesday morning might feel like. The Coachella Valley is already familiar to millions of people because of Coachella, the Indian Wells tennis tournament, Modernism Week, and the Palm Springs International Film Festival. People know how to visit here. What they do not necessarily know is how to evaluate the region as a place to build a company, open a satellite office, or begin the next chapter of their lives. The web does not make that decision particularly easy. Search engines and even capable AI agents tend to return familiar hotels, attractions, rankings, and generic itineraries. For the judgment that actually matters, people still call someone local: a commercial real estate agent, an economic development director, or a hospitality operator who knows the area. That human guidance is valuable, but a consequential decision can end up depending on whichever local person happens to answer the call. For the past year, AICV has been mapping businesses, institutions, places, and local signals across the nine-city Coachella Valley so agents can understand the region more accurately. Along the way, we discovered that the technical work was only half the challenge. Local businesses are already surrounded by noise from Google, Facebook, Yelp, Yext, Foursquare, and a growing number of consultants promising that AEO is the new SEO. Expecting every restaurant, hotel, university, workspace, and civic institution to understand the agentic web—and independently restructure itself for it—is technically possible, but culturally unrealistic. At the same time, world-scale platforms are attempting to understand and “agentify” millions of places around the globe. They can provide enormous reach, but they cannot easily capture every local distinction: whether two places are genuinely close, whether an institution requires an introduction, whether a supposed innovation district is a finished ecosystem or still a promising collection of institutions, or whether a recommendation makes sense for the particular human asking. That is where we believe WebMCP changes the equation. Instead of waiting for every local entity to become agent-ready on its own, a trusted regional layer can organize the local context and expose it directly to agents as usable tools. The agent no longer has to scrape a directory, infer meaning from buttons, or assemble a decision from generic search results. It can ask the region for a city brief, search locally curated intelligence, compare options, check routes and constraints, build a scouting itinerary, and prepare the next step for human approval. Getting a region ready starts with getting one city ready. We chose Palm Desert because it sits at the center of the Coachella Valley and brings together many of the ingredients a founder or executive would need to evaluate: business support, universities and workforce, retreat infrastructure, hospitality, culture, coffee, outdoor life, and future growth. For this Challenge, we took a deliberately small corpus of AICV’s mapped Palm Desert intelligence and asked a focused question: Could WebMCP help an AI agent deliver something closer to the judgment of a trusted local—not merely tell someone what is here, but help them imagine whether they could build part of their life here? Agent-Ready Palm Desert is our first answer. What it does Agent-Ready Palm Desert helps a founder or executive evaluate Palm Desert for a leadership retreat, satellite office, relocation, or longer-term build path. A person can explore the website directly. Through five WebMCP tools, an AI agent can use the same local intelligence to: Understand the city Search relevant places and institutions Open individual Agent Previews Compare several options Build a route-aware scouting itinerary Prepare an inquiry for human approval - manual The demonstration uses 22 source-linked Palm Desert records. Each Agent Preview separates the official facts from AICV’s local judgment: why the place matters, when it should be considered, and what constraint the agent must preserve. That local context changes the answer. Rutina Coffee may be a good quiet-coffee stop, for example, but it is not walkable from the Entrepreneurship Resource Center. The routing tool identifies approximately 5.5 miles and ten minutes by car. The result is closer to a white-glove relocation conversation than a generic travel itinerary. It helps someone ask not only, “What is in Palm Desert?” but, “Could my team and I actually imagine ourselves here?” How we built it We built Agent-Ready Palm Desert as a standalone ChatGPT Site using React and TypeScript. Its WebMCP tools are registered directly in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool() . The visible interface and the agent tools use the same underlying data and decision logic, so the human and agent are not working from two different versions of Palm Desert. The corpus is stored as structured JSON with source links, geographic information, access conditions, local signals, and comparison guidance. Routing uses OpenStreetMap road data through OSRM. Five tools are read-only. The sixth will prepare an inquiry or update request, but it cannot send one. It returns sent: false and requires human confirmation. Currently not enabled. AICV’s regional mapping and source material began before the Challenge. During the Challenge, we turned a focused portion of that work into a standalone WebMCP experience with six callable tools, structured Agent Previews, shared human-agent workflows, routing safeguards, and a confirmation-gated handoff. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was not registering five tools. It was deciding what an agent needs to know before it should make a recommendation about a real place. Local knowledge is full of distinctions that rarely survive conventional search. Two places may sound nearby but be several miles apart. A resource may be valuable but require an appointment or introduction. An area may be described as an innovation corridor while still functioning as a collection of institutions rather than a finished, walkable district. We had to convert those human observations into structured intelligence without presenting AICV’s judgment as an official fact. A second challenge was scope. The Coachella Valley contains thousands of businesses and institutions across nine cities. Trying to make every entity independently WebMCP-ready would reproduce the same adoption problem we had already encountered. For this experiment, we chose a much smaller question: could one regional intelligence layer make one city meaningfully easier for an agent to understand? The final challenge was trust. We wanted the agent to be useful without allowing it to overstate live conditions, overlook access restrictions, or take action before the human was ready. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project became a complete human-agent decision experience rather than simply a technical demonstration. The public Site works without an account. All five WebMCP tools are discoverable and functional. The human interface and agent tools share the same 22-record corpus, and every recommendation remains connected to a source, a local explanation, and something the user may need to verify. We are especially proud that the system knows where to stop. It can research, compare, route, and prepare—but the consequential next step remains with the human. What we learned We learned that making a place agent-ready is not primarily a website problem or a listings problem. It is a context problem. Global platforms are very good at indexing enormous amounts of information. Local intelligence layers can contribute something different: the lived distinctions, constraints, relationships, and judgment that make the information useful for a particular human decision. We also learned that expecting every local business to independently adapt to every new AI platform is unlikely to work. A shared regional layer may be a more practical approach. It can organize local truth once and make it available to multiple agents through a common interface such as WebMCP. Most importantly, we learned that constraints are part of the answer. “Not walkable,” “appointment required,” “not live traffic,” and “not yet sent” are not disclaimers added after the recommendation. They are part of what makes the recommendation tr

title: SharableWorlds
pitch: An agent that builds with you, not for you.
about_excerpt: An agent that builds with you, not for you. Like 1 Comment Story Updates SharableWorlds A 3D miniature studio in the browser, where you and an agent build on the same canvas. What inspired me I was tired of the usual AI 3D demo: you type a prompt, a pile of objects appears, and you’re left wondering if it actually understood what you asked for. There’s no real way to work with the scene. You just watch it happen. WebMCP clicked for me because the page can be what the agent uses, not some API off to the side. Tools live on the site. A person can still be there, placing pieces, locking lots, arguing with the result. I wanted that to feel what we were accustomed to. A grid. A bunch of assets. You say "a harbor," or you drop a boat yourself, and the agent has to work in that same language. How I built it Everything runs in the browser. Next.js as a static export, React, Three.js for the isometric view, Zustand for the world. It deploys on a Cloudflare Worker. No login. Nothing on a server that "is" the scene. When the page loads it registers tools on document.modelContext . If something changes the world, it goes through one of those tools. Surprise Me button, share, the kit assets, and a connected agent all hit the same functions. Three.js only reads the state, the agent never talks to the renderer. I made the agent go through and follow a sequence instead of dumping pieces: get_occupancy → plan_scene → compose_scene → populate_zones → create_environment → inspect → validate_scene → repair_scene It thinks in lots ( C4 ), zones ( picnic ), and things like "east of the grill." validate_scene scores the result on six dimensions. Done means the score is high enough, not that a bunch of calls returned in an ok state. The assets are Kenney , CC0. Roughly 1,800 pieces in 22 packs. What I learned An agent can call place_piece 47 times and still not build a picnic. I had been treating a successful tool call as progress. It is not. I ended up scoring the scene and handing back repairs, otherwise it would stop early and look finished. Coordinates were a dead end. "Put this in the picnic zone, facing the grill" is something a model can actually use. (12.4, 0, -3.1) is not. If the agent can knock over what you just placed, you are not collaborating. That is why locks on human placed pieces and "build on this" matter as much as the fancy compose step. WebMCP being the only write path was annoying at first and then useful. I also needed to see what it was doing. The Details panel, the trace, the percentage all dove into what was happening behind the scenes. Otherwise it still feels like a black box, just a prettier one. Challenges I faced The first version technically used WebMCP and still sprayed pieces. My own runner was looping place_piece so the cursor had something to do. The model got a paragraph of instructions instead of a real sequence. Validation was so loose a picnic with no table could score 100. So I split it up. plan_scene does not mutate anything. Layout and objects are compose_scene and populate_zones . Twenty rules, each with a { tool, args, why } if it fails. repair_scene runs those. build_scene is the whole loop for hosts that will not steer. extend_scene is there because "add a harbor" should not delete the village. Then the small stuff started breaking the feeling of it. The cursor spawned under the kit and jumped when the camera moved. An empty board still looked like leftover scenery. You could not rotate the view. Share links replay a seed, which I wanted, until a leftover test URL made it look like a default world had kept rendering. Most of those bugs were the same issue: the person and the agent are looking at one stage. If that stage is lying, the whole thing falls apart. Getting registerTool working was the easy part. The work was making the tools a language two sides can share, and knowing when the harbor is actually a harbor. title: AI-slop-check
pitch: Catching AI slop requires zero AI. Twelve rules, runs in your browser, and your agent can swipe through the findings with you
about_excerpt: Catching AI slop requires zero AI. Twelve rules, runs in your browser, and your agent can swipe through the findings with you Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I vibe-code a lot. And a lot of what comes back is slop. Not broken code. Code that looks finished. A catch block that swallows the error so nothing ever turns red. A comment that says // In a real implementation, validate this sitting exactly where the validation should be. A default that no caller has ever overridden, because the model invented a knob nobody asked for. It runs. It passes. It is not done. My usual fix for this was to paste the file into a better model and ask it to look. Which works, and costs tokens, and takes a minute, and I have done it for mistakes that a grep would have caught. That felt stupid enough to build around. So slop-check has no AI in it. Twelve rules, plain text matching, one pass over the source. It scans a repo, a diff, or a pull request and hands back a 0-100 score, a grade, and every hit quoted as file:line . Instant, offline, deterministic, and the same input gives the same output forever. The scoring is deliberately boring so you can argue with it: $$\text{score} = \min\left(100,\ \frac{100 \times \sum_{r} w_r \cdot d(h_r)}{1000 \times \max(L_{\text{eff}},\ 420)}\right)$$ where $w_r$ is a rule's weight, $h_r$ its hit count, $d$ a damping function so one repeated house idiom cannot fail a whole codebase, and $L_{\text{eff}}$ the effective scanned lines. --explain prints that arithmetic per run. No black box to trust. why it is a card game A wall of 200 findings is a linter, and linters get disabled. So findings come back as a deck you swipe. Left says the finding is fair. Right says it is a false positive, and disputed cards come back out as slop-disable directives you paste into your code, which the CLI and the GitHub Action then honour on every later run. Your disagreement becomes configuration instead of a shrug. There is also a confession mode on the share card. It stamps YES, I WROTE THIS WITH AI on the image. Everyone is doing it. The pretending is the annoying part. It has already earned its keep on repos much larger than mine. Pointed at openai/openai-python (1,542 files) it surfaced real findings, and the same run surfaced six defects in my own rules. what I actually learned A scanner's most important property is staying quiet. I spent most of my time not adding rules. I read every finding on a large, well-written repo by hand and asked whether a maintainer would act on it. 61 findings became 12. None of the six bugs I found this way would have surfaced from unit tests, because every rule passed its own fixtures. Some of them were embarrassing in a useful way. dead-defaults split parameter lists on bare commas, so a comma inside dict[str, Any] invented parameters that did not exist. happy-path-only matched \bopen( , which caught tarfile.open() and wave.open() and read every with open(...) as unhandled I/O, when a context manager is the failure path. duplicate-helper flagged every f / async_f pair in an async library at 95% similarity, which is a Python constraint and not a mistake. swallowed-error flagged __del__ , where suppressing exceptions is correct and the tool was asking for the code to be made worse. And the one I liked most: every rule read prose as code. A rule that matches source text will happily match a sentence describing the pattern it looks for. This repo scored itself a grade worse because two of its own explanatory comments contain .catch(() => {}) . Comments are masked before matching now. Each of those is pinned in test/false-positives.test.ts , which exists for one job: keep fixed rules fixed. Then WebMCP. I liked it immediately, and for a reason that is more about how I work than about the spec. I am usually looking at a page and I want my agent looking at the same page. Not a copy of it, not a scrape of it, the actual thing in front of me. And half the time I am lazy and would rather ask than click, but I still want to watch it happen. Every other integration shape makes you pick one: either the agent works somewhere you cannot see, or you do it yourself. WebMCP is the first one where the agent presses the buttons you can see it pressing. how I built it One TypeScript source ships three things: the slop-check CLI, a GitHub Action, and the web app. The rules run in a Web Worker in the tab, so a scan never uploads your code anywhere. The WebMCP layer is web/webmcp.ts . Seven tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool() : list_rules , explain_rule , scan_repository , scan_diff , list_findings , judge_finding , export_suppressions . The rule I gave myself was that the tool layer owns no state at all. It gets a small handle assembled in main.ts out of the exact functions the click handlers call. There is no second code path, so there is no way for an agent to reach a result the page is not showing, or to record a verdict the deck does not reflect. A tool-driven scan fills the visible input, flips the visible tab, and runs the same progress panel a click does. Three tools are meaningless before a scan exists, so they are not registered until one lands and are unregistered when results clear, using the AbortSignal that registerTool takes as its second argument. The page emits its own state event, the WebMCP layer syncs registration to it, the browser fires toolchange . An agent reading the tool list is reading the page's real state rather than a manifest. Cancellation is threaded all the way down. execute receives a signal , it reaches githubFiles and every fetch under it, composed with the existing per-request timeout through AbortSignal.any . challenges False positives, by a distance. Everything above about the openai-python pass was the hard part of the project, not a footnote to it. It is still not fully solved. hardcoded-config is my noisiest rule and I will tell you exactly how: it flags process.env.SITE_URL || 'https://example.com' , which is a literal inside an environment-variable fallback, which is the configuration it is demanding. It flags a project's own canonical URL, which belongs in a sitemap. swallowed-error still cannot tell recovery from silence, so .catch(() => null) whose value gets branched on reads the same to it as a bare .catch(() => {}) . Both get reported. One is a fallback and one is a shrug. I also know the rule set came from my intuition rather than data. There is empirical work on LLM code smells finding magic numbers and missing documentation most over-represented, which barely overlaps with my twelve rules, and their method is better than mine: compare a codebase's smell profile against a human-written baseline instead of scoring it alone. Deciding how far the agent gets to reach. My first version let judge_finding walk the whole deck and decide everything. Technically better tool use. Completely wrong product. An agent that judges every card has replaced the user, and the verdict was the only part I wanted a human doing. The shipped version can move one card the user can see, one verdict at a time, and the tool's own description tells the agent to ask first. Judging out of order. The deck is a stack, but an agent asked about one specific rule wants that card now, not in fourteen swipes. Re-rendering the stack broke the animation on cards already leaving, so swapToFront swaps the rendered contents of two positions instead. The deck's order was a sampling artefact, never meaning, so nothing is lost. what it does not claim slop-check cannot tell you code was written by an AI and does not try. There is no reliable authorship signal in source text and anything claiming otherwise is guessing. It measures whether code carries the patterns that AI-assisted code carries more often. A human can write all of them, and I regularly do. Read the score as a description of the code, never as an accusation about who wrote it. title: AIEndpoint - Service Discovery for the Agentic Web
pitch: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. An open standard and live registry that lets browser agents discover which service can do the job before they ever navigate.
about_excerpt: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. An open standard and live registry that lets browser agents discover which service can do the job before they ever navigate. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP integration docs: declare support in your manifest, promote it into page tools with @aiendpoint/webmcp DemoWeather: live Open-Meteo data. WebMCP tools generated from its /.well-known/ai manifest update this card when an agent calls them aiendpoint.dev - the open /ai standard: ~800 tokens of pure signal instead of 10k-50k tokens of page noise Registry search results with the ⚡ WebMCP badge - DemoWeather (verified, score 100) tops the results agents and humans both see Real Chrome with the WebMCP flag: tools registered, executeTool call received - the visible counter proves the loop works Inspiration WebMCP gives an agent structured tools for the page it is already on. But watching agents work, we kept hitting the step that comes before that: which page should the agent open in the first place? An agent that needs weather data or a currency rate still guesses URLs or scrapes search results. We had been building that missing step for months: AIEndpoint, an open standard where any site publishes a capability manifest at /.well-known/ai (an IETF Internet-Draft), plus a live registry indexing thousands of services. When WebMCP appeared, the two ideas snapped together: AIEndpoint finds the right website. WebMCP operates it. We are honest with ourselves: an independent project like this may never become the standard. The giants are drafting their own, and there is only so far one person can push. But robots.txt also started with one individual and an idea the web happened to need. We simply wanted to cut the traffic LLM agents waste crawling site after site just to figure out what each one can do - and we entered this challenge hoping more people will join us. What it does On aiendpoint.dev , an in-browser agent calls find_services ("a weather service with no auth"). The results the agent receives render as cards on the page the human is looking at. select_service opens the detail view with a live "Open service" link. One click later, on weather.aiendpoint.dev , the agent calls current_weather and the weather card in front of the user updates with live Open-Meteo data. Human and agent share one screen at every step. Nothing happens in a hidden console: every tool call has a visible consequence on the page. Before WebMCP, a service directory for agents could only be a server-side HTTP API, unreachable exactly where users work. Now discovery, selection, and execution all happen inside one browsing session, visibly shared between the user and the agent. How we built it @aiendpoint/webmcp (new package, ESM + IIFE): promotes a site's /.well-known/ai manifest into WebMCP tools. Tool names, descriptions, and JSON input schemas are derived from the manifest: the spec's compact parameter notation ( "string, required -- city name" ) is parsed into schema types and required lists. Execution stays in explicit per-capability handlers, so a site never exposes anything it did not consciously wire up. aiendpoint.dev (Next.js) registers find_services / select_service on every page; tool calls navigate the visible UI. A /webmcp/ping diagnostics page reports the browser's actual WebMCP surface and shows a live call counter. DemoWeather (FastAPI) serves its manifest, loads the adapter's IIFE bundle, and wires three handlers that drive the page's weather card, backed by live Open-Meteo data with a labeled stale-cache fallback. Challenges we ran into The API surface is still moving. Registration probes document.modelContext , navigator.modelContext (now deprecated), and older entry points, preferring registerTool with AbortSignal cleanup. We learned by experiment that executeTool takes the registered tool object plus a JSON string , so our handlers normalize both parsed objects and raw strings. provideContext replaces the whole tool set on every call , so independent components clobbered each other until we kept a page-wide union of registered tools. React Strict Mode silently unregistered tools in development via the register/cleanup/register cycle until we made registration fully idempotent. Making discovery honest: we rewrote our registry search to match capability keywords against descriptions, and fixed count/filter bugs the new browser-driven usage exposed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The full loop is verified in a real browser , not just designed: tool registration, an actual executeTool call, and a visible UI change on the page. The discovery chain runs on live production data : the registry indexes 3,600+ services, and DemoWeather registers itself, passes our own validator at 100/100, and tops the "weather" search results agents actually see. One adapter call makes any /.well-known/ai site agent-operable - schemas included - while keeping execution in explicit handlers the site controls. We migrated the entire platform (registry, validator, CLI, MCP server, three demos, and every framework adapter) to the well-known location during the hackathon window, and cleared all 71 dependency audit vulnerabilities while we were at it. What we learned ogfooding an open spec against a second standard is the fastest way to find its weak points. Migrating /ai to /.well-known/ai (draft-01), parsing our own compact notation into JSON Schema, and watching a real browser call our tools taught us more in three days than months of design. What's next for AIEndpoint - Service Discovery for the Agentic Web Schema-typed params in spec v1.1, mutations with confirmation UI, auth-scoped tools, and a "WebMCP-ready" tier on the registry's verification badge, so agents can filter for sites that are operable , not just discoverable. Built With cloudflare esbuild fastapi fastify next.js open-meteo python react redis supabase typescript vercel webmcp Try it out www.aiendpoint.dev weather.aiendpoint.dev github.com www.aiendpoint.dev Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo builder. I created the /ai spec, the registry, and the site before the hackathon, and built everything WebMCP during the submission period: the @aiendpoint/webmcp adapter, the registry's find_services/select_service tools, the DemoWeather page, and an in-page agent that drives the tools with natural language. WebMCP was so new that its API surface changed mid-hackathon - reverse-engineering executeTool in the DevTools console at 2am was intimidating, but watching a model call my page's tools and the UI react for the first time made it all worth it. I paired heavily with AI coding agents throughout, which felt fitting for a project about making the web agent-ready. title: Recovery Radar
pitch: An agent that finds money your transactions should have returned.
about_excerpt:
An agent that finds money your transactions should have returned.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for Recovery Radar 

 Inspiration 

 People lose money because a delay, cancellation, outage, failed delivery, cancelled subscription or provider promise is rarely matched back to the transaction that should have been settled. Recovery Radar turns that missed connection into a reviewable recovery lead. 

 What it does 

 Recovery Radar looks for a verifiable gap between a purchase or booking, an incident or provider promise, the applicable rule, and the final settlement. It then prepares the next step for the person to review. 

 The demo covers three synthetic recovery leads: 

 
 a transport delay with a possible EUR 400 compensation; 
 a subscription cancelled before a later EUR 17.99 charge; and 
 a telecom outage with a possible EUR 20 service credit. 
 

 The product is intentionally not a chatbot that writes a generic complaint. It builds an evidence chain and shows why a recovery may exist. 

 Why WebMCP 

 This workflow normally spans several web surfaces: a booking or receipt, transport or provider records, a policy page, a billing record and a claim workspace. WebMCP gives the agent a structured way to discover and operate the meaningful actions exposed by the page. 

 Recovery Radar registers seven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool: 

 
 scan_for_recoverable_money 
 select_recovery_case 
 inspect_recovery_evidence 
 prepare_recovery_claim 
 approve_recovery_workspace 
 reconcile_recovery 
 reset_recovery_demo 
 

 These represent the product operations: discover, select, prove, prepare, approve and reconcile. The tools validate inputs, preserve an audit trail and keep external submission behind a human approval boundary. 

 What people and agents do together 

 The agent performs the repetitive discovery and evidence assembly. The person chooses the scope, reviews the proof, confirms the amount and decides whether to open the prepared workspace. Preparation can be agent-assisted, but submission and money handling remain outside the project. 

 How it was built 

 Recovery Radar is a local-first static web application built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It uses synthetic cases and deterministic state transitions so the complete flow can be tested safely. The main challenge was making WebMCP meaningful instead of decorative: each registered tool maps to a real product operation and produces visible evidence or state changes. 

 Impact and scope 

 Recovery Radar starts with transport, subscriptions, purchases and paid services, where the evidence chain can be made concrete without immediately entering higher-risk areas such as banking, insurance or litigation. 

 How to test 

 Open the live demo in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Ask: 

 “Scan for recoverable money, select the highest-confidence transport case, inspect its evidence, and prepare the claim packet. Do not approve or submit anything.” 

 The expected result is three findings, EUR 437.99 in synthetic potential recovery, and a transport lead for EUR 400. Review the evidence, prepare the packet and approve the local workspace manually. No provider form is submitted and no funds are handled. 

 Disclosure 

 All records and amounts in the demo are synthetic. The project makes no provider requests, does not use credentials, does not send claims and does not receive money.

title: API Canvas
pitch: API Canvas is a local-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents can discover public data, connect APIs,create reusable cards and visualizations,and reason across the resulting dashboard together.
about_excerpt: API Canvas is a local-first WebMCP workspace where people and agents can discover public data, connect APIs,create reusable cards and visualizations,and reason across the resulting dashboard together. Like Comment Story Updates Api Canvas build a dashboard Canvas View Inspiration Building a useful dashboard usually involves a surprising amount of repetitive work. You have to find an API, understand its documentation, construct the request, inspect the response, identify useful fields, create a visualization, connect those fields to a component, and repeat the process for every additional source. I wanted to see whether WebMCP could make that process dramatically more direct. Instead of only asking: "Can an agent operate this application?" API Canvas asks: "Can an agent help construct the application experience using primitives the website intentionally exposes?" What I Built API Canvas is a local-first workspace for turning public data into reusable connected cards. A dashboard can contain components such as: Tables Charts Maps Metrics Lists Notes Text and explanation blocks Search results Media Raw datasets API responses Question blocks Agent-generated answer blocks Sources and presentation are kept separate. That means one API response can power several different visualizations without repeatedly requesting the data. Users can also transform and combine information through declarative mappings including filtering, sorting, grouping, arithmetic, field selection, and joins. WebMCP Tools API Canvas exposes a large WebMCP tool surface covering dashboard and data workflows. An agent can perform operations such as: Create or switch dashboards Add data sources Request public API data Add cards Select appropriate visualizations Connect source fields to cards Transform data Update layout Resize or reorder cards Inspect dashboard state Read selected cards Answer questions using dashboard context Create new explanation blocks Export or present results This lets a simple request expand into a multi-step application workflow. For example: Build me an earthquake research dashboard. Find magnitude 5 or greater earthquakes from the past week, map the events, create a table, identify the strongest earthquake, and summarize it. API Canvas can break that request into structured operations and leave behind a real editable dashboard. Why WebMCP Dashboard construction is naturally compositional. The user usually knows the outcome they want but should not need to manually specify every intermediate API call and UI operation. WebMCP lets the application expose those intermediate operations directly. The agent gets structured tools instead of having to simulate: click Add Card → select source → open another menu → map a field → choose visualization → repeat. This makes workflows faster and substantially easier for an agent to reason about. Human + Agent Collaboration The most interesting part of API Canvas is that the resulting dashboard becomes shared context. Imagine the agent has created an earthquake dashboard containing a map, table, and several metrics. The user can then ask: Using all of the information currently on this page, which earthquake was strongest? The agent can inspect the existing structured cards, reason across them, produce an answer, and create another normal dashboard card containing that explanation. The workflow becomes: Data → Visualization → Context → Reasoning → New Visualization Everything remains editable by the human. How I Built It API Canvas is built with Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, IndexedDB, ECharts, AJV, and WebMCP. The workspace has a reusable block system that separates: data sources raw responses normalized values transformations bindings presentation The normal UI and WebMCP tools call into the same underlying workspace actions. AJV validates structured WebMCP inputs. IndexedDB stores larger browser-local response caches and workspace information. Public data adapters support structured formats including JSON, CSV, XML, feeds, permitted HTML tables, and embedded JSON. The application intentionally does not provide an unrestricted proxy or execute arbitrary supplied scripts. The /webmcp documentation page is generated from the same canonical WebMCP contracts used by the application. Challenges I Faced The largest challenge was building something generic without making it unpredictable. An unrestricted "call any API and run any code" tool would be powerful but would also make the application difficult to reason about. Instead, API Canvas uses bounded requests, validated schemas, explicit source handling, and declarative transformations. Another challenge was keeping data, provenance, presentation, and transformations sufficiently independent. That separation is what allows an agent to replace a chart with a table without losing the underlying source. What I Learned API Canvas changed how I think about agent interfaces. The visual dashboard does not need to be replaced by chat. Instead, the dashboard can become the persistent shared artifact that the human and agent construct together. WebMCP then acts as the structured editing and orchestration layer. What's Next I would like to expand API Canvas with more public data adapters, richer visualization components, reusable dashboard templates, local analytical queries, and collaborative sharing. The broader idea is an open, composable workspace where agents can assemble useful specialized interfaces on demand. title: Origami Gratis
pitch: I stopped asking how to make agents work with Office and started asking why Office still exists. Origami: deck, doc, sketch and chart as one HTML file, authored over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: I stopped asking how to make agents work with Office and started asking why Office still exists. Origami: deck, doc, sketch and chart as one HTML file, authored over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Have clean reports instantly Agents and humans can make together. No more need for MS Visio A Hub of MCP's that will keep growing Why cant my Spreadsheet be in my Presentation My document can be my spreadsheet And i can choose what in that sheet is shown in the presentation Validated working with GPT Cloud Browser Inspiration When a new technology arrives, we ask "how do I make it work with the old thing?" almost never do we ask "does the old thing deserve a future?" I hit this thought when making agents try to make the perfect PowerPoint at work. Why am I parsing zipped XML from two decades ago? Why is it three separate programs? Why can't my presentation have the document as a Slide? why cant i have a full spreadsheet in my report? What the hell is Visio? Surely we can combine Excel, PowerPoint and Word into one tool by now? Also, I find HTML presentations just look way more professional — anyone can scrape together a PowerPoint, but a slick HTML deck? Far less… until now. And that's why I built Origami Folio, my eyes set on a Chrome extension because it was the best way for agent and human to work together. That was until I randomly saw a post about this hackathon and WebMCP. What it does Origami Folio is a full next-generation Office suite built in HTML. Make presentations, word documents and spreadsheets from scratch. The word document doesn't link to the spreadsheet or paste a picture of it — it's in the document! And it all saves to a single file that opens in any browser around the world, ready to present and edit further. The Chrome extension version already allowed MCP control, but it required the extension. With this version, agents just need a website — they can make everything, save it, open files and resume where they left off. How we built it WebMCP is new enough that we measured most of it ourselves. The launch flag isn't documented — we found --enable-features=WebMCP by string-searching chrome.dll. Chrome silently drops destructiveHint , so every destructive warning had to move into the description itself. inputSchema arrives as a string. Halfway through, Chrome 152 removed navigator.modelContext under our feet. Challenges we ran into The hardest design work was honest saving: a page can't just write to your disk. So save_deck reports exactly which of three things happened: a real write through a file handle, a backstop copy in the browser's own storage, a started download. It never says "saved" when it can't verify bytes landed. Agents are also blind without native vision — not an issue for OpenAI models, but I want it supportable by all models. So inspect_render lays the deck out off-screen and reports the geometry — including the fold that validated perfectly and rendered as nothing. Accomplishments that we're proud of An agent with no prior knowledge of Origami self-onboards from one origami_guide call and builds a complete deck. Venn diagrams, sketches, charts, flowcharts, Gantts — all unattended, through Chrome's own WebMCP surface. No mocks, no shim. The demo video is 54 native executeTool calls, and the file it produces plays on double-click, full screen, forever. This isn't a demo of a concept — it's something users can keep coming back to again and again as part of their tech stack. What we learned WebMCP inverts distribution. Instead of installing your tools into the agent, the page hands its tools to whatever agent shows up. Distribution becomes easy it's all self-contained. Once it's loaded, an agent can call the tools once or a million times and it costs me nothing either way. (Unless agents reload the page every time, which they don't need to — then I'd be thankful for Cloudflare Pages' generous scaling.) What's next for Origami Gratis Honestly, my mission statement has been the same from the start: I want to displace Microsoft Office. People, AI and the future of tech should not be beholden to the dead weight of a 25-year-old solution of zipped XML files masquerading as three different executables — and then paying extra for Visio. WebMCP is new, and because I saw this hackathon late I only had three days to port this — so I'll keep polishing the experience and adding features until it holds full parity with the extension. Anything your agent can make, you can edit; anything you make, the agent can pick up. Origami Gratis will be my hub: each petal added to the flower is a new WebMCP tool, until Origami Gratis is known as one of the go-to libraries of tooling for all agents.
