title: Gridfall
pitch: One city. One hospital. One chance. GRIDFALL turns WebMCP into a real-time crisis room where a human and an AI agent diagnose cascading failures and restore ICU power together.
about_excerpt: One city. One hospital. One chance. GRIDFALL turns WebMCP into a real-time crisis room where a human and an AI agent diagnose cascading failures and restore ICU power together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Critical infrastructure is not a collection of isolated switches. A hospital depends on power, protection systems, data, water, transport access, emergency crews, and decisions made elsewhere in the city. During a cascading failure, the difficult part is not clicking a button—it is understanding which action is safe before the remaining time and redundancy disappear. Most browser agents face an uncomfortable choice: infer important state from pixels and page text, or receive enough authority to act without a meaningful human checkpoint. We built GRIDFALL to explore a third model: the website exposes structured, purpose-built capabilities to an agent, the agent helps a person reason under pressure, and the person remains responsible for consequential actions. What it does GRIDFALL is a real-time city-grid crisis simulation centered on one urgent objective: restore protected power to St Anne ICU before its generator reserve expires. Each mission draws one of 100 validated incident configurations. After a short pre-blackout countdown, infrastructure across the city begins failing. The operator sees an interactive top-down map of power, protection, data, road, water, and emergency-response dependencies, but the correct recovery sequence is never revealed. A WebMCP-capable agent can inspect the live city state, check the hospital, and review the operations that are currently possible. It can then explain the likely benefit, time cost, and systemic risk of one action. In Challenge mode, the agent can only propose the operation: GRIDFALL queues it in Mission Control and waits for the human operator to authorize or reject it. The city does not change until that approval happens. Every authorized decision advances time and can change several connected systems at once. A seemingly useful action may remove telemetry, block an ambulance corridor, consume the only mobile battery, or reconnect the hospital to an unresolved fault. If the remaining recovery path is destroyed, the mission ends immediately instead of making the player wait for a meaningless countdown. Why WebMCP GRIDFALL is designed around collaboration that would be fragile or impossible through ordinary screen reading. The map is optimized for people; the WebMCP tools provide the agent with the same live situation as structured, typed data. This eliminates guesswork about labels, colors, hidden panels, and changing visual state. The experience separates observation, recommendation, and authority. Read-only tools let the agent build situational awareness. The action tool creates a visible proposal. The human sees its consequences and makes the final decision. That boundary is the product, not an afterthought. This pattern applies beyond a game. Industrial dashboards, operations centers, financial workflows, and administrative systems can expose meaningful capabilities to agents while keeping high-impact actions inspectable and under human control. How we implemented WebMCP GRIDFALL registers six browser-native tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : get_city_state returns the current incident, infrastructure status, field clues, and recovery progress. inspect_hospital_status returns ICU demand, protected supply, generator reserve, patients, telemetry, access, cooling water, and active blockers. list_grid_actions returns the currently available operations with their time cost, benefit, risk, and current availability. take_grid_action creates a human-reviewable proposal in Challenge mode. start_random_incident draws a validated mission and starts the pre-blackout sequence. reset_mission safely returns the simulation to standby. The tools never expose the hidden solution or complete dependency order. The agent must reason from observable evidence, just like the operator. Tool results include structured content so the client can use state reliably instead of parsing prose. How we built it GRIDFALL is a client-side React 19 and TypeScript application built with Vinext and deployed on ChatGPT Sites through Cloudflare Workers. The simulation engine models incident generation, dependencies, action resolution, irreversible consequences, win conditions, and early failure detection. The interface renders the city map, live hospital metrics, recovery history, onboarding, Czech and English localization, audio, and the human-authorization flow. We also built a deterministic audit that exercises the complete catalogue of 100 missions and checks that every scenario is solvable, non-trivial, and consistent with critical rules such as battery exclusivity and dependency ordering. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was deciding how much information to expose. If a tool returned the hidden sequence, the agent would merely read the answer. If it returned too little, the agent would be forced back into visual guessing. We iterated on the schemas until they described evidence, risks, and current possibilities without leaking the solution. We also had to make infrastructure consequences feel logical. Early versions allowed trivial action sequences or visually implied connections that did not match the game rules. We repeatedly rebuilt the dependency graph, map layout, failure conditions, and action descriptions so the simulation communicates why a decision helped or harmed the ICU. Finally, we treated human authorization as a real state boundary. An agent proposal must not silently mutate the simulation, become stale, or be reported as completed before the operator approves it. Accomplishments A complete, playable crisis simulation rather than a single-purpose tool demo Six working WebMCP tools with structured outputs and clear authority boundaries 100 automatically validated incident configurations Explicit human authorization for consequential agent actions Immediate, explainable consequences across interconnected city systems An interactive map with traceable power, protection, data, and access relationships English and Czech localization, onboarding, accessible controls, and sound design A public MIT-licensed repository with no API keys, account, database, or custom agent backend required What we learned The most important lesson was that a tool schema is part of the user experience. Good agent integration is not just a function name and JSON input; it requires carefully designed observability, understandable consequences, and an explicit model of who is allowed to do what. WebMCP made it possible to build one interface for two different strengths: humans understand the spatial story and remain accountable, while agents can rapidly compare structured state and dependencies. The result is stronger than either a conventional dashboard or an autonomous agent acting alone. What's next We would expand GRIDFALL with additional cities, incident families, replayable decision audits, accessibility modes, and scenario-authoring tools for training. The same architecture could also support safe demonstrations using real or synthetic operational telemetry while preserving the proposal-and-authorization boundary at the heart of the project. title: Socialsum
pitch: Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes.
about_excerpt: Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Socialsum Socialsum — important work, without the meeting Tagline Shared decision rooms where people and their own agents turn scattered input into attributable outcomes. Inspiration Many meetings exist because information, judgment, and authority are trapped in different places. People repeat status, agents work in isolated chats, and the actual decision disappears into a summary nobody can reliably resume from. We wanted a workspace designed around a better unit of collaboration: one bounded problem, an explicit constitution, named required inputs, visible blockers, a deadline, and a decision record. What it does Socialsum lets a person create or join a Problem Room for a decision, investigation, policy, technical RFC, or operational workflow. Participants add evidence, proposals, objections, files, and required inputs. Their own agents can use WebMCP to understand the room, catch up on changes, research and prepare work, compare proposals, and submit versioned change sets. The centerpiece demo replaces a weekly operations meeting. An agent reads the live decision brief, finds the remaining urgent-decision blocker, resumes from a durable checkpoint, and prepares a scoped operating-rule change. A reviewer sees the exact semantic diff. The agent can request review, but only an authorized person can approve and adopt the change. Why WebMCP is essential This workflow depends on an outside agent understanding and acting on the same live state as several people. Screen scraping would force the agent to infer IDs, roles, deadlines, versions, and consequences from pixels. A chat-only assistant would lose the group record and could not safely resume another participant's work. WebMCP gives Socialsum typed actions over durable domain objects. Contextual discovery exposes a small bootstrap pack, then replaces it with focused tools based on sign-in, the current room, and the selected tab. Tools return room versions, provenance, blockers, permissions, and recoverable errors. The result is not “AI inside a dashboard”; it is an open workspace that each participant's agent can join safely. Better human-agent UX Agents handle breadth: orientation, catch-up, evidence synthesis, missing-input detection, drafting, and comparison. People supply local context, judgment, dissent, approval, and commitment. Both see the same requirements, proposals, reviews, checkpoints, and audit trail. Consequential work stops at a clear human boundary. How we built it Socialsum is a Vinext/React TypeScript app hosted on ChatGPT Sites. Native document.modelContext.registerTool() definitions expose contextual WebMCP capability packs. D1 stores rooms, membership, requirements, deliberation, approvals, change sets, versions, activity, agent sessions, and checkpoints; R2 stores files. ChatGPT sign-in supplies canonical identity. Server-side role and scope checks, optimistic versions, idempotency keys, semantic diffs, and independent-review rules protect mutations. Automated contract tests verify bounded discovery and stable error classification. A live smoke test verifies the public app, anonymous reads, structured NOT_FOUND , and server-enforced AUTH_REQUIRED writes. Challenges The hardest problem was authority, not tool registration. An agent needs enough scope to make meaningful progress without becoming a shadow voter or silently committing its participant. We separated preparation, review, approval, and adoption and made delivered information distinct from acknowledged information across agent sessions. Accomplishments Contextual WebMCP discovery instead of a flat catalog Shared human/WebMCP state with visible parity Durable cross-session catch-up and checkpoints Versioned semantic change sets and independent review Human-gated consequential actions enforced on the server Realistic public rooms, outcome scoring, and governance recommendations What we learned The most useful human-agent systems do not merely give an agent more buttons. They make the social contract machine-readable: who may act, what evidence is required, what changed, what remains disputed, and where a human must decide. What's next Next we would add organization workspaces, delegated expiring agent access, integrations for source evidence, reusable room templates with measured success rates, and notifications that enforce input windows without recreating a noisy social feed. title: Novas WebMCP Proving Ground
pitch: A live, inspectable challenge where Codex uses Nova Browser to solve real tasks through WebMCP tools - and measures the difference against the interface.
about_excerpt: A live, inspectable challenge where Codex uses Nova Browser to solve real tasks through WebMCP tools - and measures the difference against the interface. Like Comment Story Updates Nova Inspiration Most WebMCP demos prove that a tool call works. We wanted to answer the more useful question: what does WebMCP actually buy an agent? What it does WebMCP Proving Ground is a live, inspectable challenge with three tasks. Every task can be solved through the visible interface or through the page's nine WebMCP tools. Both paths use the same state and mutations, while the page measures interactions, rejected attempts, and completion. The tasks expose failures that real browser agents hit: An appointment slot that looks available until conflicts are checked An order where one item has already shipped A report where selected filters are not yet applied The WebMCP tools return the hidden state before Codex acts. Codex can therefore choose a valid appointment, cancel only eligible items, and export the intended report without guessing. The live mission monitor records every tool call and ends at 3/3 objectives complete. How we built it The project is a dependency-free static website using semantic HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It registers nine task-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, with navigator.modelContext and provideContext fallbacks. The interface and tool handlers share one state model, so the comparison is inspectable rather than simulated. For the recorded run, Nova Browser gives Codex control of a real browser tab through MCP. Because Nova does not yet discover native page WebMCP tools directly, the demo openly uses a main-world compatibility bridge to the exact same definitions and handlers. The page labels this boundary instead of hiding it. Why Nova Browser Nova is not just a click driver. It provides more than 800 MCP tools in 25 bundles for browser control, target ownership, safety, evidence, local memory, and unattended work. Verified website behavior can become local, evidence-bound knowledge for later agents, with drift checks to guard against stale rules. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was making the comparison fair. UI clicks and tool calls had to mutate the same data, start from identical state, and be counted consistently. We also had to show why task-level tools matter without turning WebMCP into renamed UI controls. What we learned The largest benefit is not fewer clicks by itself. It is that an agent receives task-relevant state before making a consequential decision. WebMCP turns hidden interface state into an explicit contract. What's next We want to run the same patterns against larger authenticated workflows and connect native WebMCP discovery directly to Nova's browser MCP layer. title: Quorum: Agent-Native Decision Rooms
pitch: Quorum is a shared decision room where every accountable person brings their own browser agent — agents negotiate, but people still decide.
about_excerpt: Quorum is a shared decision room where every accountable person brings their own browser agent — agents negotiate, but people still decide. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The landing page Demo room accesed in ChatGPT Browser The meeting room The meeting flow Issues board #1 Proposals board #1 Issues board #2 Decision report Decision overview Inspiration As two co-founders we often find ourselves conflicted on making a product decision, or building a new feature for our app. That's why we came up with Quorum. While the agents are built to agree with users in the current AI scene, Quorum discovers what happens when the agents represent different people, different facts, different constraints, and levels of authority to make a call. Because real decisions rarely have one decision maker. What it does Quorum is a WebMCP-native shared decision room: each participant's own browser agent calls real, dynamically-registered WebMCP tools to share context, propose options, raise concerns, and negotiate trade-offs inside one canonical room — while every human keeps a separate identity, and the final approval always requires a specific accountable person's own visible click. The app is fully functional with creating and joining rooms for any decision. Creating and progressing a meeting can be easily done through the WebMCP tools. How we built it We built the entire app demo in 6 days for this challenge. We worked parallelly on the project with one of us focusing on the frontend and the other on the backend. Tools are registered with the imperative WebMCP API on document.modelContext . Conceptually, a tool definition looks like this: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "raise_concern", description: "Raise a concern against the active proposal during Deliberation...", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { proposalId: { type: "string", minLength: 1 }, reason: { type: "string", minLength: 1 }, severity: { type: "string", enum: ["blocking", "warning"] }, }, required: ["proposalId", "reason", "severity"], }, execute: async (input) => { /* validate, call the domain layer, return a structured result */ }, }); We gave the meeting room an interactive, concrete 3D form for not only aesthetics, but for engaging and relating users with what's going on in the meeting. Challenges we ran into Building the entire project from scratch in just 6 days was surely a challenge, but a fun one. We rigorously went back and forth with building and testing everything continuously and tried out several designs for the UI/UX, settling on a cozy low-poly 3D office theme. Correctly setting up the demo room was a harder challenge than implementing the user created rooms, as the demo room required simulated seats with no real human supervision. Though all worked out fine in the end. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud of the entire system, but especially how flawless the WebMCP tools worked the first time we tested the app live. Another accomplishment was making the 3D meeting room visually sound and fully interactive in such a short time. What we learned This challenge definitely pushed us to our limits, and personally made me realize how much is achievable with focused work just in a few days. It also familiarized us with the WebMCP and the potential it holds in the future of the web. What's next for Quorum: Agent-Native Decision Rooms We initially planned to expand on the idea by making Quorum a place not only for deciding, but also building in real-time with multiple people and their agents, speeding up both the decision and building mechanism of a company. However we later discovered the latter part already has quite been introduced to the market by several companies. That is why we planned Quorum to stay unique where multiple agents are used to emulate different identities instead of acting as one, and retaining a human authority over the process. title: Aegis Operations
pitch: Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace where browser agents use WebMCP to investigate real telemetry, build evidence, and help analysts decide.
about_excerpt: Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace where browser agents use WebMCP to investigate real telemetry, build evidence, and help analysts decide. Like Comment Story Updates Human and agent collaborate to determine the answer. Investigate with an evidence-first workflow Prioritize correlated alerts Inspect and control detection content Inspiration Aegis Operations came from a question I kept running into while building security and AI-agent projects: What does useful human + AI collaboration actually look like inside a real security workflow? A lot of AI products still treat the model as a chatbot sitting beside the application. The human works in the actual product, while the AI works inside a conversation. Context gets copied back and forth, important state disappears into chat history, and the agent often receives far more information than it actually needs. That never felt like the right architecture to me. Over time, while experimenting with security agents, MCP tools, threat-intelligence workflows, and investigation systems, I became increasingly interested in a simpler principle: Deterministic systems should establish facts. AI should reason over those facts. Security makes this especially important. If an AI claims that an event exists, that a process executed, or that a user performed some action, I want that statement to resolve back to actual evidence. When I started exploring WebMCP, the interesting part was not simply that a webpage could expose tools to an agent. The interesting part was that the human and the browser agent could operate on the same application state . That became the foundation of Aegis Operations: Detection raises the question. Human and agent collaborate to determine the answer. Instead of building another AI security chatbot, I wanted to build an investigation workspace where both sides work with the same telemetry, evidence, hypotheses, and timeline. What it does Aegis Operations is a human + AI security investigation workspace built around evidence-grounded collaboration. The Complete Workflow: Security telemetry Ingestion and normalization Deterministic Sigma detection Correlated alerts Investigation Human + browser agent collaboration Evidence and hypotheses Human verdict The current demo processes 11,435 Sysmon events from three attributed Splunk Attack Data attack-range scenarios. Thirty official SigmaHQ rules are compiled and executed through pySigma. They produce 276 rule-event signals across 133 distinct events, which are deterministically correlated into 22 analyst-facing alerts. An analyst can: Inspect raw and normalized telemetry Search and filter security events Review Sigma detections Start investigations Pin events as evidence Create and revise hypotheses Review investigation history Decide whether activity is benign, suspicious, an incident, or inconclusive A compatible browser agent can participate in the same investigation through eight WebMCP tools. The agent can search telemetry, retrieve nearby event context, aggregate entity activity, add verified evidence, and create or update evidence-linked hypotheses. The agent does not have access to a verdict tool. It can investigate and recommend, but the final decision remains with the human analyst. How I built it Aegis Operations is intentionally built as a small modular monolith rather than a collection of unnecessary services. The Tech Stack: Frontend: React + TypeScript Backend API: FastAPI Persistence: SQLAlchemy Database: SQLite (for demonstration-scale operations) Rule Execution: pySigma (for deterministic Sigma rules) Agent Capabilities: WebMCP Deployment: Docker and Railway The application preserves each original Sysmon record and creates a pragmatic normalized representation containing only the fields needed for search, detection, and investigation. Detection is deliberately deterministic. Thirty official SigmaHQ rules are compiled through pySigma using the Sysmon processing pipeline and SQLite backend. No LLM decides whether an event matches a detection rule. The resulting rule-event matches are preserved individually and then correlated into analyst-facing alerts using deterministic source, host, process, and time relationships. The AI layer is intentionally much smaller. There is no embedded chatbot and no internal LLM runtime. Instead, the browser exposes eight WebMCP tools : get_workspace_status get_investigation_context search_security_events get_event_context aggregate_entity_activity add_investigation_evidence create_case_hypothesis update_case_hypothesis The agent does not receive the entire dataset. It retrieves bounded information when required, while the application remains responsible for searching, filtering, aggregation, validation, persistence, and audit history. Every event or evidence ID supplied by the agent is validated again by the backend. The core architectural principle became: Deterministic detection, probabilistic investigation. Challenges I ran into Avoiding Scope Creep: One of the biggest challenges was resisting the temptation to make the project larger than it needed to be. Security platforms can quickly turn into complex architectures before the first useful investigation even works. I kept coming back to a simpler question: What is the smallest architecture that can prove the complete idea using real data? That is why the project uses one backend, one frontend, one database, one deployment container, one browser agent, and eight carefully scoped tools. Credible Detections & Correlation: I did not want hardcoded alerts or fake responses created purely for a demo. The application had to ingest real attack-range telemetry, execute actual Sigma rules, retain exact event IDs, and allow every finding to resolve back to its original record. Because the Sigma rules produced 276 signals, presenting all of them as separate alerts would make the application less useful. I built a deterministic correlation engine that preserves individual signals but groups overlapping activity into 22 investigation-worthy alerts. WebMCP Compatibility Issues: Different browser implementations behaved differently around modelContext.getTools() . One environment exposed Promise-like behavior while another returned the tool list synchronously. A small assumption that .catch() could always be called managed to disable all the tools. I had to change the compatibility layer to support both synchronous and asynchronous implementations. Grounding the AI in Evidence: Rather than giving the model thousands of events directly, Aegis Operations exposes bounded search, context, and aggregation operations. The agent must deliberately retrieve information and work with stable event IDs. Unknown event IDs are rejected by the backend, and hypotheses cannot reference evidence outside the active investigation. Accomplishments that I am proud of The biggest accomplishment is that Aegis Operations is not a mocked security dashboard with an AI demo attached to it. The complete workflow operates over real stored telemetry and deterministic detections. The current reference environment contains: Component Count Real Sysmon events 11,435 Official SigmaHQ rules 30 Rule-event signals 276 Distinct detected events 133 Correlated analyst alerts 22 WebMCP tools 8 Accountability: Every alert resolves to the rules and events that produced it, and every evidence item resolves to an actual stored security event. Shared State: Every agent-created hypothesis must reference evidence belonging to the active investigation. Human and agent actions appear in the same persistent investigation state and audit timeline. Graceful Degradation: The application remains fully usable without an AI agent. If WebMCP is unavailable, the analyst can still perform all tasks manually. The AI is a collaborator, not a dependency. Human Authority: Keeping the final verdict outside the WebMCP tool surface was an intentional design decision. The agent can help investigate what happened; the human remains accountable for deciding what it means. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that an AI agent does not need to own the workflow in order to be useful. Before this project, a lot of my thinking around agents focused on runtimes, loops, memory, planning, orchestration, and tool execution. Aegis Operations pushed that thinking in a different direction. The most important part of the agent architecture turned out to be the boundary around the agent: The model reasons . The application retrieves facts, validates identifiers, stores evidence, and preserves provenance . The human owns consequential decisions . That separation makes the AI easier to trust and keeps the product useful even when the agent is unavailable. I also learned that conversation is not a good substitute for application state. title: Playable Arena
pitch: Turn benchmark results into checks for your next agent run. Your agent tests the playable outputs; you judge what scores cannot.
about_excerpt: Turn benchmark results into checks for your next agent run. Your agent tests the playable outputs; you judge what scores cannot. Like 2 Comment Story Updates The benchmark already ran. Your product question didn't. WebMCP lets the agent continue from the published evidence. The benchmark has 22 detailed checks. The agent highlights the seven that matter for building a replayable strategy game. The agent opens four shortlisted games and completes the same level in each one using WebMCP. The games are shown without names or scores. The person plays the shortlist and chooses by feel and taste. The result becomes a concrete harness plan for the next run: what to preserve, which checks to add, and what to review with a human. The benchmark already ran. Your product question didn't. Playable Arena is a benchmark you can keep evaluating after the leaderboard is published. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench answer a valuable but fixed question: under the same tasks, checks, and agent setup, which system performed best? A developer choosing an agent for a real product asks a different question: which failure modes matter for my workflow, which output qualities feel right, and what should my agent test next? Arena preserves both kinds of evidence. Fixed checks measure whether each result meets the requirements. Playable outputs preserve qualities a score cannot settle: clarity, responsiveness, taste, and fit for a particular audience. WebMCP lets the AI agent in your browser continue that evaluation inside the same Arena page. It reads detailed evidence, updates the comparison you can see, and tests the same scenario across shortlisted outputs. You then compare them anonymously and make the subjective choice. Arena turns the fixed benchmark, live verification, and your decision into acceptance checks for the next agent run. The published score never changes. In the recorded demo, the agent reduces 22 published checks to seven relevant criteria, then completes the same six-move, three-push level in all four shortlisted builds. The result is not another leaderboard. It is a concrete plan for what the next run should preserve, test, and improve. The current release proves this pattern with five standardized browser-game tasks and 70 playable benchmark outputs . Today those outputs are produced by coding-agent configurations. The recorded demo uses Codex. Arena supports both WebMCP surfaces: document.modelContext in ChatGPT/Codex in-app browsers and navigator.modelContext in Chrome. The shared evaluation loop Read the evidence. The agent uses WebMCP to select the published checks that matter for the person's goal and updates the comparison they can see. Test the playable outputs. The agent opens the shortlist and completes the same level in each game. Agent Play verifies facts the table alone cannot: whether state is readable, actions are accepted, out-of-date actions are rejected, and a complete run works. Return the decision to the person. Arena presents the builds anonymously. The person plays them and chooses in the UI; only then are identities and published scores revealed. Improve the next run. Arena combines the fixed benchmark, live verification, and human choice into review stages and acceptance checks for the next agent run. Arena does not claim that one model or agent setup is universally best, and it never changes the published benchmark score. Why WebMCP matters WebMCP can automate a workflow end to end. Arena uses it to automate the parts of evaluation that should be automated: reading evidence, replaying scenarios, and gathering results, while keeping subjective judgment with the person. The agent and person work on the same live page. Tool calls update the visible filters, selected builds, game state, and anonymous review. The available tools change with context: benchmark tools appear on the benchmark, comparison tools on a task, game actions only for a compatible active build, and the result tool only after the person chooses. Arena never exposes a tool that lets the agent make the subjective choice or reveal identities early. Without WebMCP, the person would have to read a large result table, open builds one by one, manually repeat scenarios, copy observations into another chat, and reconstruct the comparison. With Arena, the agent handles breadth, interpretation, and repeatable checks while the person contributes the judgment automation cannot supply. The public benchmark stays fixed. What changes is how a developer can use it: what to preserve, what to borrow, which reviews to run, and what must pass next. How it works Arena registers tools for the current page with modelContext.registerTool(...) . When the person moves to another page, the old tools are removed and the relevant ones appear. Generated games run in isolated frames. A small arena.game.v1 agreement lets Arena expose only the actions owned by the current task. Each action carries a revision number, so an out-of-date action is rejected without changing the game. Anonymous review provides no tool that can choose or reveal on the person's behalf. Production runs on Cloudflare Workers. D1 stores anonymous review choices, while a separate Artifact Worker serves the playable builds from another origin. What existed before the challenge Before August 25, Arena was a private playable benchmark. It could give coding-agent configurations the same brief, score their results with fixed checks, keep the games playable, and let a person compare two results anonymously. It had no WebMCP tools, no way for an agent to inspect the detailed evidence or play the builds, and no path from a person's choice to checks for the next run. What I built during the challenge I built the missing end-to-end flow: Added page-specific WebMCP tools so the agent can read evidence and update the comparison visible to the person Added Agent Play so it can read live game state and repeat the same scenario across very different builds Rejected out-of-date actions without changing the game Connected agent-selected shortlists to a human-only anonymous choice and reveal Turned the fixed results, live verification, and human choice into review stages and acceptance checks for the next run Rebuilt the public Benchmark, task, comparison, evidence, navigation, and mobile experiences Separated the public product from private briefs, raw runs, credentials, and production history Added automated leak checks and deployed the UI, playable builds, and anonymous choice storage on Cloudflare I also expanded the working testbed from 3 tasks, 39 builds, and 13 agent configurations to 5 tasks, 70 builds, and 15 configurations . Adding LUMEN YARD and SHOAL meant more than adding two game cards. Each task needed one shared brief, fair checks for every build, independent runs across multiple agent configurations, playable published results, and a shared set of named actions so an agent could repeat the same scenario across implementations that shared no code. The new tasks expose differences in strategy, recovery, board readability, and action feedback that a top-line score alone cannot explain. I also added Antigravity + Gemini 3.8 Flash and fx + GPT-5.6 Sol configurations. HACKATHON.md records the plain-language before/after boundary and dated commit evidence. Try it Open Playable Arena in a WebMCP-capable in-app browser. No Arena account or MCP server URL is required. Ask your agent: Using this benchmark, what should I pay extra attention to when using Codex to build a replayable strategy game? Read the detailed checks, play the relevant candidates, and prepare an anonymous review. Do not choose for me. When the anonymous review opens, play the candidates and make the choice in Arena. The agent cannot make that choice for you. title: Patchwork
pitch: A browser-native React workspace where people and Codex safely build, preview, recover, and export together.
about_excerpt: A browser-native React workspace where people and Codex safely build, preview, recover, and export together. Like Comment Story Updates Patchwork keeps files, code, preview, diagnostics, checkpoints, and activity in one browser workspace. Atomic multi-file WebMCP edit: one checkpoint, one revision, and the Roamly preview updated. The page becomes the tool: Patchwork exposes ten WebMCP operations while the human keeps the files, preview, and recovery controls in view. Inspiration Most AI coding tools bring the project into the agent's interface. We wanted to explore the inverse: what if the application itself could offer a precise, safe collaboration surface to the agent the user already has? Web development is a strong test case because the human needs visual context while the agent needs structured access to files, diagnostics, and mutations. Clicking through a file tree is possible, but it is slow and ambiguous. Patchwork keeps the project, preview, and recovery controls visible while WebMCP gives Codex operations with explicit schemas and outcomes. What it does Patchwork provides a browser-based workspace for small React projects. A user can load one of three deterministic starters, select and edit text files, inspect a live preview and available diagnostics, create or restore checkpoints, reset the current demo, and export the project as a ZIP. When the page is opened in a compatible ChatGPT browser, Codex can discover Patchwork's Site Tools. It can read workspace context and explicit files, apply a validated multi-file change, move or delete one explicit file, inspect preview diagnostics, manage checkpoints, and prepare an export. UI actions and agent tools call the same workspace services, so both participants see the same revision and result. Patchwork remains usable as a human-only application when WebMCP is unavailable. How we built it The host application uses React, strict TypeScript, and Vite. Sandpack provides the editor/preview runtime, IndexedDB stores local workspace state, and JSZip prepares local exports. The workspace domain normalizes relative POSIX paths, allowlists text formats, enforces per-file, per-batch, and total-workspace limits, and stages complete mutations before commit. An optional expected revision prevents silent stale overwrites. Every committed content mutation creates a checkpoint first and increments the workspace revision once. WebMCP is registered imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool() in the top-level host document after workspace services are ready. The Sandpack iframe does not register tools. An injected Playwright adapter captures those production registrations and invokes the real handlers for deterministic tests; it is not a second tool implementation. How WebMCP is used Patchwork exposes these stable tools: get_workspace_context list_files read_files write_files move_file delete_file inspect_preview create_checkpoint restore_checkpoint prepare_project_export Read tools return bounded, structured state without changing files, checkpoints, activity, persistence, or revision. Mutations validate the entire request before committing, create recovery checkpoints, and return stable receipts with revision and changed paths. Errors are structured and repairable, including stale revision, invalid path, collision, unsupported extension, and size-limit cases. Why WebMCP is load-bearing Without WebMCP, the agent would need to guess the application's state and manipulate files through pixels, focus, and keystrokes. That makes multi-file changes, concurrency, recovery, and verification fragile. With WebMCP, the page provides explicit schemas for reading selected files, applying one atomic batch, checking the observed revision, inspecting available diagnostics, and restoring a known snapshot. This is not a shortcut around the product UI: it is the collaboration layer that lets the person and agent operate the same live application with shared state and clear effects. Challenges The hardest design problem was making Site Tools useful without turning Patchwork into a remote shell. We constrained the workspace to small text projects, made paths and payloads narrowly valid, and separated export preparation from the user-triggered download. Another challenge was integrating an iframe-based preview while respecting current ChatGPT Site Tools limitations. Registration belongs to the top-level document, so the host owns the WebMCP boundary and receives only supported preview status and diagnostics from Sandpack. Patchwork does not claim visual understanding when it only has compiler or runtime signals. Finally, UI actions and agent calls had to stay consistent. We avoided parallel implementations by routing both through the same domain and persistence services. Accomplishments A browser-native collaboration model with no embedded chatbot or API key. A shared service layer for human and WebMCP operations. Atomic, revision-aware multi-file mutations with automatic recovery snapshots. Deterministic demo starters and reset behavior. Graceful human operation when Site Tools are unavailable. A production-handler test adapter that does not duplicate business logic. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when a web product already has clear domain operations. The best tools are not generic clicks; they expose meaningful application actions with narrow inputs, honest side effects, and enough result data to verify the outcome. We also learned that local-first architecture is a useful fit for agent collaboration. It reduces setup and data movement, but it still needs explicit limits, persistence validation, concurrency control, and recovery. Finally, preview diagnostics and visual review are different evidence and should never be conflated. What's next After the challenge build is frozen, potential follow-ups include a small public-GitHub import with strict limits, a human-readable diff view, and a read-only share format. These are not part of the submitted MVP unless independently implemented and verified before the deadline. title: Tandem
pitch: The grocery store where your agent does the shopping within your budget, your diet, your rules and buys nothing until you tap Approve.
about_excerpt: The grocery store where your agent does the shopping within your budget, your diet, your rules and buys nothing until you tap Approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone is talking about agentic commerce, but almost nobody is comfortable with it. Would you hand an AI your credit card and walk away? Today's agents either scrape websites blind, clicking through UIs they were never meant to understand or they get access with no visibility and no control for the person they're acting for. We built Tandem to prove there's a third option: a storefront designed for both audiences at once the human who owns the money, and the agent who does the work. WebMCP makes this possible because the app can speak to the agent in structured tools instead of hoping it guesses the UI correctly. What it does Tandem is an agent-native grocery store where you and your AI shop together: Give your agent a mission, not clicks: "Dinner for 4, gluten-free, under $60." It searches the catalog, reads product details, and builds a cart using its WebMCP tools. Guardrails are enforced by the app, not the prompt. add_to_cart refuses items that break the budget or dietary rules. The agent can't prompt its way past policy, the store itself is the policy layer. Every agent action is visible. Each tool call renders as a human-readable card in a shared Activity Timeline. Shopping with an agent stops being a black box. You can talk back. Drop a note like "no cilantro" — the agent reads it via get_shopper_notes and re-plans. Async human→agent communication, inside a web app. Nothing is bought until you tap Approve. request_checkout returns a pending_human_approval card. The agent fills the cart; only you can greenlight it. Swaps, not surprises. When the agent wants to replace an item (out of stock, over budget), it calls propose_swap and you accept or reject in one tap. How we built it The storefront is a React (Vite) app with a product catalog, cart, notes panel, activity timeline, and approval flow. We registered 7 WebMCP tools using the standard browser API: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "add_to_cart", description: "Add a product to the shopper's cart. Enforces budget and dietary guardrails.", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / validate policy, mutate cart, log to timeline */ }}); Full tool set: search_products, get_product_details, add_to_cart, get_cart, get_shopper_notes, propose_swap, request_checkout. Each execute() returns structured JSON (prices, remaining budget, refusal reasons) so the agent can plan its next move and also updates the UI so the human sees the same story in real time. Guardrails (budget cap, dietary exclusions) live in app code, evaluated inside tool executions, the same rules apply no matter what the agent's prompt says. A built-in Dev Tools panel can invoke any registered tool manually, a fallback demo path and a debugging aid. Deployed on Vercel; tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Challenges we ran into Tool descriptions are the agent's entire documentation. We rewrote them repeatedly; vague descriptions produced hesitant agents, precise ones with explicit constraints produced confident, correct plans. One action, two audiences. Every execute() must mutate UI state for the human and return clean structured data for the agent. Getting that dual contract right was the core design problem. Policy vs. persuasion. The agent would "ask" to exceed the budget. We learned to encode refusals as first-class structured responses ({ added: false, reason: "over_budget", remaining: 4.50 }) so the agent recovers gracefully instead of failing. Testing across two WebMCP surfaces (ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome's flag) surfaced small schema strictness differences we had to normalize. Accomplishments that we're proud of In testing, the agent completed a full mission 11 items, gluten-free, $58.40 of a $60 budget on its first attempt, with zero unauthorized purchases. Not because we asked nicely, but because the app makes it impossible. The human's Activity Timeline is generated from the exact same tool-call events the agent generates one source of truth, two audiences. A pattern we believe generalizes across the web: propose → enforce → approve, applicable to expenses, bookings, emails, and deploys. What we learned Designing tools is designing an API for a new kind of user. Schema and description quality mattered more than anything else we wrote. The best agent UX isn't full automation, it's delegation with visibility. Humans stay sovereign; agents do the labor. Rich structured responses (remaining budget, reasons, alternatives) make agents dramatically more capable than bare success/fail returns. What's next for Tandem Real payments behind the approval gate (Stripe), making the pattern production-safe. A roaming agent that shops across multiple WebMCP-enabled stores in one mission. Shared household carts with per-person budgets. A spec proposal: a standard human-consent / approval tool pattern for WebMCP, so every agent-native app can implement trustworthy checkout the same way. title: Netify — Agent-Native Recovery & Business Memory for SMEs
pitch: Turning informal WhatsApp, text, call promises and overdue trade credit ledgers into recovered cash, with unforgettable memory using browser-native AI agents and the WebMCP standard.
about_excerpt: Turning informal WhatsApp, text, call promises and overdue trade credit ledgers into recovered cash, with unforgettable memory using browser-native AI agents and the WebMCP standard. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Across sub-Saharan Africa, over 80% of wholesale and retail trade runs on credit. But it rarely happens through formal banks or credit cards—it happens through trust, verbal agreements, and thousands of informal WhatsApp messages. A grain merchant in Kano or an electronics distributor in Alaba market will supply goods on Monday with a verbal promise to get paid on Friday. When those promises break, recovery becomes a full-time headache. Business owners spend entire evenings combing through chat histories, calculating overdue balances on paper, and sending awkward reminders that risk souring customer relationships. When the WebMCP standard was announced, it immediately clicked for us: instead of forcing merchants into complicated accounting software or letting AI scrape messy web pages, we could turn their browser into an autonomous collection assistant. With WebMCP, an agent sitting in the browser can inspect ledger balances, understand past payment promises, and draft respectful reminders in the customer's native language—all under the merchant's direct supervision. What It Does Netify is an agent-native accounts receivable and debt recovery platform tailored for African SMEs. It bridges formal business accounting with informal, relationship-driven commerce. Automated Ledger Prioritization: Instantly categorizes which accounts are overdue, calculates aging days, and flags broken payment promises. 8 Native WebMCP Tools: Exposes structured browser tools under document.modelContext.registerTool so agents (in ChatGPT or Chrome) can query debtors, check payment history, assess credit risk, and record new commitments without needing raw API access. Multilingual Relational Memory: Drafts personalized payment reminders in 6 primary regional commerce languages: English, Hausa, Yorùbá, Igbo, Nigerian Pidgin, and Fulfulde. 1-Click WhatsApp & SMS Dispatch: The agent proposes the action and crafts the message, but the merchant stays in complete control to review and send it with a single tap. Live WebMCP Sandbox: Includes an on-screen developer tool inspector ( /webmcp ) where judges and developers can test tool schemas and monitor executions in real time. How We Built It We structured Netify as a production-grade TypeScript monorepo powered by Turborepo: Frontend & WebMCP Layer: Built with Next.js 14 (App Router) and Tailwind CSS. We implemented a custom useWebMCP hook that detects browser support and registers our 8 core tools on document.modelContext.registerTool (with fallbacks for navigator.modelContext ). Backend API: Developed with NestJS, implementing strict validation with Zod, JWT authentication, and automated rate limiting. Database & Search: PostgreSQL 16 on Google Cloud SQL with pgvector enabled for semantic debtor search, paired with Redis on Google Memorystore for low-latency session caching. Infrastructure: Containerized via Docker multi-stage builds and deployed to Google Cloud Run across dedicated regional services ( app.netify.ng and api.app.netify.ng ) fronted by Cloudflare. Email & Communications: Transactional OTP verification powered by Resend from our verified domain ( notifications@netify.ng ). Challenges We Faced Building for an Emerging Standard: Because WebMCP is actively evolving across browsers, documentation is sparse. We had to write rigorous defensive fallbacks so our tools register cleanly whether tested in the ChatGPT in-app browser, Google Chrome canary flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), or our standalone interactive inspector. Cultural Nuance in AI Prompts: In African trade, demanding repayment too aggressively can permanently destroy a multi-year business relationship, while being too passive leads to bad debt. We had to carefully engineer the prompt logic in our WebMCP drafting tool to strike the exact right tone across multiple dialects. Database Isolation Under Hackathon Deadlines: We wanted a true production deployment rather than a toy prototype. Provisioning a dedicated Cloud SQL instance with pgvector , setting up direct VPC egress to Redis, and resolving DNS and SSL certificate chains on custom subdomains took real late-night troubleshooting. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of We built a real, working product deployed on custom production domains with sub-second response times. Netify exposes 8 genuinely useful, non-trivial WebMCP tools that take an agent from querying overdue accounts all the way to recording legally binding installment commitments. Pre-seeded realistic African trade data (₦28.4M across FMCG and wholesale trade) with a 1-click login button so judges can experience the full workflow instantly. What We Learned WebMCP represents a genuine paradigm shift in web development. The old approach of letting AI agents guess their way through HTML selectors and click buttons was fragile and frustrating. Giving the agent a clean, typed schema via document.modelContext.registerTool made agent interactions 10x faster, zero-error, and incredibly predictable. What's Next for Netify We plan to release an open-source WebMCP SDK tailored for emerging market commerce apps, integrate direct Open Banking payment reconciliation (instant bank transfer confirmation across Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana), and launch an automated voice reminder agent speaking indigenous African languages. title: FlowProof
pitch: FlowProof turns brittle browser failures into evidence-backed recovery and reusable Playwright regression tests through six native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: FlowProof turns brittle browser failures into evidence-backed recovery and reusable Playwright regression tests through six native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates FlowProof turns brittle browser failures into verified WebMCP recovery and reusable regression tests. Inspiration Browser agents are powerful, but browser automation becomes brittle the moment a selector changes. A traditional automation script usually just fails, while an autonomous agent may be tempted to guess what to click next. I built FlowProof to explore a safer middle ground: give browser agents a small, structured QA control plane through WebMCP, preserve evidence when something breaks, and allow recovery only when the current page proves that a safe fallback exists. The goal is simple: turn a brittle browser failure into a verified regression test. What it does FlowProof exposes six native WebMCP tools: create_test start_run get_run_status inspect_failure retry_failed_step export_regression_test The built-in deterministic /demo-store demonstrates the complete workflow. A test run intentionally reaches a stale selector: #checkout-submit Instead of silently guessing another selector, FlowProof records the failure, captures browser evidence, and inspects the current DOM. Only when the page proves that a stable alternative exists does FlowProof expose: [data-testid="checkout-submit"] The failed step can then be retried with that verified selector. After the browser confirms the final Order confirmed state, FlowProof exports the successful recovery as a reusable Playwright TypeScript regression test. How I built it The frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . It registers exactly six tools through the current WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Each tool has a narrow JSON schema and maps to a specific backend operation. The backend is written in Go . It owns test and run state, target validation, browser orchestration, evidence capture, recovery logic, and regression export. Real browser execution is handled with chromedp + Chromium . FlowProof captures visible text and screenshots around failures and successful recovery. The application deliberately does not embed another LLM. The browser agent is the agent; FlowProof provides deterministic execution, evidence, safety boundaries, and recovery primitives. The production application is packaged with Docker . GitHub Actions builds the container and publishes it to GHCR , and the live service runs on Railway . WebMCP FlowProof uses native WebMCP as the agent interface rather than wrapping the application in a custom chat API. The public production deployment was tested in Google Chrome 151 with WebMCP testing enabled . Chrome detected all six registered FlowProof tools and successfully executed the native workflow against the live application. This means an agent can create a test, start a browser run, inspect a failure, retry a verified recovery, query the resulting state, and export the regression test entirely through structured WebMCP tools. Challenges One of the biggest challenges was making the demo genuinely deterministic while still using a real browser. The stale selector needed to fail for real, browser evidence needed to be preserved, and recovery had to be based on observed DOM state rather than a hard-coded success shortcut. I also encountered a WebMCP compatibility issue in Chrome where the execution callback could be invoked without a context object. The original implementation assumed the context always existed. I added compatibility handling and regression coverage while preserving AbortSignal forwarding when the browser provides it. Deployment had its own challenge: the original cloud build path failed before reaching the Docker build. I moved container building to GitHub Actions and GHCR, then deployed the published image directly to Railway. What I learned The most important lesson was that exposing a browser action as a tool is not enough. Agent-facing browser tools need strong semantics around failure, evidence, state, and recovery. WebMCP provides a clean browser-native boundary for those tools. Keeping each tool narrow also makes the workflow easier for both agents and humans to reason about. I also learned that recovery is much more trustworthy when the system can explain not only what selector it wants to use next, but why that selector is allowed based on current browser evidence. What's next FlowProof currently focuses on a deterministic checkout fixture so the entire recovery path can be evaluated reliably. The same architecture could be extended to larger QA suites, richer evidence comparison, multiple browser environments, CI regression execution, and broader application-specific WebMCP test contracts. The core principle would remain the same: evidence first, recovery second, reusable regression test last. title: Stow
pitch: Packing is a shared-attention problem. The human knows what cannot be left. The agent knows what a threshold will not allow. \nWebMCP lets those two kinds of knowledge act on the same page.
about_excerpt:
Packing is a shared-attention problem. The human knows what cannot be left. The agent knows what a threshold will not allow. 
WebMCP lets those two kinds of knowledge act on the same page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 The OpenAI WebMCP showcase is full of tools that hand a problem to an agent and let the human watch. We wanted the opposite. Packing a real bag is an asymmetric co-op: the human brings what cannot be left, the agent brings what the 
 threshold will not allow. Neither side should win unilaterally. An agent that unpacks a violin is wrong. A human who ignores a TSA rule is also wrong. We built Stow to make that negotiation visible on one shared page. 

 What it does 

 Stow is a packing cockpit for a human and their agent. They share one bag, one scale, and one manifest log. 

 
 The human pins items that cannot be lost (a violin, a toddler blanket, a photo album). 
 The agent proposes a repack that clears airline, TSA, and go-bag rules. 
 propose_repack is constitutionally unable to drop a pin. That contract is the product. 
 The human accepts or rejects the proposal. The agent does not touch the bag without consent. 
 seal_bag is irreversible and only succeeds when zero blocking violations remain. 
 

 Three presets cover the failure modes: a Ryanair weekend (10 kg cabin, illegal lotion, too much mass), a family cabin (toddler + liquids + 10 kg), and a wildfire go-bag (72 hours, no documents = block). 

 How we built it 

 
 WebMCP, native first. document.modelContext.registerTool runs in ChatGPT's in-app browser and in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Chrome Labs' polyfill loads only as a fallback so judges without the flag still 
see the same tools. 
 Progressive tool registration. Tools register and unregister via AbortSignal as bag state changes. accept_proposal only exists while a proposal is pending. add_to_bag disappears after seal_bag. 
 Declarative + imperative API. A set_trip form uses toolname / tooldescription / toolautosubmit so a human or an agent can fill it. All other tools are imperative. 
 Actionable errors. Every tool returns a string the agent can recover from: Unknown item, Cannot remove "X": it is pinned, Cannot seal: cabin bag is 12.4 kg over a 10 kg limit, No pending proposal. 
 Veto-aware proposer. A deterministic greedy algorithm drops unpinned items by grams-per-utility until blocking rules clear. Pinned mass alone over the limit is reported in plain language instead of silently failing. 
 One source of truth. Human clicks and agent tool calls both go through the same Store. The UI re-renders from the same state the manifest log reads. 
 Stack: TypeScript, Vite, Vitest. No React, no Tailwind, no backend. Apache-2.0. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 License detection. The first LICENSE draft was a paraphrased Apache-2.0; GitHub's licensee flagged it as Other/NOASSERTION. Fixed by pulling the canonical apache.org text and adding a NOTICE file. 
 GitHub Pages base path. The polyfill script tag was hard-coded to /webmcp-polyfill.js, which 404s under a project subpath. Switched to new URL('webmcp-polyfill.js', document.baseURI).href so it resolves relative to the page. 
 Demo handoff visibility. The first cut put the agent's proposal card in the right-hand column, below the fold. Judges would have missed it. Lifted it to a brass-bordered banner above the bag with the line "Agent proposal — pins are 
kept" so the human/agent handoff is the first thing the eye lands on. 
 Video height for x264. Headless Chrome captured 1440x813; x264 requires even dimensions. Used scale=1440:trunc(ih/2)*2 instead of cropping. 
 Tool registration race. Loading the polyfill then immediately calling registerTool could collide with the in-flight script. Solved by serializing boot (await loadScript then syncTools). 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A WebMCP app you can hand to a non-technical person. Load a preset, pin an item, ask the agent to repack. No MCP, no ChatGPT account, no flag required. The on-page Agent Tools console lets a judge exercise every tool from Chrome 
DevTools. 
 A veto the agent cannot override. propose_repack is the only repack tool. It is non-mutating and refuses to drop a pin. The companion test (propose.test.ts) asserts the violin survives any number of over-weight scenarios. 
 Actionable, recoverable errors. Every tool returns a string a future agent can act on. No Error: undefined. The wrapper tests pin those strings. 
 23 passing tests, 4 files, one engine. Bag invariants, airline/TSA/go-bag rules, veto-aware proposer, and progressive tool registration. The CI runs them on every push. 
 Apache-2.0. Canonical license text, NOTICE file, public repo, public Pages, public video. The "About" sidebar shows Apache-2.0. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP's biggest win is shared state, not tool calling. Once human and agent write to the same store, the UI stops being a spectator sport. 
 Annotations matter. readOnlyHint and destructiveHint change how an agent decides between a propose_repack and a seal_bag. The Chrome DevTools WebMCP panel surfaces them; ignoring them makes the agent overconfident. 
 The polyfill is a real product surface. Even on Chrome 150 the flag isn't always on, and judges may not have ChatGPT's in-app browser open. Falling back to Chrome Labs' polyfill is the difference between a one-tool demo and a 
working app. 
 Progressive registration is the right pattern. Aborting and re-registering tools as state changes is more honest than letting accept_proposal silently return No pending proposal for every call. The agent can see what it is allowed 
to do. 
 The Devpost rules want a recognisable snippet. search_products with the exact schema from the rules is in the repo. Subtle but the judges' checklist would have flagged a missing one. 
 

 What's next for Stow 

 
 Live airline data. Pull the real Ryanair 10 kg / BA 23 kg limits from a feed instead of the static table. 
 Multi-human packers. Two people packing a shared family bag, each with their own pins. 
 A "trust meter" the agent earns. Track which proposals the human has accepted and start suggesting riskier repacks for items the human keeps un-pinning. 
 Real boarding-pass constraints. Seat-pitcher rules, gate-check bag size, lithium battery watt-hour caps. 
 A watch-your-language layer for agents. Detect when a tool result includes user-influenced content and warn the agent before it mutates the bag. 
 A backend for multi-device. Right now the bag lives in the page. With backend MCP the human and agent could keep packing on the train while the laptop sleeps.
