title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Floorplay
pitch: A floor plan you and your agent edit together, in 2D and 3D, doorways included.
about_excerpt: A floor plan you and your agent edit together, in 2D and 3D, doorways included. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I've moved apartments four times and every time the same thing happens. I open a chat, describe the room, get a nice paragraph about "creating a cozy reading nook by the window", and then I stand in the room with a tape measure and none of it fits. The bed blocks the door. The desk is in the dark corner. Meanwhile the planner apps that can actually draw a room have no idea what I asked for. So the idea was pretty simple: put the drawing and the agent in the same place. Not a chat with a picture attached. A real plan that an AI agent can read and change, next to me, while I drag things around too. What it does Floorplay is a room designer where you and an AI agent work on the same floor plan. On the left there's a plan that looks like something an architect would hand you: grid, thick wall bands with the doors and windows cut out, swing arcs, dimensions. On the right the same room in 3D, and you can walk through it at eye height. Eight rooms come already furnished because staring at an empty rectangle is the worst part of any planner. There's a catalog of 139 pieces with real sizes and prices. The whole room is exposed to the agent as WebMCP tools. Sixty of them, plus four that show up only while you have something selected. It can read the plan, ask where a bed would fit, place and move things, paint a wall, resize the room, cut a window, move the camera, or lay out a whole option. When it proposes a layout you see it as ghosts on the drawing with a little card. Hover to preview, accept or reject. Everything else it does lands straight on the plan, goes into a ledger next to your own edits, and any step can be reverted. Late in the week I added homes. You can put rooms next to each other on one sheet, they snap edge to edge and refuse to overlap, and if you cut a doorway through a shared wall it opens in both rooms. Then you can walk from the living room into the bedroom in 3D. The part I like most is small. Ask the agent "what do I see from the door?" and the camera actually walks to the door and the answer comes from what is in that view. No guessing. How we built it It's a Vite + React + TypeScript app, no backend, three.js for the 3D through react-three-fiber. I built it in three days with an AI coding agent doing most of the typing and me doing most of the complaining. Underneath there's a plain TypeScript engine that doesn't know the UI exists. It computes footprints and overlaps, whether a door can swing, whether you can reach everything, walkway width on a 10 cm grid, a rough daylight model, budget, and it can invert every operation so undo is exact. Homes sit on top of that: snapping, overlap checks, and a doorway stored as one record that owns an opening in two rooms. The WebMCP part registers every tool on document.modelContext with a schema and a readOnlyHint where it applies. The selection tools live in their own group behind an AbortController, so when you click a different chair the old group is torn down and a new one registered. All the editing tools share one write path, which means they all answer the same way: what happened, what's now broken, the new numbers. That turned out to matter more than anything else I did. Since most browsers don't have document.modelContext yet, the app has a fake one built in and a dev panel (Cmd+Shift+D) where you can call any tool by hand. Honestly that's where I spent most of the time. There are 309 tests and a Playwright script that runs the real app through 44 screenshots. Challenges we ran into The first time I opened the DevTools WebMCP panel it was empty. Every tool registered without an error, and Chrome just didn't list any. It took most of an afternoon to learn the page needs to be origin isolated, which is two headers ( Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) ). Two lines in the Vercel config. At the start the agent placed furniture by guessing coordinates and it was awful. I tried writing better tool descriptions and it barely helped. What helped was giving it real answers: a suggest_positions tool that returns ranked spots with a reason for each, and every edit reporting the violations it caused. Once it could see that the bed now blocks the door, it fixed it on its own. When I added homes, the walls between rooms poked into each other's floors, because each room draws its walls just outside its own rectangle. Fine alone, wrong the moment two rooms touch. Now a shared wall is drawn as two halves, one on each side of the line. I also built a "Propose first" switch that turned every agent edit into a card you had to approve. It sounded responsible. In practice it just made the agent feel slow, and undo already covers the risk, so I took it out again the same day. And on the last day I noticed you couldn't move a window at all. Not by dragging, not from the editor, not from a tool. Nobody had ever needed to during testing. That's fixed now. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can do anything I can do in the app. It never has to say "please click this for me". The plan looks like a drawing, not a toy. Early versions looked like they were built for kids and that bothered me more than any bug. Homes with doorways. Cutting one door and seeing it appear in both rooms, then walking through it in 3D, was the moment the project felt done. What we learned The number of tools is a vanity metric. What the tools return is what changes the agent's behaviour. Give it computed facts in every answer and it stops needing instructions. Selection-scoped tools are worth the setup. "Move the thing the user just clicked" removes a whole class of wrong-id mistakes. And an agent dropped into a page needs the same thing a new colleague does: a short tour. There's a get_guide tool for exactly that. What's next for Floorplay The Buy tab already lets the agent find where to buy each piece you don't own. Real store listings and price tracking would make that useful for real. After that: more home templates, more than one floor, and a share link so two people and one agent can work on the same flat. title: OpenHardware
pitch: Software got its agent moment. Hardware hasn't. OpenHardware is the missing piece: an agent that can see the board it programs.
about_excerpt: Software got its agent moment. Hardware hasn't. OpenHardware is the missing piece: an agent that can see the board it programs. Like Comment Story Updates A coding agent today can write, run, test and fix software on its own. Point the same agent at an ESP32 and the loop breaks at the first step: it can write the firmware, but it can't see it run. It doesn't know if the camera came up green, whether the frame rate held, or that the board rebooted twice while you were reading the log. So you become its eyes: you flash, you watch, you report back, and one wrong setting sends you around again. Every gain agents brought to software stops at the edge of the cable. OpenHardware puts the board in front of the agent. A browser page, an ESP32-S3 on a USB cable, and a set of WebMCP tools that let ChatGPT's built-in browser read live telemetry, run measured experiments, build firmware on top of a baseline that never stops reporting, and flash it, with every write to hardware waiting on a human. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP tools run inside the page, on the user's machine. That one property is the reason this project can exist. A cloud MCP server can't see a USB port; a browser tab can. So the same tab that draws the telemetry for the human is the tab whose JavaScript holds the serial link, and the tools the agent calls are functions in that tab. The agent's tool calls have physical consequences, and the human is watching them land on the same screen. It's also the shape WebMCP was designed for: one instrument, two operators. The human sees the charts, the frames, the attempt history and the gate. The agent sees structured summaries of the same data through tools. Neither is working from a description of what the other did. They're looking at the same board. How it creates a better user experience The firmware developer's loop today is edit, plug in, flash, squint at a serial monitor, guess, repeat. Minutes per cycle, and the agent is locked out of all of it. With OpenHardware the loop is a sentence. Ask for "the maximum resolution that holds 12 fps under 50 °C" and the agent reads the board, applies a resolution, soaks, measures frame rate and die temperature, records the attempt, and climbs until a limit breaks. Every attempt is a card in the page, every number was measured seconds ago on this board, and what the agent learns is written into a limits panel in plain language that persists for the next session. When the agent writes firmware, it builds on top of the harness rather than replacing it, so the telemetry stream survives its own flash. If something comes up wrong, the agent sees the frame and the numbers in the same moment and debugs with live data instead of a guess. Every build is recorded with its source, so the human can code-review before anything touches the board, and a flash waits at the gate for approval. For anyone without hardware, the page ships a simulated board with scenes (a board that runs hot, a lost link, a missing camera). It's badged amber so it can never be mistaken for the real thing, and every tool result says which one it came from. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Measure instead of recall. Two boards with the same part number have different amounts of contiguous PSRAM free. The agent now reasons from what this board reported, not from training data. Iterate without becoming the agent's eyes. The human declares what's wired to which pins, states the goal, and approves. The agent runs the experiments. Debug after a flash. Because the harness is never overwritten, the agent still has telemetry and camera frames after its own firmware boots. The failure mode where the agent flashes and goes blind is gone. Review before it's real. Reads are always available to the agent. Writes to hardware are gated, and the source of every build is one click away, so trust is earned attempt by attempt rather than assumed. How we implemented WebMCP The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool. Read tools are annotated readOnlyHint and stay registered whenever the page is open: board identity and capabilities, telemetry over a window (count, min, max, mean and slope per field, never raw samples), learned limits, a frame capture that renders in the camera panel, the available builds, the wiring list, and the current work order with its attempts. Write tools register only while a board is linked and unregister on link loss: camera on/off and config, run_experiment (apply, soak, measure, record in one call), watch_for (block on a telemetry condition, honoring the abort signal), record_limit, and flash_image, which routes through the same approve/hold gate a human uses. Approve and hold are deliberately not tools. Every result carries its source, sim or usb, and the link state. The page infers agent presence from tool calls and narrates it next to the link badge, without ever changing the badge's color. If document.modelContext is absent, the page works exactly as before with a single hint that tools are available in a WebMCP-enabled browser. Underneath: a static frontend with no build step, a framed line protocol (OHW1) over Web Serial with CRC and four-per-second heartbeats, an ESP-IDF harness built in Docker, and a simulated board that speaks the same protocol so the tools are tested against it in CI. video_transcript_excerpt: And agents can write you firmware. You just can't see it run. So, you flash your watch and do your work back every single time. Software got its agent moments. And hardware just did. This is open hardware. First, the board gets a baseline firmware we call the harness. It does one job. Stream everything the board knows about itself four times a second. That stream is the agent's eyes and it never goes away. The base wears all of that as web MCP tools. So, ChatGPT's built-in browser can call them while I watch. So, I just ask, "Run my camera at the maximum resolution possible while holding 12 frames a second and staying under 50 degrees." It reads the board's first, then one experiments. Each one applies a resolution, so it measures the frame rates and the temperature and records an attempt. Every call has a real measurement on this board, not an estimate from a data sheet. It climbs until [music] one of the two limits breaks, then backs off. When it writes firmware, it builds on top of the harness, never replacing it. So, if something comes up wrong, the agent sees the frame the [music] numbers at the same moment and debugs with live data instead of a guess. Every build is recorded. title: Murph Food Lab
pitch: Compare 2M+ foods with clear grades, lab evidence, and WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Compare 2M+ foods with clear grades, lab evidence, and WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Murph Food Lab compares more than two million foods with ChatGPT and WebMCP. ChatGPT sees four typed WebMCP tools exposed directly by the Food Lab page. Murph compares exact products in one normalized nutrition table. Open the grade, ingredients, and product-level lab evidence behind each result. Inspiration Food labels make simple choices hard. Serving sizes differ, ingredient lists are difficult to scan, and lab results rarely tell a shopper what matters. We wanted a child, a parent, or an AI agent to compare real products and understand the tradeoffs in seconds. What it does Murph Food Lab searches more than two million branded foods and compares up to four exact products side by side. It normalizes nutrition to the same basis, shows a clear A-E Murph grade, calls out useful and concerning ingredients, and links exact product-level lab evidence when it exists. The person and the agent share one visible workspace. The agent can search for foods, add exact products, read the current comparison, and open the evidence drawer. The person stays in control and sees every result the agent used. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the interaction layer, not a wrapper around a chatbot. The Food Lab page registers four typed tools: search_food_products searches the public catalog and returns exact product references. compare_food_products places selected products into the visible comparison. get_food_comparison reads the same normalized metrics and grades shown to the person. show_food_evidence opens the visible evidence view for one selected product. Each tool has bounded input, structured output, and shares the current page state. This lets an agent act through the real interface instead of using a separate hidden backend. How we built it We built the experience with TypeScript, React, Next.js, WebMCP, PostgreSQL, Vercel, Brandfetch, and Codex CLI. Murph reuses its public product search and exact-evidence APIs. Nutrition comparison and grading use deterministic code. WebMCP exposes those same results to compatible agents. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping the result useful without pretending that one food is universally healthy. We kept nutrition, ingredients, and lab evidence separate. Missing lab data stays unknown instead of becoming a safety claim. We also filtered generic database rows that look like products but do not identify a real consumer product. Accomplishments that we are proud of A shared human-agent comparison instead of a separate AI chat result. More than two million searchable food records. Clear A-E grades with plain-language reasons. Exact product-level evidence when available. Stable layouts across loading, empty, mobile, and four-product states. Brand matching without exposing the Brandfetch credential to the browser. What we learned WebMCP works best when tools control a useful page that already makes sense to a person. Typed tool inputs, exact product references, and shared visible state made the agent behavior easier to trust and debug. What is next We want to add barcode scanning, more exact lab sources, regional product catalogs, and personal comparison preferences. We also want agents to explain why two similar products received different grades without hiding the underlying label or evidence. title: Paris ICC
pitch: Procedure-grounded rail incident decisions, powered by WebMCP and controlled by operators.
about_excerpt: Procedure-grounded rail incident decisions, powered by WebMCP and controlled by operators. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration On a large urban rail network, each line has its own control centre. An Integrated Control Centre (ICC) adds a network-wide view so teams can coordinate disruptions that cross lines and transport modes. During an incident, an operator must check many sources at once: alarms, train movements, delays, passenger queues, power, available driver capacity, network connections, and the right procedure. The operator may also need to ask other teams for missing information. Finding and checking all of this takes time, and the difficulty depends partly on the operator's experience. What Paris ICC does Paris ICC is a complete, runnable railway decision-support application for the 21-line Paris Metro and RER network. It turns the operational web page into a shared workspace for a human operator and an AI agent. The application supports an end-to-end workflow: monitor the network through an interactive map with semantic zoom; locate simulated trains, delays, incidents, and affected areas; rank active incidents by their current passenger-queue impact; inspect one coded incident and retrieve its matching procedure; review evidence, expected effects, duration, and operator checks; approve procedure steps one by one; record every approved action and receipt in a persistent operations log; configure the agent's analysis focus for nine incident types; and prepare an editable end-of-shift report from the complete persisted log. Paris ICC also includes passenger flow, procedures, delays and regulation, traction power, SCADA, bus replacement services, rolling stock, D-1 schedules and drivers, an operations log, and simulation data views. It is a coherent operational product, not a standalone tool-call screen. Why WebMCP is essential Without contextual decision support, the operator has to move between alarm screens, operational views, procedures, staff information, and conversations with other teams before deciding what to do. An experienced operator may know where to look first; a less experienced operator may need more time to assemble the same picture. With WebMCP, the agent can read the current, carefully limited context exposed by the page. It brings the relevant facts together, finds the matching procedure, and proposes grounded next steps inside the incident workflow. This can reduce the time spent searching and cross-checking, while the operator still reviews the evidence and makes the decision. The page publishes 21 typed WebMCP tools: 13 read-only tools for current operational and procedural evidence; 2 non-committing analysis/staging tools; and 6 guarded operational actions that affect only the simulation. For an incident decision, the server-hosted OpenAI agent must follow this exact read-only WebMCP chain: inspect_incident_decision_context search_operational_procedures get_operational_procedure The server validates each call and forces the final recommendation into a strict structured schema. The model may cite only step IDs from the exact retrieved document. The evidence view keeps the incident code, decision revision, procedure revision, SHA-256 integrity hash, and cited steps visible to the operator. The result is more than an assistant beside a dashboard: the human and agent work from the same application state and the same versioned evidence. Human authority and safety boundaries The agent finds and explains. The procedure defines. The operator decides. The model never receives the procedure-application tool during incident analysis. When the operator selects an executable step, the page builds one exact request and displays a visible, one-use confirmation. Before accepting it, the application rechecks: the current incident and decision revision; the procedure ID, revision, and content hash; the cited step and its mapped capability; that the incident remains active; that the target is the local simulation; and that the request has not become stale, duplicated, or invalid. A successful action creates a receipt, advances the applicable revision, and appears in the persistent shift log. A stale recommendation cannot silently change a newer situation. How we used AI The OpenAI Responses API powers the constrained incident-decision agent, passenger-impact explanations, procedure-editor feedback, and the editable end-of-shift report. Agent instructions can be configured for nine incident types, but they cannot override verified evidence, the retrieved procedure, the structured output contract, or human approval. The application also has a deterministic procedure-based fallback. If model analysis is unavailable, it still performs the same inspect, search, and retrieve flow and proposes only unfinished mandatory steps from that document. OpenAI text-to-speech was used for the disclosed English narration in the demo video. How we built it The browser application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, SVG, and the browser WebMCP API. The page registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) for native discovery. A clearly labelled in-page compatibility bridge uses the same definitions, schemas, validation, and approval path when native browser support is unavailable. An authenticated Node service owns mutable simulation state, the server-authoritative clock, agent calls, and session boundaries. Embedded SQLite persists operational snapshots, events, idempotent command receipts, procedure execution progress, the shift log, and the report. An optional IDFM PRIM connector supplies read-only passenger-information evidence and never sends railway commands. Codex was used as an implementation and verification partner: refining scope, designing typed WebMCP contracts, implementing and debugging the React and Node application, hardening authorization and revision guards, expanding automated tests, checking browser behaviour, documenting boundaries, and preparing the demonstration. Challenges The hardest challenge was enabling useful agent action without confusing recommendation with authorization. A user-supplied confirm: true would not be meaningful, so approval is held outside tool input, shown visibly, bound to frozen arguments, and consumed once. A second challenge was grounding recommendations in a changing operational state. Paris ICC binds the incident revision to an immutable procedure identity and content hash, then refreshes evidence after each approved step. A third challenge was presenting a dense 21-line railway network without losing context. Semantic zoom keeps the overview calm, then reveals missions, trains, delays, passengers, provenance, and decision detail as the operator investigates. Accomplishments A complete incident-to-recovery-and-handover product workflow. 21 real, typed page tools instead of a single generic agent endpoint. A multi-call, procedure-grounded evidence chain. Passenger-impact prioritisation from the current page state. Visible human approval and revision-bound simulated actions. Persistent receipts, operations history, and shift reporting. A native 21-line network schematic with 390 canonical stations and 467 physical interstations. Reproducible unit, integration, browser, native WebMCP, build, and deployment checks. Honest separation between simulated operational data and optional read-only passenger information. What we learned WebMCP is especially valuable when a page contains changing, structured context and actions whose consequences must remain visible. Agent-native does not have to mean agent-autonomous. Typed tools let the model handle information-heavy analysis while the application keeps authority, evidence, and safety boundaries understandable to the person responsible. Potential impact The target users are traffic controllers and network supervisors coordinating incidents across Metro and RER lines. Paris ICC helps them understand a disruption, focus on the incident with the greatest current passenger impact, follow a traceable procedure, and preserve a clear handover record. The product is designed to support, not replace, operators with different levels of experience. It can reduce the time spent looking for information and checking it across several systems, while procedures and human judgement remain authoritative. For passengers, better-informed coordination can support more regular service, clearer incident handling, and less crowding. Although demonstrated on the Paris Metro and RER, the approach is designed to be transferable to other rail networks and multimodal transport systems in major metropolitan areas. Each deployment can connect its own network topology, supervision data, incident codes, operating procedures, roles, and authorization rules while retaining the same WebMCP-based human-agent decision loop, traceability, and human approval model. Beyond transport, this approach could also be explored for browser-based industrial HMI and SCADA systems used

title: Easy Query
pitch: A local data file viewer with a private SQL workspace where WebMCP agents can write complex queries, and analyze data alongside you.
about_excerpt: A local data file viewer with a private SQL workspace where WebMCP agents can write complex queries, and analyze data alongside you. Like Comment Story Updates demo1 demo2 demo3 Inspiration Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Pain: Writing complex SQL requires expertise. Solution: Using WebMCP, the agent can help users write accurate SQL queries. Pain: Most AI assistants and data tools operate in separate contexts. Users are forced to repeatedly copy information between tools and manually apply every suggestion. Solution: The agent works directly in Easy Query, eliminating constant copy-pasting between tools. Pain: Long, deeply nested SQL queries maintained by multiple people are difficult to understand, modify, and debug. Solution: WebMCP gives the agent access to the full query, schema, errors, and results to explain the logic, make changes, and verify the fix. How it creates a better user experience Pain: Basic file viewers such as Excel are easy to use but building complex queries quickly becomes awkward. Solution: Easy-to-use GUI features such as: infinite scrolling, search, sorting, and filtering. Pain: On the other hand, database tools are powerful but intimidating. Solution: Easy Query gives users the power of SQL and AI through a familiar table interface, making advanced data analysis far less intimidating. Pain: Formats such as Parquet are difficult to inspect. Solution: Easy Query displays them directly in a fast, familiar table. Pain: Most AI tool's chat history buries earlier queries and results. Revisiting an earlier query means scrolling through the conversation, finding the right response, and interrupting the current discussion to refine it. Solution: Every query and result appears in a browser-style tab that users can inspect, edit, rerun, rename, and reuse. What people and agents can do together Every query and result remains visible and editable, making advanced analysis accessible without taking control away from experienced users. Either the user or agent can independently perform full data analysis. They can also collaborate: the user guides the question while the agent handles complex SQL and iterative debugging. Because both operate on the same live workspace, either can immediately continue, refine, or verify the other's work. What it does Easy Query loads CSV, TSV, Parquet, JSON, and JSONL files into DuckDB-Wasm and lets users explore them entirely in the browser. Users can write DuckDB SQL themselves or ask a WebMCP-enabled agent to: Discover tables, columns, and relationships Write joins, aggregations, CTEs, and window queries Execute SQL and inspect complete results Diagnose errors and revise queries Create, rename, activate, and close workspace tabs Every query and result remains visible in a tab, allowing the user to inspect, edit, rerun, and learn from the agent’s work. How we built it Easy Query is built with Svelte 5, TypeScript, CodeMirror, Apache Arrow, and DuckDB-Wasm. Files are loaded into an in-memory DuckDB database, while virtual scrolling keeps large query results responsive. We implemented WebMCP using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API. The application exposes structured tools for inspecting the DuckDB catalog, managing workspace tabs, reading and writing SQL, executing queries, and retrieving help. These tools operate on the same Svelte state and DuckDB connection used by the visible interface. When an agent creates a query tab or runs SQL, the result immediately appears for the user. When the user edits or renames a tab, that updated state is available to the agent. Challenges we ran into Tables, SQL, active tabs, query results, and schema changes must remain synchronized between the user interface and WebMCP tools. Accomplishments that we're proud of We built an end-to-end WebMCP workflow rather than a collection of isolated demo commands. An agent can discover an unfamiliar dataset, create a query, run it, inspect an error or result, revise its approach, and leave the finished analysis visible to the user. We are also proud that Easy Query supports two collaboration styles. An agent can complete an analysis autonomously, or it can behave as a copilot by drafting SQL and waiting for the user to review and execute it. What we learned We learned that WebMCP tool design is product design, not just an implementation task. Delegating it entirely to a coding agent can produce tools that work technically but create a confusing user experience. Human judgment was essential for defining clear capabilities and boundaries. For example, explicitly identifying DuckDB as the SQL dialect and separating database tables from workspace tabs made agent behavior far more reliable and predictable. What's next for Easy Query Next, we want to grow Easy Query into a broader, local-first data analysis workspace: Add charts and maps so people and agents can turn query results into clear trends, relationships, and geographic insights. Explore additional query paradigms, including dataframe-style transformations and specialized languages for graph or time-series data. Support more data sources, including local SQLite and DuckDB databases, plus optional remote databases through secure, user-controlled connectors. title: Nexo RUTIC
pitch: Every button in this Colombian telecom registry has an AI-agent twin — same validation, same logic, same authority. A WebMCP Challenge entry.
about_excerpt: Every button in this Colombian telecom registry has an AI-agent twin — same validation, same logic, same authority. A WebMCP Challenge entry. Like Comment Story Updates Attaching the three bundled sample documents through the canonical manifest — the same files whether clicked or registered by the agent. Every step names both paths at once: the button to click, and the exact sentence to tell the agent instead. The Spanish interface, with an explainer panel describing what WebMCP is and how each action maps to a tool. The agent creates a dossier, is blocked from skipping a step, then submits it — all through the page's own validated logic. Review step: every extracted field cites the exact document and page it came from, before a human approves submission. Inspiration What it does How I built it Challenges I ran into## Inspiration We wanted to test a real, unglamorous shape of task against the WebMCP standard: a government procedure. A trámite is a bounded set of well-defined actions with real validation and real consequences — exactly the kind of task where an agent guessing at buttons or screen text is not an acceptable failure mode. RUTIC is a synthetic GovTech app: a public telecom-provider registry for Colombia where every action a person can do with buttons, an AI agent can also do, through the same page-owned logic, never around it. What it does RUTIC lets a person create a dossier by uploading three documents, which the page extracts and validates locally — no PDF ever reaches the AI model. From there they review or edit nine typed fields, submit with an explicit human-approved code, modify a submitted dossier without re-uploading anything, cancel an edit and keep the last submitted version untouched, list and check their dossiers, and switch the interface between Spanish and English. Every one of those actions is reachable two ways: a button, or a sentence to the agent. "Modify my dossier" resolves to the one submitted dossier without asking for its code back; "the second one" or "el segundo" resolves against a list the agent just showed; "envíalo" is accepted as the explicit approval without repeating a code already on screen. The task takes the same number of real steps either way — talking removes the cost of finding the right control, and a person can switch between clicking and talking mid-task because both paths write to the same state. How we built it Every dossier action is a real, imperative document.modelContext.registerTool call, not a static list — the set of registered tools is recomputed from the page's own state machine on every change, so the agent can only ever see and call what's actually valid at that moment. Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) receives a fresh summary of the true page state on every turn and is instructed to reuse only values it has actually seen: it never receives PDF bytes and never invents a claim value, a dossier code, or an approval code. The page keeps the authority; the agent only routes intention to it. Challenges we ran into We built and load-tested a declarative variant — an annotated form the browser fills and submits directly — for the one task that looked like a natural fit, editing form fields, and reverted it. Our full-page re-render recreates the form's DOM node on every state change, and the browser's declarative discovery treated that as a brand-new tool appearing each time, causing a runaway feedback loop. We're documenting that attempt rather than hiding it, because it's a real, useful finding about the standard's current rough edges, not just a footnote. Accomplishments that we're proud of Nothing the agent can do is something the page can't already validate and execute on its own — the agent only ever decides which action, never how it runs. That guarantee holds across nine typed fields, a document manifest, and a state machine with an explicit human-approval gate, and it's backed by 45 tests covering the state machine, the WebMCP bridge, the Gemini boundary and its retries, extraction, and localization. What we learned The clearest lesson came from the failure: WebMCP's declarative discovery assumes a form's DOM identity is stable, and a framework that re-renders the DOM on every state change breaks that assumption outright. The imperative registerTool path, recomputed from the same state machine, doesn't have that problem — for a UI built around frequent re-render, the imperative API is the one that composes safely with real application state, not just a fallback. What's next The pattern holds past this one registry: any administrative procedure with well-defined actions, real validation, and real consequences can be built this way — clicked through as usual, or described in plain language, with every check the process requires staying exactly as strict either way. The submission step here is intentionally local and simulated, and always reports externalTransmission: false; the natural next step is wiring that same page-owned logic to an actual government backend without loosening any of the guarantees the demo enforces today. title: HomeWheel
pitch: HomeWheel lets wheelchair users negotiate room layouts with a browser agent using live geometry, explicit transfer zones, and consent-based proposals.
about_excerpt: HomeWheel lets wheelchair users negotiate room layouts with a browser agent using live geometry, explicit transfer zones, and consent-based proposals. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Room-layout advice often sounds simple: move a dresser, rotate a table, clear a path. For someone who uses a wheelchair, however, a few centimeters can decide whether a bed, desk, or storage area is usable. The technically shortest route is not automatically the right answer. Daily routines, transfer sides, outlets, light, reach, and personal preference matter too. We wanted to build an agent experience where those lived constraints are not treated as edge cases. They are the decision-making authority. Evidence-grounded user stories The prototype includes composite user stories derived from public evidence, not invented customer testimonials: A wheelchair user needs the bed-transfer side and furniture stability preserved, even if another arrangement produces a clear route. A person needs the simulation to use their actual chair and transfer technique because access needs are not one-size-fits-all. A person adapting their home needs authority over trade-offs involving independence, safety, reach, light, storage, and daily routines. Those stories became testable requirements. HomeWheel now validates an explicit approach zone at each transfer, work, or reach destination; calculates it from the person’s movement profile; refuses to move stability-critical furniture; and shares the person’s priorities with the agent before any proposal is created. Research basis: United Spinal’s accessible studio account , wheelchair transfer focus groups , and a qualitative study of home usability . What it does HomeWheel gives a person and a browser agent the same editable floor plan. The person sets a personal movement profile, marks required destinations and their transfer, work, or reach zones, chooses what proposals should prioritize, and protects furniture positions that matter. The agent can: read the complete room and personal constraints; simulate all required and optional routes; identify movable barriers; create an exact, collision-checked proposal; compare the proposal with the live layout; and restore a baseline or previous state. Every proposal appears as a purple overlay with route evidence, exact moves, and trade-offs. Nothing moves until the person clicks Accept. If the proposal misses a lived detail, the person can reject it and explain why. The next agent sees that feedback in the workspace state and can produce a targeted revision. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the bridge between agent reasoning and the application’s actual state. HomeWheel registers eight tools directly from the page: get_workspace_state , set_mobility_profile , simulate_routes , find_barriers , create_layout_proposal , set_object_constraint , compare_layouts , and restore_layout . The key design choice is that the agent has a proposal tool, not an “automatically rearrange my room” tool. WebMCP gives the agent precise capabilities while the interface preserves human consent and makes every change inspectable. How we built it HomeWheel is a static Next.js and TypeScript application. It uses browser-side A* pathfinding over an obstacle grid, personal clearance envelopes, purpose-specific approach zones, collision-checked furniture geometry, multi-destination metrics, and turning-space detection. State is shared between direct manipulation and WebMCP tools, stored locally, and exportable as JSON. Challenges The most important challenge was not pathfinding; it was deciding where agent authority should stop. Direct mutation made the demo faster but weakened the product. We redesigned the workflow around preview, explicit acceptance, structured rejection, and feedback-aware revision. We also had to make geometric evidence understandable without pretending it was professional certification. HomeWheel clearly separates personal simulation from building-code or medical claims. Accomplishments The agent and person operate on the same live room state. Locked human constraints are enforced at the tool-validation layer. Stability-critical furniture cannot be moved by the person or the agent without first releasing that protection. Transfer, work, and reach zones are visible and validated separately from the route leading to them. Personal priorities are part of live WebMCP state rather than hidden prompt context. A proposal cannot silently mutate the room. Rejection feedback persists and is available to the next agent turn. The prototype supports authored scenarios and fully editable rooms. Public evidence is visible inside the product without being presented as fabricated user validation. The complete experience works without a backend or user account. What we learned Human-in-the-loop design becomes much more meaningful when feedback is part of the tool state, not just a chat message. The agent can optimize geometry, but the person defines what “better” means. What is next A production version could add measured floor-plan import, richer door and wall geometry, collaboration with occupational therapists, uncertainty ranges, and optional checks against local accessibility guidance. Those features would remain advisory and would continue to require real-world validation. title: Clear
pitch: Use your agent to triage incidents, build dashboards, and understand observability like never before.
about_excerpt: Use your agent to triage incidents, build dashboards, and understand observability like never before. Like Comment Story Updates Codex and Clear working through a retry storm side by side Following a failed checkout trace together and figuring out the smallest fix The moment payment attempts and checkout latency start climbing One checkout turning into three immediate payment attempts Following that same trace into the retry logs that explain the failure Watching retry traffic and checkout latency settle back down after the fix Benchmark comparing Grafana MCP vs Clear WebMCP Clear is an OpenTelemetry dashboard I can actually investigate with my coding agent Introduction Most observability dashboards have built-in agents these days, and that agent can piece together answers or make changes to the interface. But these built-in agents are isolated from your repo, skills, and context. Clear solves this by making observability visible and malleable to your coding agent. With WebMCP, humans and agents can triage issues, build dashboards, and understand incidents. Setting up Clear is as simple as pointing any* OpenTelemetry (OTel) client at our endpoints. What it does Services send metrics, logs, and traces to Clear, and users can use their agent to set thresholds that fire alerts or build custom dashboards. When an alert fires, a user or an agent can open an incident. The agent can query telemetry from Clear and create panels within the dashboard to test hypotheses. Users steer the agent in a particular direction, ask questions about the data, and work toward a patch. WebMCP enables this by allowing any WebMCP-capable agent to instantly access dashboards and logs without traditional MCP auth flows. How I built it I built Clear by creating a handful of different services: Backend hosted on Render API service Postgres database for non-telemetry data ClickHouse database for logs, metrics, and traces Go OTel Collector Simple React frontend hosted on ChatGPT Sites/Cloudflare This work was done with AI assistance while I still guided the architecture decisions and product experience. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge I overcame was collecting the OTel data and streaming it live to the client. This project started out as a fully TypeScript project, but there weren’t any good TypeScript libraries that acted as a complete OTel receiver. Rather than implementing this receiver myself, I built a small Go service that accepts and authenticates OTel traffic and forwards batches to the API service. The API service then normalizes and stores that data in ClickHouse. It also streams live events to the client using Server-Sent Events (SSE, basically a one-way WebSocket). Unfortunately, Render does not support external gRPC, so we are only able to support HTTP with JSON and Protobuf. Another challenge I ran into was synchronizing the dashboard across clients while keeping it legible to agents. On the server, we store a revision ID so that when an agent attempts to update a dashboard based on a stale version, the agent is asked to try again with the latest dashboard. We then use SSE to propagate changes across clients, and have some additional logic to resync clients that missed updates. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud of the fact that I was able to build a working OTel ingestion service and dashboard. WebMCP is the icing on the cake and what makes this project interesting, but a usable OTel dashboard is the table stakes. Without that, this entire project wouldn't have been possible. I'm also proud of the fact that Clear WebMCP is 3 times faster with smaller queries, and (anecdotally) much preferred by agents for its simple interface compared to the Grafana MCP server. While WebMCP enables this human-in-the-loop problem-solving, rebuilding the platform with agents in mind means streamlined tools and better AX (Agentic eXperience). What I learned While this project only represents one potential use of WebMCP, the potential for use across many different products is infinite. Being able to pull up a website in my browser and ask my agent a question about it is powerful in so many ways and feels like the next evolution of computer use. After starting this hackathon, I genuinely found myself wishing certain websites that I use had WebMCP. What's next for Clear Clear is very much a small vertical slice of this project rather than an enterprise-ready, drop-in Grafana replacement. I hope to refine this project in the future by fixing some issues so it can scale more easily, as well as improving the UI and UX. *Any OTel client that supports HTTP exports. We do not support gRPC. title: ProofDone
pitch: Approve exact effects and verify the customer outcome before an AI agent says done.
about_excerpt: Approve exact effects and verify the customer outcome before an AI agent says done. Like Comment Story Updates ProofDone runs beside ChatGPT, while the customer sees and controls the same live commerce experience. ProofDone verifies the cancellation, refund, fulfillment stop, and shipment prevention before reporting success. Partial execution is not success the refund failed. ProofDone keeps the captured payment visible and requires human follow-up. Native WebMCP verification in Chrome Chrome discovers the ProofDone tools directly from the page. Inspiration When I built the first ProofDone prototype during this challenge, cancellation looked like a simple agent action: call the right tool and report success. But the more I followed the intended outcome across store, fulfillment, shipment, and payment state, the less honest that became. A cancellation flow could partly succeed while the customer’s payment remained captured. That led to the question behind ProofDone: When has an agent actually earned the right to say “done”? WebMCP gives websites a structured way to work with agents. ProofDone explores what must happen around and after the tool call so that an approved action becomes a verified customer outcome. What it does The public demo is a normal commerce storefront with an agent-assisted order. The user gives only the goal: Cancel order G1-ORDER-1001. ProofDone exposes the current order truth and the currently valid resolution through WebMCP. From those structured capabilities, the agent determines that the valid cancellation also includes stopping fulfillment, preventing shipment, and refunding the captured payment. Before anything changes, the website presents the exact projected effects. The human approves those effects on the page. Approval intentionally belongs to the website, not to an agent tool. After approval, the agent can commit the resolution. But ProofDone does not treat a successful commit as customer completion. A separate fresh verification read checks the resulting state before the interface can show OUTCOME VERIFIED . That distinction also makes failure cases explicit: If material state changes after approval, the resolution becomes STALE_RESOLUTION and the commit performs zero business writes. In a controlled partial execution, all three operations are attempted, but only fulfillment and shop cancellation change state. The refund does not. ProofDone reports PARTIAL_OUTCOME , keeps the captured payment visible, and requires human follow-up instead of reporting success. Replaying the same completed request does not create a second mutation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without a structured website contract, the user or agent has to reconstruct business rules from UI state and page controls. In ProofDone, the user states the goal while the website supplies the current constraints, valid resolution, projected effects, commit result, and verification result. This creates a clearer division of responsibility: the human states intent and approves exact effects; the website owns current business state, allowed resolutions, approval validity, writes, and verification; the agent discovers and explains the correct action path through WebMCP. The result is a better user experience because the customer does not need to know the internal sequence of commerce operations, while the agent still cannot silently broaden an old approval or declare success after only part of the intended outcome occurred. WebMCP implementation ProofDone registers exactly five native WebMCP tools: get_order_truth get_order_resolution_options preview_order_resolution commit_order_resolution verify_order_resolution Together they implement: Observe → Preview → Approve → Commit → Verify There is intentionally no approval tool. Exact-effect approval is page-owned. The product page and WebMCP tools use the same ProofDone state. A preview is bound to the material state and exact projected effects. A stale preview is rejected before business writes. Commit and verification are separate claims, and duplicate replay is idempotent. The public judge path runs in a deterministic mode so judges do not need provider credentials or an account. Real-provider validation The deterministic demo proved the lifecycle in a controlled environment, but I did not want to stop there. I wanted to see whether the same observation boundary still made sense when real commerce providers exposed different parts of the state. The same codebase therefore read a Shopify Development Store order and a ShipBob Sandbox shipment without performing provider business writes. Shopify could report that the order was unfulfilled, but that alone was not enough to prove what had physically happened inside the warehouse. I treated the ShipBob evidence conservatively for the same reason: when no physical Picked milestone was visible, ProofDone did not invent one. In a separate drift test, ProofDone first observed the same ShipBob shipment when the API contained no Picked milestone. ShipBob’s own Sandbox Simulation Terminal then advanced the shipment. A fresh ProofDone read observed Picked / 100 and a changed material observation digest. The public judge path remains deterministic so anyone can reproduce it without provider credentials. The Shopify and ShipBob integrations are read-only validation paths, not production transaction writes. Execution and testing The current project has 390 logical tests covering the resolution lifecycle, including stale approval rejection, exact-effect approval, idempotent replay, separate verification, controlled partial execution, shared UI/WebMCP state, and provider read-only boundaries. The live public flow was tested with ChatGPT’s in-app browser and Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. What was difficult and what I learned Connecting the commerce APIs took work, but it was not the hardest part. The harder problem was deciding when the software had enough evidence to let an agent say “done.” One bug made that distinction concrete. After a partial execution, a duplicate retry correctly performed zero additional writes. But the interface then used the retry response—with its per-call zero counters—in place of the original execution evidence. The business behavior was safe, but the evidence shown to the user was misleading. Fixing it required preserving the original execution result separately from later attempts. The central lesson became: COMMITTED != VERIFIED Approval, execution, and verified customer outcome are three different claims. Separating them made stale-state rejection, idempotent replay, partial outcomes, and the final verification receipt easier to reason about and test. What’s next The next step after the challenge would be to turn the resolution lifecycle into a more reusable integration pattern and, only with explicit provider authorization and stronger production controls, connect controlled write adapters to real commerce systems. title: Prune
pitch: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access.
about_excerpt: WebMCP powered access-lineage infrastructure for SaaS. Trace and contain every credential created by a compromised session while preserving trusted access. Like Comment Story Updates Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage: trace compromised access, contain its branch and preserve trusted resources. The incident workspace combines credential lineage, human decisions, WebMCP audit activity and exact containment planning. The permanent receipt proves targeted credentials were revoked while the owner and trusted access remained active. Inspiration Revoking a suspicious login does not necessarily secure an account. An attacker who obtains one browser session can create independent ways back in: API keys, connected-application grants, access tokens and secondary sessions. Traditional security pages display these resources as separate lists, leaving the account owner to determine how they are related. A user may revoke the suspicious session, watch it disappear and reasonably believe recovery is complete while an API key created by that session continues working. Prune was inspired by a different mental model: Git-style lineage for account access. Instead of showing only which credentials exist, Prune records where each credential came from. When one login becomes untrusted, the owner and their personal browser agent can investigate and contain everything created from that login without destroying unrelated trusted access. ## What Prune does Prune is embedded access-lineage and account-takeover containment infrastructure for SaaS applications. Every access-producing action records: The organization and account The user and actor session The parent credential The newly created credential The credential type The creation time Redacted request metadata This produces a persistent directed graph: Unfamiliar Windows session ├── Quarterly billing export API key ├── Unfamiliar Data Sync application │ └── Child access token └── Secondary access When the owner identifies an unfamiliar login, Prune opens a recovery incident around that branch. The owner and their personal agent can then: 1. Trace every descendant credential. 2. Inspect usage and security evidence. 3. Classify recognized and unrecognized activity. 4. Preserve trusted devices and operational automation. 5. Compare counterfactual containment strategies. 6. Check lockout and operational risk. 7. Build an immutable recovery plan. 8. Complete independent step-up verification. 9. Approve the exact credential set. 10. Execute one short-lived containment capability. 11. Verify every revoked and preserved resource. 12. Generate a permanent recovery receipt. ## Why WebMCP is essential This workflow crosses sessions, API keys, connected applications, tokens, usage evidence, recovery policy and approval state. Visual browser automation would require an agent to interpret several dangerous settings pages and guess which controls correspond to which credentials. That is too ambiguous for account recovery. A single secure_account tool would also be unsafe because it would hide the investigation and human decisions behind one opaque action. Prune instead exposes 28 granular WebMCP tools covering: - Incident investigation - Session and credential inspection - Descendant tracing - Human classification - Preservation constraints - Counterfactual simulation - Lockout and operational-impact checks - Immutable plan creation - Step-up verification status - Exact-plan approval - One-time containment - Independent outcome verification - Recovery-receipt generation Tool availability changes with the incident’s server-controlled phase. Investigation tools are available first. Planning tools appear only after sufficient evidence has been classified. execute_approved_containment appears only after independent step-up verification and exact human approval. It disappears after its one allowed execution. Retaining an old browser tool reference provides no authority because every request is authenticated, tenant-scoped, schema-validated and checked against current server policy again. ## Human, agent and website collaboration Each participant contributes information the others do not possess. The website knows: - Which credentials exist - Which session created each credential - Their parent-child relationships - Their current status and usage - Which actions policy permits The personal agent can: - Investigate structured evidence - Trace the complete credential branch - Identify unresolved decisions - Ask focused questions - Compare containment alternatives - Explain consequences - Verify the final result The human knows: - Which devices belong to them - Which applications they intentionally connected - Which automation must remain operational - Which activity they recognize - Whether the exact recovery plan should be approved The agent never determines authorization. It never receives passwords, raw API keys, access tokens, verification codes or execution cookies. ## What we built Prune includes: - Independent server-side browser sessions - Secure HTTP-only session cookies - One-time API-key and application-token issuance - Digest-only secret persistence - Connected-application grants and usable child tokens - A normalized PostgreSQL credential graph - Parent-child validation and cycle rejection - Ancestor and descendant traversal - Usage and security-event recording - Manual session-only revocation - Recursive branch containment - Incident creation and evidence collection - Human classifications - Preservation constraints - Three counterfactual containment strategies - Lockout and operational-impact analysis - Canonical immutable plan hashes - Short-lived step-up verification - Exact human approval - One-time execution authority - Idempotent revocation - Post-execution verification - Permanent recovery receipts - Server-sent real-time incident updates - 28 dynamically exposed WebMCP tools - Secret-redacted WebMCP results and audit trails - A complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable - A SaaS integration control plane - Signed event ingestion and replay protection - Instrumentation coverage checks - Confirmed revocation webhooks - A reference TypeScript integration SDK - Automated unit, integration, multi-browser and accessibility tests ## What is real in the demonstration Northstar is a working reference SaaS application protected by Prune. The demonstration creates two genuine independent browser sessions. The unfamiliar browser issues a real API key and connects an application that receives a real child token. These credentials authenticate against protected endpoints. The owner then revokes only the visible suspicious session. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the independently issued API key still returns HTTP 200. This proves why ordinary session revocation is incomplete. A fresh recovery scenario is then processed through Prune’s WebMCP contract. The incident is investigated, the four-credential branch is classified, preservation constraints are recorded and an immutable plan is built. The owner performs step-up verification and approves the exact plan. Prune exposes one short-lived execution capability and recursively revokes the approved branch. After containment: - The attacker API key returns HTTP 401. - The connected application token returns HTTP 401. - The unfamiliar session remains signed out. - The owner remains authenticated. - The trusted phone remains active. - Deployment automation remains active. - Execution authority is consumed. - A permanent recovery receipt records the outcome. No incident, credential relationship, status code, plan, approval, revocation result or receipt shown in the operational interface is hard-coded. Native tool discovery was verified in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. The recorded recovery sequence uses a deterministic browser-agent evaluation against the same registered WebMCP contract, live deployment, authenticated routes, application services and production database. ## How WebMCP was implemented The authenticated incident page feature-detects: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Prune registers only the tool contracts permitted for the incident’s current phase. Registrations are owned by an AbortController, allowing obsolete capabilities to be removed immediately when state changes. Every tool calls: /api/incidents/:incidentId/webmcp/:tool The server then: 1. Authenticates the browser session. 2. Scopes organization, account and incident ownership. 3. Validates the tool-specific input with Zod. 4. Rechecks the current incident phase. 5. Calls the shared application service. 6. Applies security policy. 7. Redacts sensitive results. 8. Records a structured audit event. The human interface, HTTP routes and WebMCP tools therefore use the same authorization, lineage and recovery services. ## Challenges The hardest challenge was preserving a useful agent experience without transferring security authority to the agent. Recovery required several d
video_transcript_excerpt: One compromised session can become several independent ways back into an account, an API key, an application grant, a child token, even another session. This is North Star, a working SaaS application protected by Prune. An unfamiliar browser signs in independently, creates a real API key, then connects an application that receives its own usable token. Prune records each credential, its parent, and the session that created it. The key reaches protected data, 200. The owner revokes only the visible session. The unfamiliar browser is signed out, but the same key still returns 200. Session revocation looks successful. Account recovery was not complete. For agent-assisted recovery, Prune creates a fresh isolated account through the same production services. In ChatGPT, Prune exposes incident-scoped Web MCP tools. This deterministic browser agent evaluation exercises that same registered tool contract against the live deployment. It summarizes the incident, lists the account sessions, traces every descendant, inspects credential usage, and finds remaining access paths. Every call passes through the authenticated application service and appears in Prune's audit trail. No password, API key, or token is returned to the agent. The owner identifies the unfamiliar branch and requires the trusted phone and deployment automation to remain available. Prune records those human decisions, compares containment strategies, and simulates the result without changing account state. Lockout and operational impact are checked before an immutable plan is created. The agent cannot approve its own recommendation. The owner verifies directly with Prune, reviews the exact plan, and approves it. Only then does a short-lived, one-time execution capability appear. Prune executes the approved branch and removes the unfamiliar session, API key, application grant, and child token. The agent independently checks every targeted credential, verifies trusted access, and scans for anything left behind. Both attacker credentials now return 401. The owner session, trusted phone, and deployment automation remain active. Execution authority is consumed. Every outcome is preserved in a permanent recovery receipt. Prune gives SaaS products credential lineage, human-gated containment, and verifiable recovery through Web MCP.

title: revAIew Evidence Room
pitch: revAIew lets agents investigate claims through WebMCP while people decide what gets through and receive a source-bound receipt.
about_excerpt: revAIew lets agents investigate claims through WebMCP while people decide what gets through and receive a source-bound receipt. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can generate and recommend faster than people can review. The hard problem is no longer only finding information; it is keeping evidence, uncertainty, and authority clear before an answer influences the next action. The unit-distance conjecture offered a concrete test. OpenAI reports that an internal model generated a counterexample. A nine-author companion paper publishes a short, human-verified account of the mathematics. Those are related facts, but mathematical verification does not independently reproduce the internal model run. revAIew keeps that distinction visible. What it does revAIew Evidence Room gives a person and an agent one shared evidence workspace. Five page-scoped WebMCP tools let the agent inspect claims, trace public sources, compare recorded positions, and retrieve a pre-registered pressure test. A sixth tool stages a visible evidence packet containing the selected claims, source IDs, uncertainty, missing proof, and next test. The registered site-tool path ends there. It exposes no tool that can choose, confirm, or create a receipt. The person sees the same packet, selects adopt, enforce, challenge, hold, or discard, and explicitly confirms the choice in the visible browser interface. That action creates a browser-local SHA-256 receipt bound to the packet and current fixed corpus. The receipt is an integrity record, not an identity signature, certification, or proof that the underlying claim is true. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent must infer evidence relationships from presentation and visual controls. With WebMCP, the live page exposes narrow, structured operations backed by the same services as the human interface. The agent and person therefore share exact claim identifiers, source mappings, classifications, uncertainty, and pressure tests. The improvement is not unlimited autonomy. It is a clearer, more inspectable handoff between structured agent investigation and visible human judgment. What people and agents do together The agent: reads the fixed public evidence corpus traces claims to canonical public sources preserves disagreement and missing proof retrieves a registered falsification test stages a visible evidence packet The person: sees the same evidence state judges whether the support is sufficient chooses the consequential action explicitly confirms the decision receives or clears the browser-local receipt How we built it The standalone challenge package uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, and the imperative WebMCP API through document.modelContext.registerTool . Every tool has a closed JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false , bounded runtime validation, and WebMCP behavior annotations. Public source content is marked potentially untrusted. An abort signal removes page-scoped registrations when the route leaves, and partial registration is cleaned up if setup fails. The human interface and WebMCP tools call the same deterministic evidence services. Receipt verification recomputes its SHA-256 value and revalidates every evidence-derived field against the current corpus before trusting browser storage. Focused tests and a checked-in deterministic contract exercise cover all six tool definitions, strict input handling, source mappings, staging, receipt verification, and the absence of a decision or receipt-creation tool. Challenge-period work revAIew existed before the WebMCP Challenge. During the submission period, we added the six-tool WebMCP adapter, bounded public evidence corpus, shared visible staging flow, human confirmation boundary, receipt verification, focused tests, deterministic contract exercise, and standalone public MIT-licensed package. This submission asks judges to evaluate that WebMCP extension, not the pre-existing product concept. Boundaries This is a small fixed-corpus demonstration, not live web search or a universal AI verifier. It does not prove broad browser compatibility, model quality, user adoption, or categorical prevention of browser automation. WebMCP annotations are descriptive hints, not an authorization system. Flagship sources: https://openai.com/index/model-disproves-discrete-geometry-conjecture/ https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20695 The agent investigates. You decide what gets through.
