title: Peira
pitch: An instrument for the US benefits system. Earn one more dollar at the wrong income and a family can lose thousands in benefits at once. Peira simplifies this complexity one step at a time.
about_excerpt: An instrument for the US benefits system. Earn one more dollar at the wrong income and a family can lose thousands in benefits at once. Peira simplifies this complexity one step at a time. Like Comment Story Updates What if you wanted to fix the cliff at 80k as a policy maker What you first see after entering your details Inspiration I work in AI safety, in mechanistic interpretability. We understand something as complex as a transformer with a few simple probes: knock a component out and see what breaks, trace a behavior to the circuit that causes it, look for the smallest intervention that changes the output. The US benefits system is another machine nobody can see inside — thousands of pages of interacting rules. So I pointed the same probes at it. Peira is Greek for "probe." It's the root of the word empirical . What it does Peira maps what a Colorado family actually keeps at every income level, and pins every benefit cliff to the program that causes it. Then it gives you the tools to investigate your own map: Knock a program out and see which other programs move. Trace a cliff to the exact eligibility rule that flips. Overlay a changed life — marriage, a new baby, different hours — on top of today's. Search an income × childcare grid for safe regions. Find the smallest legal rule change that would make a cliff disappear, and watch it heal on screen. Why WebMCP Cliff charts already exist. PolicyEngine's CliffWatch and the Atlanta Fed's CLIFF suite are good ones. But a chart can't answer "why?" or "what if?". A chatbot can answer, but it can't compute anything trustworthy or show its work. WebMCP puts the tools inside the page, next to the chart. The agent runs the probes. The person edits the household card, clicks the cliffs, scrubs the map, and decides what matters. Every action lands in one shared log — human moves in green, agent moves in purple. That's the thing that wasn't possible before. The person can't drive a 600MB rules engine. The agent doesn't know this family's life. Together, "is my raise actually worth it?" gets a real answer — and the person learns why , instead of taking a chatbot's word for it. There's no retrieval anywhere in Peira. The thousands a family loses at the wrong income isn't written in any document — it only exists once you run the law. Every answer here is a computed experiment on a real rules engine, not a search result. How I built it The engine is policyengine-us, the open-source model of actual US tax and benefit law. A FastAPI backend on Render runs it. A React frontend on Netlify draws the map. Eleven WebMCP tools connect the two, registered through document.modelContext and validated with zod. Two rules shaped every tool. First: the agent can't see the canvas, so every reply is about a kilobyte of findings — cliffs, recovery points, safe regions — never raw data dumps. The screen keeps the detail; the reply says what it means. Second: the agent can't be trusted with the engine, so policy edits pass through a server-side whitelist with bounds. A parameter path the agent makes up never reaches the engine. Challenges I ran into Getting the balance between person and agent right. I didn't want a chatbot that hands out answers — today's benefits tools already do that, and the person learns nothing. So everything the agent can do, a person can do by hand, and each side can see what the other did. The person is a participant, not a spectator. Accomplishments that I'm proud of WebMCP is pull-only: the page can never tell the agent "the human just changed something." So every tool reply includes a digest of what the person did since the agent's last call — card edits, cliff clicks, probes run by hand. Change the daycare cost yourself, ask "what do you make of what I just did?", and the agent answers from the digest. It saw you. What I learned The programs are secretly wired together. Remove TANF and this family silently loses $5,139 of SNAP, through a rule called broad-based categorical eligibility. No chart shows that dependency. I found it the same way you find circuits in a transformer: by knocking something out and watching what else broke. What I learned The programs are secretly wired together. Remove TANF and this family silently loses $5,139 of SNAP, through a rule called broad-based categorical eligibility. No chart shows that dependency. I found it the same way you find circuits in a transformer: by knocking something out and watching what else broke. What's next for Peira More states. Colorado is the verified wedge, and the instrument is built state-parameterized — other states with full childcare-subsidy models are next.  What if that B2B SaaS could support WebMCP without the vendor needing to make any changes? A WebMCP browser extension could uplift it to the latest tech, until the next version - possibly years away - supports WebMCP natively. 

 What it does 

 The product is a browser framework that uplifts a legacy SaaS to support WebMCP, even if the SaaS itself does not expose tools to the agent. The browser extension jumps in. It provides full context to the agent: backend power plus browser tab content.

title: Dwellwise
pitch: Plan an apartment with an AI agent, supercharged with WebMCP
about_excerpt: Plan an apartment with an AI agent, supercharged with WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Main screen Fully furnished apartment layout ChatGPT using webMCP 3D Preview Inspiration Apartment hunting is a high-stakes guessing game. A floor plan can look spacious while hiding the things that matter: whether a bed fits, whether a dining table blocks circulation, or whether a room still feels livable once real furniture is inside it. We wanted to make apartment planning more honest and more collaborative. A person should be able to edit a plan visually, while an AI agent can understand the same apartment through safe, structured actions, not by guessing where to click. What it does Dwellwise is an apartment planner for testing a real layout before committing to it. You can create a private apartment project, draw and reshape its exterior and interior walls, add doors and windows, furnish rooms with real-world dimensions, and inspect the same saved layout in 2D and 3D. The 3D view includes an illustrative sunlight preview, editable supported finishes, and camera controls. The important difference is that Dwellwise is WebMCP-ready . Compatible browser agents can inspect the open apartment and use semantic tools to add or update furniture, walls, openings, exterior corners, finishes, preview settings, and history. They do not need to simulate clicks or drag pixels. How we built it Dwellwise is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, PostgreSQL, and WebMCP. One meter-based scene document powers the 2D editor, saved project data, furniture-fit checks, and 3D renderer. Walls, exterior corners, doors, and windows define the apartment; rooms are derived from the closed wall network; furniture keeps its own dimensions, position, rotation, and room assignment. For agent interaction, Dwellwise progressively registers page-scoped WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . Dashboard tools manage the current browser’s projects. Editor tools inspect and modify only the apartment already open in that browser. Both people and agents use the same application commands. That means agent edits receive the same geometry validation, collision checks, optimistic revision protection, save queue, undo/redo history, and visible UI updates as human edits. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not exposing buttons as tools. It was preserving the product’s rules when an agent changes geometry. Wall edits can split or merge rooms, change furniture assignments, and affect doors and windows. Openings need to stay attached to their host wall, respect wall boundaries, and behave predictably when they meet another opening. A stale browser tab must never silently overwrite a newer apartment state. We addressed this by building shared, atomic architecture commands and using revision-checked saves. WebMCP tools call those same commands rather than maintaining a separate AI-only editing path. We also kept sunlight honest: it is presented as a visual planning aid, not as a quantitative daylight or building-code analysis. Accomplishments that we’re proud of A complete private multi-project apartment workspace without requiring an account. One shared scene model for 2D planning, 3D rendering, geometry validation, and furniture fit. Semantic WebMCP tools for the dashboard and editor, with 32 distinct registered tool names. Shared human and agent editing commands for furniture, architecture, finishes, preview controls, and undo/redo. Revision-safe saving that prevents stale tabs from overwriting newer work. Browser-owned project isolation: tools never receive cookies, owner IDs, raw database access, or unrestricted scene writes. A normal visual editor that remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned An agent-ready app is not just a traditional UI with an AI layer attached. The tools need to express the real product concepts: walls, openings, rooms, furniture, revisions, and confirmation, not pointer gestures. WebMCP works best when it makes the safe path the easy path: bounded tools, clear inputs, shared validation, visible results, and a person still in control of destructive actions. What’s next We want to make complex floor-plan recreation more reliable, improve the visual fidelity of 3D apartment previews, and continue hardening the geometry and agent workflows against messy real-world plans. title: thinkPuff
pitch: A WebMCP powered bakery operations board where an AI agent discovers live tools in the dashboard and resolves real time shop crises.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP powered bakery operations board where an AI agent discovers live tools in the dashboard and resolves real time shop crises.

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 At 8:03 a.m., the bakery is already losing the morning. 

 The butter delivery never arrived. There are butter croissants on the menu, two orders that depend on them, a sourdough order that should have gone out three minutes ago, and two customers waiting for a reply. None of these problems is catastrophic. Together, they are exactly the sort of mess that makes a one-person shop feel impossible. 

 That was the starting point for thinkPuff . 

 We wanted to make a bakery back office that felt like a place someone might actually work: slightly chaotic, a little charming, and full of small decisions that matter. The cat in the sidebar is called Brioche. The language is warm. But underneath it is an operations board with real dependencies: stock affects the menu, the menu affects orders, and all of it affects what needs attention. 

 Then we gave the board a second kind of user: an AI agent. 

 What it does 

 thinkPuff is a bakery operations board that opens on a deliberately bad morning. Seven urgent problems are red, three are amber. 

 Butter is out. Three menu items still need butter. Marc’s croissants and Sofia’s walnut levain cannot be fulfilled. Leïla’s sourdough is overdue. Walnuts are low. Two customers have been waiting for an answer. 

 A baker can handle all of it by clicking the normal action buttons beside each alert. There is no AI-only version of the product. 

 But the same page publishes 16 WebMCP tools. An agent can ask what is wrong, inspect stock, menu items, orders, and messages, then decide what to do. It can reorder butter, mark Leïla’s order ready, restock walnuts, and reply to Marc and Théo. 

 The satisfying part is what happens after the butter order. One action changes the state of the shop. Butter is back in stock; the three affected menu items are no longer impossible; Marc and Sofia’s orders can be fulfilled again. Six red alerts disappear because they were all consequences of the same missing delivery. 

 There is no hidden fix_morning() command. The agent has to discover the available tools and connect the dots itself. 

 How we built it 

 We built thinkPuff as a single-page bakery operations simulation. Its data model holds supplies, menu items, orders, customer messages, shop status, and a running activity log. 

 The important part is that alerts are derived rather than stored as a static list. When the butter supply changes, the app recalculates which menu items depend on it, which orders are affected, and which alerts still deserve to exist. That makes the red-to-green moment a consequence of the model instead of a visual trick. 

 WebMCP tools are registered in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The page exposes read tools such as get_alerts , get_supplies , get_menu , get_orders , and get_messages . It also exposes action tools including reorder_supply , mark_86 , put_back_on_menu , mark_order_ready , reply_to_message , and text_customer . 

 Two tools, set_price and set_shop_open , intentionally have no matching interface buttons. We added them to prove the point of runtime discovery: an agent can find a capability that a person cannot see on the current screen, such as raising the chocolate tart to 7 euros. 

 Actions that would feel like real work—reordering, replying, or texting—pause briefly before finishing. It is a small detail, but it keeps the demo from feeling like the dashboard is teleporting between states. Every manual or agent action also appears in the activity log. 

 Challenges we faced 

 The first challenge was resisting the obvious shortcut. 

 A polished demo could have faked the whole experience with a single script: show a crisis, press a button, turn everything green. We wanted the opposite. The agent needed enough individual tools to make choices, and the board needed enough real relationships that those choices had consequences. 

 That meant spending time on unglamorous questions. Does a product go off the menu as soon as a required supply is unavailable? Should an order be blocked or refunded? What happens to the alert when the supply comes back? How do we make the UI explain that chain without making it look like a spreadsheet? 

 We also had to make the agent’s actions understandable. If an agent changes the board without leaving a trace, it feels magical for about five seconds and suspicious after that. The activity log became our receipt: it shows what happened, whether it was done manually or by the agent, and lets the changing alerts explain the outcome. 

 Finally, we were trying to avoid the usual sterile dashboard look. A bakery is not a bank. We used a quieter, more editorial visual language, then let the urgency come from the information itself: pulsing red dots, overdue orders, and a board that visibly relaxes as the work gets done. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP made more sense to us once we stopped thinking about it as a way to let an AI “read a webpage.” 

 Reading the board is useful, but it is only the beginning. The interesting part is that the page can describe what it is able to do, and an agent can combine those capabilities in response to a situation it has never seen before. 

 We also learned that the model is only as useful as the system it is allowed to operate. Clear tools, honest state, and visible side effects make the interaction feel much less like a trick. The agent does not need to be told that butter affects croissants; it can inspect the board, use the tools available, and watch the result come back through the same live state the baker sees. 

 What’s next 

 The next version would keep the bakery feel but make the simulation more operationally deep: saved data, scheduled supplier deliveries, order timing, customer preferences, and permission levels for actions that contact someone outside the shop. 

 For this project, though, we wanted to stay with one morning, one missing delivery, and one useful idea: an agent should not just point at the mess. It should be able to help clean it up.

title: AdGate
pitch: AdGate creates ad opportunities for the AI-native era: pay a small fee for instant AI access, or unlock the same insight free through a sponsor-supported experience. Which do you choose?
about_excerpt: AdGate creates ad opportunities for the AI-native era: pay a small fee for instant AI access, or unlock the same insight free through a sponsor-supported experience. Which do you choose? Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The arrival of AI agents is dramatically changing how people consume web content. In the past, people would visit and read websites one by one. Today, AI can collect information on their behalf by scraping sources such as technical blogs. This is a great user experience for end users. However, it can also mean that website operators and the businesses that advertise on those sites lose their opportunity to reach users. This product was inspired by that problem. I wanted agents to be able to use a publisher’s structured capabilities while keeping people clearly in control of how access is granted. By combining WebMCP with x402, I wanted to explore a model where users who value convenience can make a micropayment for a nearly automated experience, while users who do not want to pay can access premium content by viewing a short advertisement. What it does For this project, I created a fictional recipe website. It includes a WebMCP-compatible tool called analyze_recipe , which provides more detailed analysis as a premium feature. There are two ways to access the premium feature: View an owned sponsor message (advertisement) for eight seconds. Explicitly approve a 0.01 testnet USDC x402 payment on Base Sepolia. Both paths authorize the same protected analysis endpoint. The original tool invocation then resumes with one structured result containing a recipe summary, nutrition notes, practical suggestions, and a general-information disclaimer. The same gate is also used by the visible Analyze this recipe button, so people and agents use one coherent product flow rather than separate experiences. I felt WebMCP was a good fit because agents can discover and invoke typed, page-owned capabilities instead of scraping a page or guessing which buttons to click. Users can make an important decision in the middle of the same invocation without losing the shared context. How we built it The React/Vite frontend registers analyze_recipe with document.modelContext.registerTool , with a navigator.modelContext compatibility fallback. A shared GateCoordinator keeps one request alive while the page renders the sponsor or payment experience, propagates cancellation, and resolves the result exactly once. The x402-enabled resource server, built with Hono, manages authorization and canonical deterministic analysis. Sponsor sessions, single-use grants, and their consumption state are stored in a named Cloudflare Durable Object. For the payment path, the app displays Base Sepolia terms before wallet access and then uses x402 exact-payment authorization. An optional Hono/viem facilitator verifies and settles the testnet payment. The browser never holds a private key, and the AI never controls the wallet. I used Codex to turn product decisions into executable specifications, build the frontend/server/facilitator boundaries, write focused tests, diagnose lifecycle and payment-receipt issues, create fake-host browser journeys, and run the final release checks. Human decisions remained explicit for product scope, payment policy, security constraints, deployment, and publication. Both the frontend and backend are deployed on Cloudflare. Challenges we ran into One challenge was deciding how to combine WebMCP and x402, as well as who should manage the wallet and where it should be managed. For the smoothest user experience, a server-managed wallet such as Privy could be a good option. However, this project focuses on WebMCP, where people and AI work together in a visible browser environment. For that reason, I deliberately chose a conventional MetaMask wallet for this demo. This is only a choice for the current demo. In the future, I believe the product should support WalletConnect and allow users to choose flexibly between wallet options such as MetaMask and Privy. With this architecture, I separated the responsibilities of AI and human interaction. The AI handles the process automatically up to the payment step. As the human-in-the-loop, the person reviews the payment details. If they decide not to pay, they can view an advertisement and be guided to premium access instead. Designing this architecture was the most difficult part of the project. Accomplishments that we're proud of Although the development period was short, I am proud that I was able to learn WebMCP and combine it with x402 and Cloudflare technologies to turn this idea into a working product. I spent more time than usual thinking through the idea and designing the architecture. It is a very simple demo, but I am proud that I was able to build it as a new advertising model for the AI-native era. What we learned The biggest lesson was gaining a practical understanding of WebMCP. Building with it helped me understand how it differs from MCP. Because WebMCP is based in a visible browser environment, I think it makes it easier to build products with a clear separation of responsibilities between people and AI. I also found this to be highly compatible with x402. What's next for AdGate Next, I would like to expand this gate to other structured publisher resources, such as news, research, and creator tools. To make it more broadly useful, I would like to build a dashboard for sponsors and make the supported blockchains and assets more flexible. For production, the payment path would need authentication, rate limits, monitoring, treasury controls, stronger key management, and evaluation of production payment rails. I would also like to explore privacy-preserving sponsor measurement and observability while maintaining a clear boundary for explicit human choice. title: LivingPage
pitch: A page that changes with your questions.
about_excerpt: A page that changes with your questions. Like Comment Story Updates The original reading view before any agent actions. Agent-generated explanations and verification appear directly beside the relevant passages. The Layers panel shows the agent’s changes, sources, and resolved requests alongside the article. Inspiration When something on a page raises a question, we usually have to look it up. We copy passages one by one, search in another tab or paste them into a chat, read the explanation, and then return to the original page. I wanted to eliminate this back-and-forth and make it possible to complete the whole process without leaving the page. What it does While reading an article, you can leave marks such as Explain, Simplify, and more on the parts you are interested in, and send those requests all at once. Instead of asking the agent one question at a time whenever something comes up, you can keep reading while leaving your questions on the page, then ask the agent only once when you are ready . The agent processes the queued requests together and makes the results available directly on the page. How we built it The page exposes both reading and editing capabilities to the agent as WebMCP tools. We also implemented web page and PDF importing, research layers, Undo / Redo, maps using Leaflet, and sandboxed interactive widgets generated by the agent . Originally, I wanted LivingPage to work directly with the web page the user is already viewing, instead of requiring them to import a URL into LivingPage. However, because development time was limited, the current version uses an import-based approach. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest parts was coming up with an idea that felt like a new experience unique to WebMCP. Many of the ideas I considered ended up moving toward things similar to existing demos, such as agent-controlled UIs or games, so I struggled to find a different direction. The idea for LivingPage came from something that felt like it should already be possible with chat AI, but still was not commonly done in practice. Instead of bringing information from the page into the chat, bring the AI's results back into the original page. I arrived at this idea only three days before the deadline , so from that point on, it became a race against time. Accomplishments that we're proud of I decided to enter the WebMCP Challenge, and although LivingPage is not perfect, I was able to turn the idea into something that actually works and make it all the way to submission. I think the rapid progress of AI tools made it possible for one person to build this much in such a short period of time. LivingPage is also the first program I have ever publicly released. More than achieving a perfect level of polish, I am proud that I was able to turn the idea into a working project and release it to the public. What we learned By actually using WebMCP, I realized that when an agent needs to operate multiple tools one after another, it can still take a noticeable amount of time. For an experience like LivingPage, where multiple requests are processed at once, processing speed has a major impact on the user experience . I also learned that if I keep working until I am completely satisfied, the project may never be finished. With limited time, it is also important to decide where to stop, finish a working version, and release it . What's next for LivingPage I expect AI agents to become faster and able to handle multiple tasks much more quickly than they can today. When that happens, an experience like LivingPage — where you leave multiple questions while reading, process them together, and have the results returned directly to the page — could become more natural and practical. I also want to develop LivingPage beyond the current approach of importing URLs into a separate reader. Ultimately, I want the web page you are already viewing to become the "Living Page" itself — changing and growing based on the user's questions. title: Asia Trend Radar — Read-Only WebMCP Tools
pitch: Six safe WebMCP tools that turn live Asian trend signals into evidence-backed answers.
about_excerpt:
Six safe WebMCP tools that turn live Asian trend signals into evidence-backed answers.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive mobile workflow — the same read-only discovery experience at a 390 × 844 viewport. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Six read-only WebMCP tools — English judge-facing interface with a safe website fallback. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Real source-backed Taiwan trends — five live results for Taiwan rising searches in the previous 24 hours. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive mobile workflow — the same read-only discovery experience at a 390 × 844 viewport. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Six read-only WebMCP tools — English judge-facing interface with a safe website fallback. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Real source-backed Taiwan trends — five live results for Taiwan rising searches in the previous 24 hours. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Responsive mobile workflow — the same read-only discovery experience at a 390 × 844 viewport. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Trend research is often fragmented across dashboards, search pages, and inconsistent source formats. An agent may find a popular topic but still lack the evidence needed to explain where it came from, how fresh it is, or whether the source is healthy. Copying results between a website and an assistant also loses structured context and uncertainty. 

 We wanted the website itself to expose a controlled interface to an agent without creating a separate plugin or giving the agent administrative access. 

 What it does 

 Asia Trend Radar exposes six browser-native, read-only tools: 

 
 search_radar_trends searches trend signals by market, category, signal type, time window, confidence, source, and sort order. 
 get_radar_trend retrieves one topic together with its supporting evidence. 
 search_radar_videos searches available video signals and returns an honest empty result when no qualifying data exists. 
 list_radar_sources reports source availability and operational status. 
 list_radar_markets lists supported markets and their enabled state. 
 list_radar_categories lists normalized categories. 
 

 A judge can request Taiwan's top five rising searches from the previous 24 hours, inspect a Chinese-language topic ID, review source status, and query markets, categories, and video signals. The six-tool WebMCP surface exposes no management, scheduling, membership, payment, publishing, or write operations. Oversized requests such as limit=500 are rejected. 

 Why WebMCP 

 A normal webpage is designed for people to read. WebMCP adds a machine-readable interaction layer that lets a compatible browser agent discover the site's capabilities, understand each input schema, and invoke the correct operation directly. 

 This project uses WebMCP as the core interaction layer. The agent no longer needs to scrape rendered text or guess button locations, and it does not receive unrestricted API access. People can still use the same responsive website when native WebMCP is unavailable. 

 Human-agent collaboration 

 The agent handles structured retrieval: it selects a read-only tool, applies the requested filters, and returns topic evidence and source status. The human remains responsible for interpretation and every downstream content or publishing decision. The agent cannot modify the radar, change sources, schedule jobs, or invoke management operations. 

 How it was built 

 The interface uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and React Router and is hosted on Cloudflare Pages with Pages Functions. 

 Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with a strict JSON Schema and read-only annotations. Tools that may return external material are marked as containing untrusted content. 

 Native WebMCP calls and visible website searches share one server-side Radar adapter. The adapter handles field normalization, sorting, cache behavior, stale-data labels, bounded retries, sanitized errors, and a fixed allowlist of read-only upstream routes. Credentials remain server-side and are never returned to the webpage or tool output. 

 Safety and truthful data handling 

 
 Every public tool is read-only. 
 Strict schemas reject unknown and unsafe inputs. 
 limit=500 is rejected because the maximum is 50. 
 Unsafe topic-ID formats and traversal attempts are rejected. 
 External titles are treated as untrusted content. 
 Missing video data produces an empty result, not fabricated records. 
 Relative popularity is not described as an exact search or view count. 
 User-supplied URLs must be public HTTPS links and are rejected before storage when they contain credentials, fragments, signed parameters, or private-access tokens. 
 Upstream records pass through field allowlists and secret redaction before cache, UI, or WebMCP output. 
 No management operation is registered as a WebMCP tool, and the Radar adapter allowlist excludes management routes. 
 

 Work completed during the challenge 

 The underlying trend product, regional discovery interface, source pipeline, scoring concepts, evidence model, filters, and original responsive interface existed before the challenge. We do not claim those foundations as new WebMCP development. 

 After August 25, 2026, the challenge work added the isolated competition edition, six read-only WebMCP Radar tools, strict schemas and safety annotations, a dedicated server-side read-only adapter, native discovery and invocation support, honest empty and stale states, safe browser fallback behavior, localized topic-ID handling, an English judging interface, and challenge-specific validation evidence. Dated commits and the repository's PREEXISTING_WORK.md and NEW_WORK_LOG.md document the boundary. 

 Challenges 

 Native WebMCP support is browser-dependent, so we had to distinguish genuine tool discovery and invocation from ordinary website automation. Native calls were verified in a compatible in-app browser. Safari was tested only as a normal website fallback; Safari native WebMCP is explicitly NOT RUN . 

 Localized identifiers were another edge case. Chinese topic IDs had to survive URL encoding and route decoding without weakening validation. 

 The central product challenge was handling uncertainty honestly. A successful query can legitimately return zero videos. The tool preserves that result rather than filling the interface with demonstration data. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Six native, discoverable, read-only WebMCP tools. 
 Real Taiwan trend results from the production competition URL. 
 Safe lookup of localized Chinese topic IDs. 
 Honest video empty states with no fabricated records. 
 Rejection of oversized inputs and absence of management tools. 
 One shared data contract for human and agent interfaces. 
 Responsive desktop, tablet, and mobile validation. 
 20 test files and 305 tests passing at the final implementation checkpoint, together with TypeScript, ESLint, production build, dependency audit, secret scanning, and whitespace checks. 
 

 What we learned 

 A trustworthy agent interface needs strict schemas, bounded inputs, explicit read-only semantics, untrusted-content warnings, safe errors, and evidence that the browser actually discovered and invoked the tools. An honest empty answer can be more valuable than an impressive-looking fake result. 

 Potential impact 

 Content teams, researchers, and analysts can ask an agent for narrowly defined trend candidates while retaining source status, timestamps, confidence, and uncertainty. More broadly, WebMCP can turn existing websites into controlled agent-ready interfaces without replacing their human experience or exposing administrative APIs. 

 What's next 

 Future work could add more authorized sources, richer provenance views, and user-controlled workflows. Any write capability would remain separate and require explicit human confirmation. The competition surface intentionally remains read-only.

title: klipvia
pitch: Video editing is a hundred precise operations, not one prompt. Klipvia exposes those operations as WebMCP tools so a person and an agent can collaborate on the same timeline.
about_excerpt: Video editing is a hundred precise operations, not one prompt. Klipvia exposes those operations as WebMCP tools so a person and an agent can collaborate on the same timeline. Like Comment Story Updates vide editor Inspiration I was cutting a nine-lesson course and had to place about forty overlays across it — a keycap where the presenter presses Ctrl, a lower third where he says his name, a callout on the part of the spreadsheet he is pointing at. Every one of those placements is trivial to describe and tedious to do. "Put the keycap where he presses Ctrl" is a complete instruction. Executing it means finding the moment in the transcript, converting source time to timeline time through the clip's in-point, building the overlay, placing it, and then looking at the frame to check it did not land on top of the save dialog. Generative video tools answer a different question. They make you a new video from a prompt. They cannot help with the video you already have and the forty small, exact decisions left in it. That work is structured, long-horizon, and needs to stay under your control — which is exactly the shape WebMCP fits. What it does Klipvia is a browser video editor. You author animations in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, cut them together with footage, audio and captions on a timeline, and export either a clip with a real alpha channel or a finished film with sound. Then it publishes itself. The editor registers 89 WebMCP tools that drive the same editor a hand drives — the same functions, the same validation, the same undo stack. An agent in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome can read your timeline, find a phrase in a transcript, cut the filler words out of a take, build a lower third, place it at the right second, screenshot the composited frame to check its own work, and render the result. You watch it happen on the timeline in front of you, and if you disagree you press ⌘Z. It also runs with no server at all . Point a static host at public/ and the whole application is the browser: projects in IndexedDB, footage in the Origin Private File System, renders encoded on the spot with WebCodecs. It decides which it is at boot by asking /api/health , and nothing above that line knows the difference. How I built it No framework and no bundler. The editor is ~27,500 lines of hand-written ES modules in public/ , served unbundled. The optional server is 4,583 lines of TypeScript on Bun and Hono. There is exactly one runtime dependency ( hono , server-side only) plus a vendored mp4-muxer . The code editor, icon set, subtitle parser, zip writer, tooltips and syntax highlighter are all hand-rolled, so the tool keeps working offline — which is exactly when you want a local video editor. Three pieces make the rest possible: A virtual clock. public/runtime.js is injected into every preview iframe before your code and replaces performance.now , Date.now , requestAnimationFrame , setTimeout , setInterval , and drives document.getAnimations() directly. That makes arbitrary HTML/CSS/JS animation seekable , which makes it frame-exact-exportable, which is what lets an animation be a real alpha overlay layer on a video timeline. One arithmetic, four render backends. public/effects.js defines crop, flip, rotate, colour, blend and shadow as numbers, and emits the CSS half for the live preview while src/sequence.ts reads the same numbers to emit the ffmpeg half, in the same fixed order. So the compositor preview, the server ffmpeg render, the browser WebCodecs render and the MediaRecorder capture all place layers identically. What you scrub is what you get. One editor facade. Every mutating operation — from the UI, from a keyboard shortcut, or from a WebMCP tool — goes through the same facade in public/app.js , which funnels into one refresh that serialises the sequence, diffs it against the last snapshot, and records the difference. That is why agent edits are undoable without a single tool having to know anything about undo. Challenges I ran into The preview cannot have one clock. Decoded <video> , real audio and virtual-clock iframes cannot share a timebase. Seeking audio to keep it aligned is an audible cut, so the compositor instead eases a wall-clock master toward the sounding footage at no more than 4ms per frame, and steers secondary media by playbackRate a few percent — inaudible — only hard-seeking past 600ms of drift. Hiding a layer breaks it. Layers are hidden with opacity, never display:none . Taking an iframe out of the render tree makes Chrome cancel its CSS animations, and they come back as objects the runtime measures from the wrong zero. That one cost an afternoon and is now a comment in composite.js . An agent's tab is always in the background. Chrome loads no media there and never fires requestAnimationFrame , and clamps setTimeout to a second. Captures now ask ffmpeg for each frame of footage, every wait has a real timer behind it, and the scheduler uses a MessageChannel macrotask instead of setTimeout . ffmpeg lies about alpha. Some libvpx builds accept -pix_fmt yuva420p , report no error, and write plain yuv420p . So on startup each alpha-capable format is encoded once and read back. Alpha is verified, not assumed. Silent argument drops. A durationMs passed to a tool that wanted durationSeconds was quietly ignored; every title came out at the default length and nothing said why. Unknown arguments are now refused with the nearest real name. Accomplishments I'm proud of That an agent's edit and a person's edit are genuinely the same edit. Not a parallel API, not a command queue — the same function call, on the same document, in the same undo history, with the same validation. It means an agent's work is inspectable while it happens and reversible after it, which is the only way I would let one near an hour of footage. And that the two tools I needed most did not exist in any editor I know of: get_narration , which answers what is said when, in this timeline's seconds , and check_layout , which answers where do my overlays actually paint, and which of them collide . What I learned Building with the tools as the agent is what produced the good ones. get_narration exists because find_in_transcript spoke source seconds and converting through each item's in-point was a script the agent kept having to write on the side. check_layout exists because the editor knew every overlay's placement but not where the content of a full-frame transparent clip actually sits, so every collision had to be found by capturing frames and looking; now each overlay is drawn offscreen, the box of what it paints is measured, and the check names the pair, the seconds, and how much is covered. The most instructive bug: sixty patch_clip_code calls with lesson 08 open had re-saved lesson 08 sixty times — its revision read 62 while its neighbours read 5 — because one dirty flag covered both the project and whatever timeline happened to be on screen. A second agent working that lesson would have hit sixty stale revisions for nothing. Multi-agent editing punishes shared mutable state very quickly. The general lesson: a good tool surface is not a wrapper over your API. It is a set of answers to the questions an agent actually has to ask, in the units it has to ask them in. What's next A real /mcp Streamable HTTP endpoint, so the same tools are reachable from Codex CLI and other out-of-page agents, not just from the page. Sandboxing agent-authored clip JS in a null-origin frame, which is the honest gap today. Richer per-call confirmation UI for write tools. And pushing more of the ffmpeg-only tools into WebCodecs so the serverless build loses nothing. Required question 1 — Why is WebMCP the right fit for this use case? Because video editing is a long, structured workflow rather than a single prompt, and because all the state that matters is already in the page. A cut is not one decision. It is: read the timeline, find the phrase, convert source time to timeline time, trim the item, ripple everything after it, check the captions still line up, look at the frame. A chat model with a text box cannot do that. A cloud MCP server could only do it by first uploading the footage, the project and the transcripts somewhere — turning a local editing session into a data transfer. WebMCP removes the transfer entirely. The tools run inside the page that already holds the state . The agent gets the open project, the decoded media, the transcripts, the undo stack and the live compositor, because it is standing in the same room as them. Klipvia takes that literally: a build with no server at all — footage in OPFS, projects in IndexedDB, renders through WebCodecs — is fully agent-drivable, and not one frame of video leaves the machine. It also means the agent inherits the app's own rules rather than reimplementing them. Items on a track cannot overlap; a stale save is rejected by revision; a locked track is not written to. Those invariants hold for the agent for free, because it is ca

This is Clip Via, a browser-based video and animation editor. An AI agent can drive through Web MCP. The agent uses structured tools connected to the same editor functions as the interface. Changes appear immediately and stay visible, editable, and undoable in this real session. Codex inspects the project, finds the media, builds the timeline, creates animated titles, and generates narration with Deep Gram. The person and agent work on one shared edit. The agent can also capture composited frames, inspect timing, and run a preflight before rendering. Clip Via keeps projects and renders in the browser and protects credentials from agent tools. The person directs the story. The agent handles the mechanics. Clip Via is built for people and agents to create together on the open web.

title: Faultline
pitch: Faultline is an AI educational app that teaches system design using WebMCP to make agents act like your favorite coworker who can see your work, see the results, and give you help without taking over.
about_excerpt: Faultline is an AI educational app that teaches system design using WebMCP to make agents act like your favorite coworker who can see your work, see the results, and give you help without taking over. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Faultline started after a friend quit his job and we began practicing system design interviews together. We could talk through architectures back and forth, but we kept asking the same question: is this actually right? I wanted a better way to practice than negotiating with an human/LLM for an answer. I wanted a game where you make a design decision and find out whether it works. What it does Faultline is a systems design/interview prep game. Fvery level gives you a problem, requirements, a workload, and a set of components; you design the system, and the simulator tells you the results. With WebMCP, an agent can join the live session, inspect the current design, and point out relevant parts of the canvas. Designed to act like another engineer in the room, the agent will help with questions but won't fully take over. Can also act to be interviewed where the agent will walk through realistic follow ups you might hear in a system design round. How we built it I started with the game itself. Parts like letting player build freely, simulator being the source of truth, and providing the agent with structured evidence from the components as opposed to the answer. Each level has its own rules, including what components are available, the performance of the components, and the requirements. For the agents I needed to decided for most states of the game what the agent might need to reasonable answer a question, and I did so through dynamically exposing tools, keeping data as fresh as possible, and intent routing for most common commands for reliable play. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping the agent reliable while a player rapidly changes an architecture. It needs the most up to date info for every call, but resending every detail was too slow. The app needed to only be frustrating with the challenges, so the agent experience for help needed to be fast just as much as it needed high quality responses. Getting the right current context to the agent efficiently and providing it with only the tools necessary for the state took a lot of fiddling around with. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud of how the agents acts. I've had friends play with it, were unable to beat the level first couple tries and begrudgingly gave into using the coach, where they were surprised with the interactions. It really keeps you as the focus as just acts as a background tool so that you don't get stuck forever. This is best shown in the interview tool that asks follow up questions to let users practice the back and forths after designing the solution by using specific interviewer tools and keeping architecture facts straight as info changes. What we learned This was my first time working with WebMCP, and I learned a lot about building for external agents inside a app. In particular, I learned more about tool routing, intent routing, and evaluations for checking whether an agent picks the best tool for the moment. Was also first time I tried to make like an app with a wide spread audience over to fill specific niches/needs. What's next for Faultline I would like to make it a daily game where you do one game a day just to keep yourself sharp. I would also like to keep expanding the coach's toolset and personality. I think during interview process if it could change the rules of the simulation and make you live build to solve a question would be pretty interesting and fun. GitHub OAuth, used only as an optional identity provider. Vercel, used to host and deploy the live application. Open source dependencies including Next.js, React, React Flow, and related packages. title: OpenSpiderWeb
pitch: An interactive pixel-art spider terrarium powered by procedural IK locomotion, WebMCP browser agent tools, and Groq natural language command planning.
about_excerpt: An interactive pixel-art spider terrarium powered by procedural IK locomotion, WebMCP browser agent tools, and Groq natural language command planning. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Larry the WebMCP Spider was inspired by the idea that websites should be designed for both people and AI agents. Instead of forcing an agent to guess which buttons to click, Larry exposes clear, structured tools that let an agent understand and control the game directly. What I built Larry is an interactive pixel-art spider terrarium built with Phaser. Players can control Larry manually, type natural-language commands, or use voice input. AI commands are interpreted through Ollama and executed through WebMCP tools exposed with document.modelContext . The available tools include inspect_game_world , move_spider , jump_spider , climb_tree , hunt_prey , get_to_ground , and stop_spider . The demo shows a user entering goals while Ollama plans and executes actions for Larry. This creates a shared-control experience where the human chooses the goal and the agent handles the detailed navigation. ## What I learned I learned how to expose state-aware browser tools with WebMCP, including input schemas, validation, cancellation, and meaningful tool results. I also learned that agents work much more reliably when tools describe the current state and their safety restrictions explicitly. Building the demo also taught me about synchronizing browser video, game sound effects, voice narration, and AI tool execution into a single recording. ## Challenges The biggest challenge was coordinating asynchronous movement, climbing, jumping, and hunting actions. Larry needs to understand whether he is on the ground, on a branch, airborne, or already pursuing prey before accepting the next action. Another challenge was making the AI interaction reliable when prey moves or an action fails. I added state validation, recovery behavior, persistent hunt attempts, and a stop tool so the agent can respond to changing conditions. WebMCP is still experimental, so testing required a compatible Chrome configuration and careful debugging through Chrome DevTools. The result is a game that remains fun for a human player while also exposing a clear interface for AI agents.  Inspiration 

 I was on a learning website and I ran out of credits to ask their bespoke AI assistant. At that time, I wished I could bring my ow agent and ask it about points that I didn't understand. When I learned of WebMCP, I knew it would be perfect for my use case. Instead of depending on other developers' implementation of AI agents, I will let my carefully personalized agent be my reading, learning and researching partner. 

 What it does 

 The website exposes several tools that the agents can use: 

 
 Get the content of the current article the user is reading 
 List all articles available on the website 
 Save the summary of an article to localStorage . 
 

 Now, users can ask the agent about concepts in the article they are reading or in other articles. They can ask the agent to summarize an article and this summary will be saved to a flyout that can be toggled with a button. Next time, when the user visits the same article again, the Summary button will be there for you! Of course, they can ask the agent to delete the summary. 

 How we built it 

 The website is nothing more than a basic React app, something that you will build whenever you learn a new frontend framework. The meaty part is the use of WebMCP imperative API to register tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Nothing significant that I can remember. Implementing WebMCP turns out to be a small project. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I think I have empowered readers to get answers for things they don't understand about a third-party website. And I would be amused if I can have a summary of a verbose article I am reading using my own agent without leaving the website. 

 What we learned 

 The most obvious use cases for WebMCP is ecommerce - you can use it to enhance storefront, booking platforms etc. However, you can also use it to create delightful experience for a humble website, even when you think it has no use for WebMCP.

 Fine-tune the existing tool to enhance the human and agent's experience. Keep the tools working seamlessly while watching the WebMCP standards evolve.

title: Algoosh Agentic Shopping
pitch: AI finds and prepares what you need. You review it, provide delivery details, and approve the payment. Offline, online, and now agentic flows are supported. Better than Shopify!
about_excerpt: AI finds and prepares what you need. You review it, provide delivery details, and approve the payment. Offline, online, and now agentic flows are supported. Better than Shopify! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Algoosh, webMCP agentic shopping Algoosh Seller Protal, client app Promo catalog Buyer application UI Infrastructure Smart Contract payment protocol Algoosh Agentic Shopping Inspiration Shopping with an AI agent should feel easier than browsing dozens of pages, comparing products, filling a cart, and repeatedly entering the same checkout information. Most websites, however, still force agents to interpret visual interfaces and simulate clicks, which can be unreliable. At the other extreme, allowing an agent to control a wallet or submit payments creates unacceptable security and trust risks. Algoosh Agentic Shopping explores a better model: let AI handle product discovery and order preparation while keeping the buyer in control of delivery details, wallet access, and payment approval. Algoosh was already a QR-first commerce platform built on Algorand. WebMCP gave us the opportunity to transform every Algoosh Promo catalogue into an agent-readable storefront, while x402 provided a structured way to connect agent-prepared orders with verifiable payments. Our guiding principle became: The AI can shop and prepare. Only the human can approve and pay. What it does Algoosh Agentic Shopping lets a shopper open an Algoosh catalogue and ask an AI agent for help using natural language. For example: I want to make mushroom risotto tonight. I already have rice, olive oil, and garlic. Find the missing ingredients in this store and prepare an order for me to review. The agent can: Read the current catalogue. Inspect individual products and prices. Select products and quantities. Prepare a durable order. Return an approval link and QR code. Check the order state before or after the buyer completes checkout. The buyer then opens the approval link in the official Algoosh application, either on the same device or by scanning the QR code with a phone. There, the buyer: Reviews the selected products and preliminary subtotal. Chooses a fulfillment method. Provides any required delivery information. Reviews the final authoritative price. Explicitly approves the transaction in their own wallet. Through this interface, the AI never receives private delivery information, unlocks the wallet, signs a transaction, or submits payment. Algoosh's WebMCP tools neither request nor return delivery plaintext or wallet credentials. After payment, the agent can retrieve a privacy-safe order summary, the payment state, the selected fulfillment option, the final total, and links to the verified payment and application transactions. How we built it We extended the existing Algoosh platform with four page-local WebMCP tools: get_current_algoosh_catalogue get_current_algoosh_product prepare_algoosh_order get_algoosh_order_status The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() only after the current catalogue has loaded. Their lifecycle is tied to an AbortSignal , so stale registrations are removed when the catalogue changes or the page unloads. No separate MCP server installation is required for this flow; the loaded catalogue page exposes the tools directly. The ordering system uses a two-stage process. First, the WebMCP tool creates a durable but non-payable preliminary intent. The agent supplies only product IDs, quantities, and an idempotency key. It cannot set authoritative prices, seller addresses, payment destinations, delivery details, or wallet information in the order request. Next, the buyer opens the approval handoff. The Algoosh application collects fulfillment information, encrypts the private delivery payload in the browser, and asks the x402 service to finalize the order. Before issuing a payment requirement, the service independently reloads the seller's catalogue and verifies: Product identities and quantities. Current prices and payment assets. Seller and payment addresses. The selected fulfillment option and its current terms and cost. The target Algorand network and application. The service then binds the buyer identity and encrypted-order commitments into the signed quote. If any important commercial term changed, the order stops before payment and the buyer must create and review a new order. Because a token transfer alone is not sufficient evidence of an Algoosh order, we implemented a custom x402 v2 scheme named algoosh-order . Settlement validation checks both the payment and the adjacent createOrderPaid smart-contract call against the signed quote. The finalized order uses an x402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED response containing the signed quote. The buyer application verifies that quote and constructs an atomic Algorand transaction group containing the payment and the Algoosh smart-contract order call. Only the buyer's wallet can approve and submit that group. Redis stores the durable state used for atomic intent creation, idempotency, settlement recovery, and duplicate-order protection. Algoosh Sync validates the resulting public on-chain evidence and correlates it with the prepared order. The approval URL is a short-lived opaque capability link. It contains no personal information, is served with Cache-Control: no-store , and cannot be redirected to an untrusted destination. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was preserving human wallet control while still creating a genuine agentic shopping experience. Many agent-payment flows assume that the agent or facilitator can sign and submit the payment. That model did not fit Algoosh. We designed the preliminary-intent and browser-approval stages so the agent can make useful progress without ever receiving payment authority. Another challenge was maintaining trust across several independent surfaces: Promo catalogue -> WebMCP agent -> x402 service -> Buyer application -> Wallet -> Algorand -> Sync The trust-critical components needed to preserve consistent bindings across the catalogue, products, mount, buyer, seller, fulfillment selection, order seed, and transaction, while exposing only the information appropriate to each surface. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that Algoosh Agentic Shopping is more than a catalogue-reading demo. It connects WebMCP product discovery to a real, human-approved commerce flow. Key accomplishments include: Four functional WebMCP tools verified in a production browser context. A cross-device approval handoff with both a link and generated QR code. A complete low-value Algorand TestNet purchase with explicit buyer approval. x402 payment requirements carrying a signed quote backed by authoritative catalogue data. A custom x402 settlement scheme that validates the complete Algoosh atomic group rather than only a token transfer. Redis-backed recovery that survives service restarts. Protection against duplicate payments during uncertain confirmation. Recovery from temporary blockchain indexer delays. Detection of changed prices or selected fulfillment terms before payment. Privacy-safe agent status responses containing no delivery details. Exact display amounts, ISO timestamps, consistent network metadata, repeated order summaries, and transaction explorer links for agents. Browser-side encryption of the buyer's delivery information. Strict separation between AI assistance and wallet authority. Most importantly, we extended the real Algoosh shopping and payment architecture instead of building a disconnected hackathon simulation. What we learned We learned that agentic commerce does not have to mean autonomous spending. The most useful experience is collaborative: the agent handles discovery, comparison, and preparation, while the person remains responsible for private information and consequential decisions. We also learned that structured WebMCP tools are far more reliable than asking an agent to interpret and click through an unfamiliar interface. Clear tool schemas improve both usability and security by limiting exactly what an agent can provide. Payment confirmation is not a single API call. It is a distributed state machine involving browser state, durable server state, wallet submission, blockchain confirmation, and delayed indexer evidence. Idempotency and recovery are therefore just as important as the successful path. Finally, WebMCP and x402 complement one another well: WebMCP helps the agent understand and use the storefront, while x402 connects the prepared intent to a verifiable payment without giving the agent control of the buyer's wallet. What's next for Algoosh Agentic Shopping Next, we plan to validate the same flow with a controlled MainNet purchase and test it across more WebMCP-capable clients as the proposal evolves. We also want to add explicit cancellation UX, privacy-safe operational telemetry, and better navigation for larger catalogues. Longer term, agents may help shoppers compare products acros

title: Captain Claw
pitch: A gaming platform where an AI agent can turn "what should we play?" into a real multiplayer session.
about_excerpt: A gaming platform where an AI agent can turn "what should we play?" into a real multiplayer session. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most AI gaming demos stop at recommending a game. But when my friends and I actually want to play something together, finding the game is only part of the problem. Someone still has to figure out who's online, what everyone owns, how many players a game supports, whether we've already played it, and whether it fits the time we have. Then someone has to create the party and invite everyone. I wanted to see what this would look like if an agent could work inside the gaming platform itself instead of just giving recommendations in chat. That's what led to Captain Claw . What it does Captain Claw is a fictional gaming platform with a Store, Library, Friends system, and multiplayer Parties. A player can give an agent a request like: "Alex, Sam and Maya are online. We have 75 minutes. Find a co-op game all four of us can play, preferably something none of us has finished." Using WebMCP, the agent can check who's online, compare player libraries, search the catalog, inspect game details, consider session length, and find a game that works for the group. If the player wants to continue, the agent can create a party and send invitations. Those aren't simulated chat responses. They change the actual state of Captain Claw. The party appears in the normal UI, and an invitation sent to another player can appear in that player's browser session. The agent handles the coordination. The player still decides what to play and presses Launch. How I built it Captain Claw is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and WebMCP , and is deployed on Netlify. The platform uses a synthetic but internally consistent dataset of games, players, friendships, libraries, presence, and play history. This keeps the demo self-contained while still giving the agent enough connected data to solve realistic requests. Captain Claw exposes 13 WebMCP tools for things such as checking online friends, comparing libraries, searching games, reading the current browser view, applying Store filters, creating parties, sending invitations, checking party status, and launching a session. Some tools are tied directly to browser context. For example, the agent can inspect the Store view the player is currently looking at and work with filters the player already applied. Tools can also appear based on application state, such as the ability to respond to an invitation when one is pending. One thing I tried to keep consistent throughout the project was that the agent should not have a separate version of the product. Agent actions use the same application logic as human actions. Game filtering uses the same filtering code as the Store, and party actions update the same party state used by the UI. Shared party state is handled through a Netlify Function and Netlify Blobs, which also lets party invitations work across browser sessions. Challenges I ran into The hardest part wasn't registering tools. It was making them feel like they belonged to a real application. Browser state matters. If a player has already filtered the Store, the agent should be able to understand that context instead of starting over. If an invitation is sent, another player should actually be able to receive it. I also ran into smaller problems that exposed bigger design questions. Session length was one example. "We have 75 minutes" sounds simple, but treating 75 minutes as a hard maximum can remove games that are still reasonable choices. The Store and WebMCP tools now share the same session-fit rule so they can't disagree with each other. Testing multi-user party state was another challenge. Each demo room needed isolated state so different users or judges wouldn't accidentally overwrite each other's party. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that WebMCP isn't just sitting beside the application as a demo API. The agent can operate the same product the player is looking at. It can use the current Store context, open a game, change visible filters, create a party, and send an invitation that another browser session can receive. The results of agent actions show up through the normal Captain Claw interface. I also built automated checks around the main recommendation funnel and WebMCP flows so the demo isn't dependent on one lucky prompt. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that useful agent tools aren't always the same thing as backend API endpoints. Giving an agent a pile of raw data isn't necessarily helpful. Tools should represent useful capabilities and expose enough context for the agent to make a good decision. I also learned how important shared context is. When the player changes something and the agent can work from it - or the agent changes something and the player immediately sees it - the interaction feels much more natural than passing information back and forth through chat. WebMCP made that idea much more concrete because the browser isn't just displaying the application anymore. It can expose the application's capabilities to the agent as well. What's next for Captain Claw Captain Claw currently uses a fictional gaming ecosystem so the demo stays deterministic and doesn't depend on external gaming APIs. The next step would be exploring how the same approach could work with real gaming services and richer social data. I'd also like to expand the session-planning side: more player preferences, scheduling, better group matching, and longer-term questions like "what should our group play this weekend?" There are also interesting actions that should require stronger human confirmation, especially purchases or other account-level changes. That's an area I'd like to explore further as agent-operated web applications become more capable. title: /signal
pitch: A Co-op Game Where Player 2 Is AI
about_excerpt: A Co-op Game Where Player 2 Is AI Like Comment Story Updates /signal — Player 2 Is an AI Most AI products are designed around the same interaction: You give the AI a task, and the AI does it for you. While looking at WebMCP, I became much more interested in a different question: What if the AI was not your assistant, but another player? That idea became /signal , an asymmetric co-op browser game where the human and an AI agent have different information, different capabilities, and genuinely need each other to finish the mission. The core rule is simple: You see things it can't. It knows things you don't. Work together. Inspiration The thing that interested me most about WebMCP was not simply letting an agent click fewer buttons or fill forms faster. It was the possibility of building software where the human interface and the agent interface are intentionally different . Traditional games already use asymmetric co-op mechanics: one player might see a map while another has the instruction manual, and the fun comes from communicating. I wanted to see what that would look like when Player 2 is an AI agent connected through WebMCP . Instead of giving ChatGPT access to everything, /signal deliberately hides some information from it. And instead of putting everything in the visual interface, some diagnostics, manuals, simulations, and actions are available only to the AI player. Neither side gets the full puzzle. What it does The player is placed inside a failing remote research station called SIGNAL-9 . Four systems must be restored: Power Cooling Navigation Signal The human plays the role of Field Ops through the visual browser interface. The AI plays Systems through WebMCP. Power The human can see a visual phase symbol and operate physical breakers. The AI can read power diagnostics and access the operating manual, but it cannot see the phase symbol. The human has to tell the AI what they see. The AI interprets that information using its manual and tells the human which breakers to activate. Cooling The human can inspect coolant colors and physically configure the valves. The AI knows the compatibility rules and can run a simulation of the proposed configuration. Even after the human configures everything correctly, the system cannot be restored until the AI player authorizes the pump through WebMCP. Navigation The human sees and interacts with a visual navigation field. The AI has access to hidden navigation constraints, hazard coordinates, destination information, and the fuel budget. They have to communicate to build a safe route together. The human plots it. The AI validates and uploads it. Signal The final system transmits a visual sequence that only the human can observe. The AI has access to the decoding rules. The human describes the sequence, the AI decodes it, the human configures the transmitter, and the AI performs the final Systems authorization. If both players did their jobs correctly: SIGNAL RESTORED. How I built it /signal is built as a fully interactive browser game using: Next.js React TypeScript Tailwind CSS WebMCP localStorage procedural HTML, CSS, and SVG graphics I intentionally avoided using an AI API inside the game. ChatGPT itself is already the reasoning engine. The game's responsibility is to provide: trusted mission state structured diagnostics operating manuals simulations system rules state-changing actions through WebMCP. The human-facing UI and the agent-facing tools interact with the same underlying game state. The AI can use WebMCP tools to inspect diagnostics, access manuals, run simulations, read event history, and perform Systems-only actions. Information asymmetry One of the most important parts of the implementation was making sure WebMCP wasn't simply another way to expose everything already visible on the page. I created separate human-facing and agent-facing information boundaries . For example: Human-only information includes: visual phase symbols coolant appearance visual navigation markers the final signal pattern Agent-only information includes: operating manuals system diagnostics hidden navigation hazards decoding rules certain authorization actions This makes communication an actual game mechanic. If the AI could retrieve the visual answer through WebMCP, there would be no reason for the human player. If the human could see the Systems manual directly, there would be no reason for Player 2. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, ChatGPT would just be sitting outside the game giving generic advice. With WebMCP, the AI becomes part of the game's state machine. It can: inspect the current system retrieve information unavailable to the human react to actions the human takes test proposed configurations perform actions that the human cannot help move the mission forward The interaction becomes: Human observes → AI investigates → both communicate → human acts → AI verifies → AI acts → game state changes. That is what makes /signal different from simply adding a chatbot to a game. WebMCP is not an interface added on top of the game. It is part of the game mechanic itself. Challenges I faced Designing puzzles that genuinely require two players The hardest part was not implementing the interface. It was making sure the AI could not accidentally solve everything by itself. Every puzzle had to answer three questions: What does the human know? What does the agent know? Why do they need to communicate? If either side had too much information, the asymmetric mechanic disappeared. Keeping WebMCP useful without making it overpowered It would have been easy to expose a tool such as: get_solution() That would technically demonstrate WebMCP but completely undermine the game. Instead, the tools expose capabilities and information , not answers. The agent still has to reason. Synchronizing two very different interfaces There are effectively two interfaces operating on the same mission: Field Ops: the visual game interface. Systems: the WebMCP tool interface. Actions performed by either side have to update the shared mission state correctly. That became especially important in modules where the human configures something and the AI must perform the final authorization. Making it feel like a real game I did not want /signal to look like a dashboard built for a hackathon. All of the visuals are built procedurally with CSS and SVG: switches, gauges, pipes, navigation fields, indicators, system traces, and controls. The goal was to make the browser feel like a piece of fictional mission-control hardware rather than an AI demo. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that agent-native software does not necessarily mean giving the agent more control . Sometimes the more interesting experience comes from deliberately giving it less information than the human . WebMCP makes it possible to design applications with two interfaces: one optimized for humans, and another optimized for agents. Those interfaces do not have to expose the same things. That opens up much more interesting forms of collaboration than simply asking an AI to operate software on our behalf. I also learned that agents become much more interesting when they are given a role with constraints . In /signal, ChatGPT is not supposed to be omniscient. It is Systems. The human is Field Ops. Both have responsibilities. And that limitation is what creates the game. What I'm proud of /signal is not a scripted animation or a fake MCP demonstration. It is a complete playable mission. A player can open the live site, connect ChatGPT through WebMCP, restore all four systems, and complete the game from beginning to end. The moment I wanted to create was simple: PLAYER 2: WAITING ChatGPT connects. PLAYER 2: ONLINE And from that point onward, the AI is no longer outside the application. It's playing with you.
