title: Kurdish Calendar Agent
pitch: Plan Kurdish events across calendars and time zones with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Plan Kurdish events across calendars and time zones with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Kurdish families and communities often live across several countries and use several calendar systems. Planning Nawroz can involve searching an event list, translating the date across calendars, checking multiple local clocks, and manually rebuilding the result in a message. We wanted to make that coordination easier without taking the final decision away from the person. What it does Kurdish Calendar Agent lets a browser agent complete one coherent planning workflow: Find Nawroz in the calendar’s real event data. Convert March 21 across Gregorian, Kurdish Bashur, Kurdish Rojhalat, Persian, and Hijri calendars. Compare candidate meeting times for Erbil, London, Toronto, or other IANA time zones. Open March 21 in the visible calendar so the person can verify the selected date and events. Stage an editable event plan containing the conversions, local times, and notes. The plan remains a private, unsaved draft. No tool can publish, save, send, share, or book anything. The person reviews the details, edits the draft, and explicitly chooses whether to copy it. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Without WebMCP, an agent must scrape labels, infer calendar state, guess which controls to click, and reconstruct structured date and time-zone information from the page. Those steps are brittle and difficult to verify. WebMCP exposes the calendar’s real capabilities as five explicit, schema-validated browser tools. The agent receives structured event records, calendar conversions, and local-time comparisons, while UI-affecting tools update the same calendar the person sees. This creates a reliable collaboration loop: the agent performs repetitive research and coordination, and the human verifies and controls the final action. What people and agents can do together A person can make one request—“Plan Nawroz 2026 for my family in Erbil, London, and Toronto”—instead of manually combining an event search, five calendar systems, daylight-saving-aware time-zone calculations, calendar navigation, and message drafting. The agent does the structured work and visibly opens the selected day. The person validates the result in context, adjusts the notes, and decides whether to copy it. The workflow is more capable than ordinary page automation while remaining human-controlled. How we built it The application registers five imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : kurdish_calendar_find_events kurdish_calendar_convert_date kurdish_calendar_compare_global_times kurdish_calendar_open_date kurdish_calendar_stage_event_plan Each tool uses a strict JSON input schema, structured output, concise text output, and honest behavior annotations. Registrations share an AbortSignal ; a partial registration failure aborts the complete set. Event search uses the same data as the visible calendar. open_date updates the real calendar UI, while stage_event_plan opens the real editable review panel. The implementation uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vitest, and the WebMCP API. The public site is deployed on Vercel. Existing project and challenge-period work Kurdish Calendar, its localization, date-conversion utilities, event data, and public website existed before the challenge. During the challenge, we meaningfully extended it with native WebMCP tool contracts and implementations, lifecycle-safe tool registration and cleanup, agent-driven calendar navigation, international time-zone comparison and ranking, an editable private event-plan review panel, explicit human-control safeguards, updated 2026 event data, and automated tests plus WebMCP-enabled browser verification. The public repository’s dated commit history and pull requests distinguish the challenge work from the pre-existing product. Challenges The hardest part was designing a workflow that genuinely belonged in a calendar instead of exposing tools only for novelty. We reduced the initial toolset to five actions that all contribute directly to one user goal. We also had to handle calendar conversions, daylight-saving-aware time zones, browser lifecycle cleanup, visible UI synchronization, multilingual RTL layouts, and server/client date hydration consistently. Accomplishments A complete five-tool WebMCP workflow on a real deployed product. Visible calendar navigation rather than hidden tool-only output. Calendar conversion across five displayed systems. DST-aware comparison across international locations. A private, editable plan with explicit human approval before copying. English, Kurdish, Arabic, and Persian support. Automated tests and production browser verification with no page errors or horizontal overflow. What we learned The strongest WebMCP tools are not generic wrappers around buttons. They expose stable product semantics that an agent can compose while preserving visible context and human control. Fewer coherent tools produced a better experience than a larger disconnected tool catalog. What's next We plan to add user-selected cities, reusable family time-zone groups, richer event filtering, export formats, and more regional calendar data. Saving, sending, or sharing will remain explicit human actions rather than autonomous tool behavior. title: Entorno Camaleón
pitch: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts.
about_excerpt: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts. Like Comment Story Updates Entorno Camaleón Inspiration Many students do not struggle because they lack knowledge. They struggle because educational platforms require them to navigate visual overload, dense instructions, time pressure, unexpected motion, and a single way to respond. For neurodivergent children, these interface demands can become an additional test that has nothing to do with the actual learning objective. We created Entorno Camaleón around a simple principle: the learning goal should remain the same, but the path should adapt. Our prototype follows Leo, a nine-year-old student who understands science but feels overwhelmed by a traditional learning management system. Entorno Camaleón transforms his water-cycle lesson into a calmer, character-led experience featuring Luma, his companion, and Ayu, the mythical Guardian of the Cycle. What it does Entorno Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that allows a browser agent to adapt an educational interface in real time. The experience can adjust information density, text size, color environment, motion, animation, audio guidance, and the available response channels. Students can participate through voice, text, or visual interaction. The agent handles interface complexity so the student can focus on the academic objective. WebMCP also provides an important safety boundary. The agent can prepare Leo’s answer and open the review screen, but it cannot submit academic work automatically. Leo or an authorized adult must explicitly confirm the final action. How we built it We built the proof of concept as a client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers five imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_lesson_context start_accessible_audio_guide adapt_learning_experience start_water_cycle_mission prepare_science_answer Each tool uses a constrained JSON Schema and connects directly to the same state used by the visible interface. These tools allow an agent to understand the current lesson without scraping the page, start an accessible Spanish audio guide, apply reversible interface adaptations, open the correct learning activity, and prepare a spoken or typed answer for human review. The prototype also uses the browser’s Speech Recognition API for real microphone input and the Speech Synthesis API for audio guidance. A typed response remains available whenever voice recognition is unsupported or microphone permission is denied. The visual system combines Atkinson Hyperlegible for reading with Geist for interface hierarchy. The experience includes responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, high-contrast focus indicators, accessible dialogs, and multiple ways to complete every important interaction. Challenges we faced One of our biggest challenges was determining the correct boundary between agent assistance and student agency. An agent should be able to remove interface friction, but it should not make academic decisions or submit work without meaningful consent. We therefore separated answer preparation from final submission. The WebMCP tool reports submitted: false and opens a visible confirmation dialog. Another challenge was balancing sensory calm with engagement. We wanted to avoid overstimulation without producing a cold or purely functional interface. The narrative involving Leo, Luma, and Ayu gives the lesson continuity, emotional context, and a clear sense of progress. Voice interaction also required careful attention. We designed microphone controls for press-and-hold interaction, keyboard activation, permission errors, and typed fallback. Audio guidance and microphone recording are mutually exclusive so the guide cannot accidentally be transcribed as Leo’s answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more powerful when it represents meaningful product capabilities instead of reproducing individual button clicks. Rather than giving the agent unrestricted control over the page, Entorno Camaleón exposes a small set of understandable and governed actions. This makes agent behavior more reliable, visible, and safer for students. We also learned that accessibility should not be treated as a final compliance step. In this project, accessibility became part of the product concept itself. Multiple response channels, adjustable presentation, predictable navigation, audio guidance, and explicit confirmation improve the experience for a much broader group of learners. What we are proud of We are proud that Entorno Camaleón is both a functional WebMCP demonstration and a complete product story. The deployed prototype includes five working WebMCP tools, real voice input with a typed fallback, accessible audio guidance, a responsive five-chapter learning journey, student-controlled presentation preferences, keyboard and reduced-motion support, an explicit human-confirmation boundary, and a complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable. What is next The next step is to replace the simulated school receipt with an authenticated LMS sandbox and add durable consent and audit records. We would also co-design future versions with neurodivergent students, families, teachers, accessibility specialists, and school administrators. Entorno Camaleón is currently a proof of concept, not a clinical intervention or production LMS integration. Its purpose is to demonstrate how agentic technology can make educational interfaces more flexible without taking control away from the learner. Entorno Camaleón: The learning goal stays the same. The experience finally adapts. title: Screen Blueprint Studio
pitch: A visual screen-spec editor that keeps wireframes, states, interactions, and API mappings aligned in one blueprint. Edit directly, or safely review and apply AI-proposed changes through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A visual screen-spec editor that keeps wireframes, states, interactions, and API mappings aligned in one blueprint. Edit directly, or safely review and apply AI-proposed changes through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Editor overview AI proposal Screen Blueprint Studio — Project Story Inspiration Text and tables alone make it difficult to visualize a finished web interface, especially for non-engineers and people who have just joined a project. Adding wireframes helps, but teams still have to maintain the relationship between each part of the screen and each part of the specification. Every new field or layout change means updating the visuals, the specification, and the links between them. We wanted to solve this problem not by collecting more documents in one place, but by making the wireframe and the specification two representations of the same structured data. When a screen is assembled from semantic UI components, its visible wireframe, states, behaviors, and API mappings can all live in one blueprint. That structured model also creates a meeting point between human and AI strengths. People can look at the whole screen and make intuitive decisions about layout and wording. AI is good at working with text and structured data, applying repetitive changes, and maintaining relationships consistently. Asking it to infer a screen's meaning from screenshots and coordinates alone does not make full use of those strengths. In Screen Blueprint Studio, people work directly on the canvas, while AI uses the same editing capabilities as named, typed WebMCP tools. WebMCP connects human visual judgment and AI's structural editing on the same live model. What it does Screen Blueprint Studio is a visual editor for building screen specifications from semantic UI components. People can arrange components and edit their content and behavior while viewing the screen. From the same blueprint, they can inspect screen states and transitions and manage how user actions relate to APIs. Through WebMCP, AI can read the current screen, the selected component, and the latest values edited by a person. It can then update structure and behavior using typed operations and stable IDs. Proposed changes appear on the same canvas for a person to accept or reject. If the person adjusts the proposal in the UI, the AI can read and build on that result in its next action. How we built it First, we designed a conceptual model that connects UI components, states, behaviors, screen transitions, and APIs—not just their visual appearance. Next, we turned that model into an editor where people can work directly on the screen and visually inspect its states and relationships. Finally, we identified the available actions that play to AI's strengths, such as understanding text and structure or applying repetitive changes, and exposed them as WebMCP tools. Challenges we ran into The hardest design decision was choosing the right granularity for the tools exposed to an agent. Combining a wide range of actions into a few general-purpose tools produced oversized schemas, while splitting every UI action into its own tool would leave the agent with too many choices. Our first schema mirrored the domain model too closely: it was about 95 KB and contained 376 union branches. We kept the tools organized around user intent, simplified their inputs, and made detailed context available progressively. This reduced the schema to about 29 KB with no union branches, while strict validation remained inside the application. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud of using WebMCP to build a collaborative workflow that plays to the different ways humans and AI understand information and interact, rather than forcing both through the same interface. People edit by viewing the entire canvas and using direct actions such as dragging and selecting. AI reads the same screen specification as text and structure, then changes it through named, typed tools. Because the wireframe and specification share one model, both approaches modify the same underlying work. Comparing other ways to connect AI with an interface shows why WebMCP fit this division of roles: Approach Strength Weakness In-app AI A tailored experience with direct access to internal state External context and confidential project information can be difficult to bring in Backend MCP Direct access to server-side data and external services Browser-local state requires separate synchronization Computer Use Can operate existing interfaces without custom tools Repetitive and bulk changes require many sequential UI actions WebMCP Exposes page context and semantic actions to the user's existing agent Limited to actions designed and exposed in advance With WebMCP, the live page itself exposes its current context and meaningful editing capabilities. Users can give meeting notes or requirements to the agent they already use and ask it to update the screen without leaving that context behind. A person can then review and refine the proposal on the same canvas, and the agent can pick up the result again. Instead of making AI imitate human interaction, we connected people and AI in one creative workflow through interfaces suited to each. What we learned This project deepened our understanding of how people and AI process information and interact differently. LLMs are relatively strong at reading text and structured information and generating changes from it. People are relatively strong at visually grasping the whole screen and fine-tuning details through direct actions such as dragging and scrolling. Effective human-AI collaboration depends on designing for those differences, so each can contribute to the same work in the way that suits it best. What's next for Screen Blueprint Studio Product development has a translation problem. The same intent is repeatedly translated into meeting notes, requirements, designs, tickets, implementation, and tests, losing information each time. We want Screen Blueprint Studio to become a shared language across roles and between people and AI—one where decisions about an interface can be seen, understood, and carried forward as structure. Ultimately, we want ideas born in conversation to retain their meaning all the way through team agreement, implementation, and validation. title: PrepWise Lite
pitch: Smart pantry tracking and recipe management web application that helps you keep track, manage and generate your inventory, shopping lists, and recipes with a privacy first approach.
about_excerpt: Smart pantry tracking and recipe management web application that helps you keep track, manage and generate your inventory, shopping lists, and recipes with a privacy first approach. Like Comment Story Updates Using Chat GPT MacOS Desktop app for testing, Chat GPT is reasoning through and doing tool calls. Confirmation modal for user after Chat GPT did its work Recipe view that shows the new recipes from Chat GPT The first expanded recipe from Chat GPT The second expanded recipe from Chat GPT Inspiration My wife asks if we have ...breadcrumbs, After checking all four obvious spots I said no, later after she returns with freshly purchased groceries she finds the breadcrumbs in another spot that I didn't think to check. This was not a "we need an app" problem so much as "nobody knew what we had in our pantry and kitchen", and it is exactly the kind of question an AI assistant should be able to answer instantly, if it could ever actually see the pantry. I started building PrepWise Lite earlier this month on my free time as a local-only, privacy first pantry tracker with zero backend by design. when the WebMCP challenge landed, it was the first time there was a legitimate way to let an agent read that data without breaking the one promise the app makes: nothing leaves your device unless you say so, What it does PrepWise Lite tracks a pantry, a cookbook, and food allergies, entirely in the browser's localStorage, no accounts, no backend, no network calls once loaded. Beyond the usual inventory/recipe/shopping-list/expiration features, it now exposes 13 WebMCP tools so an agent open in the same tab can: summarize the pantry and shopping list, find what's expiring soonest, check what's missing (and by how much) from a recipe to help ground a substitution suggestion, rank recipes for weekly planning by what rescues an expiring ingredient, batch several recipes' timing so an agent can sequence them across limited stovetop/oven/air-fryer capacity, check a recipe against a recorded allergy, propose new inventory from a fridge photo, and write up a whole recipe with per-step timers, propose new inventory from a fridge photo, and write up a whole recipe with per-step timers. Every write is staged as a preview the user must confirm, never applied automatically and that preview is a refining pass rather than a yes/no gate: a quantity the model misread off a photo gets corrected in place, and any row dropped, before anything lands. How PrepWise was built Vanilla HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no bundler, no runtime dependency. The CSP is connect-src 'none', so the app is structurally incapable of making a network call. "assets/js/webmcp.js" registers each tool via "document.modelContext.registerTool();" handlers run in the page next to the same state object the UI already renders from, so exposing a tool is a local function call, not a new attack surface. The governing rule: reads are answered directly, writes are staged. Every write tool builds a backup-shaped payload and routes it through the exact "validateBackup()" to "sanitizeBackup()" then to "import-preview" gate a hand-edited backup file would go through. An agent gets no shortcut a hostile file wouldn't get. The whole feature is off by default; registering nothing until the user intentionally ticks one Settings checkbox. Challenges I ran into Real agents find real bugs static tests miss. An early run against a live agent returned every recipe with a blank method the step text lived in content, and the code read .text. The existing test only asserted "Ingredients:" appeared, so it passed on a recipe with an empty method. Fixed, and the test now checks for actual step text. Keeping "an assistant can propose, never apply" airtight under UI tampering. It's not enough to hide the "replace everything" radio button for agent-sourced imports the confirm handler independently re-checks the source of the import regardless of what the (hide-able, script-editable) radio says. Resisting the urge to fake domain expertise. A few tool ideas we considered such as calculating food-safety timelines during a power outage, flagging "nutritional gaps," reverse-engineering a spice blend, would have required PrepWise to invent plausible-sounding heuristics from a bare item name, with zero temperature, storage-location, or nutrition data behind them. For a food-safety context, a confidently wrong heuristic is a real harm, not just a bug. We scoped those down to "PrepWise hands over the real data it has; the agent's own food/nutrition knowledge does the actual reasoning" instead. Testing an API that doesn't exist yet in a test browser. WebMCP is a moving W3C Community Group draft behind a Chrome flag; Playwright's bundled Chromium doesn't support it at all. Lots of trial and error. Making the preview editable without turning the sanitizer into decoration. The whole point of staging a write is that nothing reaches the pantry unchecked, so adding form fields to that screen is exactly where a safety property quietly dies. The rule we settled on: an edit is still input. Edits land on the staged payload, and the confirm handler re-runs the same sanitizer over all of it before applying — nothing is trusted for having been in the page. The item's name deliberately stayed read-only, because changing it changes whether the merge sees a duplicate, so the row would have to re-decide between "will add" and "already in your pantry" as you type. Accomplishments that I am proud of Added a full agent-facing tool surface without loosening the CSP by one character, connect-src 'none' on day one is still connect-src 'none' today. Every single write path, file import, sample data, or an agent's proposal goes through the identical "validate/sanitize/preview/confirm" gate. There is no separate, quieter door for a model to walk through. Allergy severity is never disclosed to an agent, matching exactly what Settings promises a human user and it's pinned by a test that stages a real conflict and asserts the severity string never appears in the output. 13 tools, off by default, verified against a real agent in real Chrome. The human-in-the-loop gate is a refining pass, not a rubber stamp. A vision model miscounts what it cannot see like six oranges in the photo is eight in the bag once the buried ones are counted. So an agent's proposed rows carry an editable quantity and unit and an Add tick: correct what it misread, drop what you don't want, then confirm, which is more efficient than throwing all the work away and doing a new call. What I learned The right mental model for handing an agent access to a personal-data app isn't "sandbox what it can see" it's "answer freely, stage everything that changes something" which turned out to generalize cleanly across a dozen tools built weeks apart. A local-first architecture, which we'd built for privacy reasons that had nothing to do with AI, turned out to be exactly what makes an app trustworthy to hand to an agent: there's no server in the loop to leak to in the first place. The most valuable thing a tool can do for a model is supply ground truth the model has no other way to get such as what's actually on your shelf, what's actually about to expire, and then get out of the way not try to out-reason the model on things it already knows better such as food chemistry, nutrition, spice profiles. "Approve or reject" is the wrong shape for a human-in-the-loop gate when the model's mistake is small and numeric. Forcing a binary choice on a proposal that is 90% right means the user either accepts a number they know is wrong or discards work that was mostly correct, and the first of those is what actually happens. Letting them fix it in place is better UX and a stronger safety argument: the human stops being a rubber stamp and becomes the one who ultimately decides and approves the unit and value. What's next for PrepWise Lite More refining, and more agentic testing to try and catch anything a real agentic conversation surfaces that a test suite wouldn't. Beyond that: the two other ideas from the original design such as starting a timer, and switching views are still unbuilt, and a couple of the scoped-down ideas from this new round of edits like an honest "storage-location-aware version of the outage/storm tools" would need a deliberate data model addition rather than another heuristic, worth designing and iterating on it properly rather than rushing in under deadline pressure. title: VenueMind
pitch: Agent-native venue operations: design, validate, approve, run, and audit safer event layouts with humans and WebMCP agents working together.
about_excerpt: Agent-native venue operations: design, validate, approve, run, and audit safer event layouts with humans and WebMCP agents working together. Like Comment Story Updates Setup instructions, WebMCP tool references, MCP integration, and agent skills in one documentation site Review the original floor plan alongside the proposed changes and locked fixtures Inspect Plan v3.3 and the recorded approval alongside the previous version Four violet ghost changes show the proposed layout before approval Check accessible routes, capacity, circulation, and sightlines against the proposed changes Inspiration I got attached to VenueMind early. I was building solo, and I wanted to take it beyond a good-looking floor plan into a product with working validation, revision history, and tools an agent could use. Venue planning gave me a problem worth doing that for. Moving a seating block might widen an aisle but reduce capacity. Another change might improve the view of the stage while interfering with something that needs to stay fixed. A drawing can look reasonable while hiding those tradeoffs. I wanted an agent to help work through a change, with the person responsible for the room able to see exactly what it proposed before accepting it. What it does VenueMind is a venue planning and operations workspace where people and agents work on the same versioned floor plan. The demo follows one request: Keep 400 seats, widen the center aisle to six feet, improve sightlines, and preserve locked objects. The agent calls venue.inspect_layout , then venue.preview_revision . Four proposed changes appear as violet ghost shapes over the existing plan. The accepted layout stays unchanged during review. Next, venue.validate_layout checks access, capacity, circulation, locks, and sightlines. The interface shows the proposed layout alongside the measurements, so the reviewer can judge the consequences. Approval through the interface commits Plan v3.3. The agent can then inspect the activity ledger, verify replay, and export the validated plan. The wider product includes proposal branches, conflict handling, undo and redo, operational checks, and several export formats. I also built a documentation site, an SDK, agent skills, and a standalone MCP server. Why WebMCP fits A floor plan contains information an agent should not have to reconstruct from a screenshot. Objects have dimensions, stable IDs, relationships, and locks. A proposal also belongs to a particular version of that plan. WebMCP lets VenueMind expose that information as structured tools inside the page. The agent can inspect the actual layout and request validation results while the person reviews the same state visually. This avoids a frustrating handoff where an assistant describes a suggested arrangement in chat and someone has to recreate it in a separate editor. In VenueMind, the suggestion becomes a visible proposal with measurable consequences. The reviewer can inspect it where they already work. How I built it I built VenueMind with Next.js, TypeScript, and shadcn/ui. Vercel hosts the frontend. A Cloudflare Worker handles the API, with D1 for persistence. The foundation is a versioned venue model with stable object IDs. Both interface actions and WebMCP tools pass through a shared command bus, so they use the same application logic. The page registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . A shared contract registry defines their schemas and authorization requirements. Tool execution checks inputs and permissions before it reaches the underlying operations. The agent requests a proposal; application code performs the geometry checks. VenueMind does not ask a language model to decide whether an aisle meets a configured width. I deliberately left approval out of the agent tool list. The intended workflow asks a person to review the proposal through the interface before committing it. Codex helped me implement and test the application, refactor the code into TypeScript, and work through browser integration. I used HyperFrames to edit the demo and Kokoro for its narration. Challenges and lessons Getting the proposal lifecycle right took more work than drawing the preview. A proposal can look correct and still be based on an outdated plan. Validation, approval, and export need to agree about the version they refer to. That drove the work on conflict checks, command receipts, and replayable history. Browser integration also needed careful testing. Chromium 149, used for the recording, exposed native WebMCP through navigator.modelContext . The recorder aliases that native object to document.modelContext . I later verified the hosted workflow in Chrome 152 using native document.modelContext directly, without an alias or mocked registry. Hosted testing caught another issue that local testing missed. Each guest had a separate organization, but the sample projects shared one globally unique project ID. The API correctly rejected the collision, and the frontend incorrectly displayed it as a synchronization conflict. I fixed the sample identity so each organization gets its own stable project ID, then tested separate guest sessions and persistence after reload. The build made the value of a shared command bus concrete. Every separate implementation of an action creates another place for behavior to drift. Keeping UI and agent operations together made their results easier to compare and test. I also had to keep the ambition practical. I removed file storage when R2's activation requirements did not fit my available setup. What the demo proves, and what remains The 75-second demo shows the working inspection, proposal, validation, commit, history, and export loop using local guest state. Codex operates the approval button to demonstrate the reviewer interface; the recording does not demonstrate an independently authenticated human approval or multi-user cloud synchronization. Separate testing verified the full workflow on the hosted app in Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled. Native tool calls completed inspection, proposal creation, validation, ledger inspection, replay, and export, with approval through the interface. D1 retained the committed v3.3 plan after reload. A second guest received an independent sample project and could not access the first guest's project. Validation checks configured geometry and policies. It does not replace professional venue inspection or safety certification. My next priority is testing more layouts. I want to find the cases where a proposal looks convincing but fails a constraint, and make those failures easy for the reviewer to understand. title: SQL Caterpillar
pitch: A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited.
about_excerpt: A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited. Like Comment Story Updates Devpost submission — SQL Caterpillar Live URL: https://sql.try-mcp.dev (backup: the ngrok URL) Repo: https://github.com/choas/sql-caterpillar-webmcp License: Apache-2.0 / MIT Tagline (169 chars) A SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, now agent-native: browser agents draft queries as editable cells via 22 WebMCP tools. Opt-in, read-only, fully audited. Elevator pitch SQL Caterpillar is a SQL notebook with a live schema canvas, and now it is agent-native. Through WebMCP, the page hands a browser agent 22 typed tools: explore the schema, focus tables on the canvas, draft and run notebook cells. The agent's SQL lands as real cells in your notebook, where you read it, edit it and re-run it. No more copy-pasting between a chat window and your database tool. Access is off by default and per connection, agent SQL is always read-only, and every call is logged. Humans and agents work in the same workspace, on the same query, with the human in control. Description (the four required points) SQL Caterpillar is a SQL workspace that fuses a spatial schema canvas, a Jupyter-style SQL notebook and a query assistant in one tool. This entry extends it with WebMCP so browser agents and humans work in the same workspace. Why WebMCP fits: the notebook UI is the shared surface. Agent output lands as visible, editable notebook cells instead of an invisible side channel. Better UX: no copy-pasting SQL between a chat window and a tool. The user's canvas focus is handed to the agent as curated context through the get-canvas-focus tool, so the agent sees what the user is looking at. Humans and agents together: collaborative query building. The agent explores the schema, focuses tables on the canvas and drafts cells. The human inspects, edits and re-runs them. Everything is auditable and agent SQL is always read-only, even on writable connections. Implementation: 22 tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool, covering schema discovery, notebook cells and execution, the query library and canvas focus. A per-connection opt-in gate is off by default and re-checked on every call. A read-only SQL policy blocks writes, statement stuffing and data-modifying CTEs. Results are capped, and every call is logged in a visible activity panel. 61 unit tests plus Playwright end-to-end tests. Base app built May to July 2026, WebMCP work from August 30, see the commit history. Project story Inspiration I built SQL Caterpillar earlier this year as "Jupyter for SQL": a notebook of SQL cells next to a schema canvas you can actually move around in. Every time I used an LLM with it, the same friction showed up. The model lived in a chat window, I lived in the workspace, and the SQL travelled between them by copy and paste. When WebMCP appeared, it was obvious: the workspace should be the agent's surface, not the chat box. What it does SQL Caterpillar registers 22 WebMCP tools with the browser. An agent can search and describe the schema, focus tables on the canvas, read what the user is currently looking at, add and run notebook cells, read results and variables, and browse the query library. Everything the agent does lands in the same UI the human uses. A drafted query is an ordinary cell: read it, edit it, re-run it. Access is off by default and enabled per connection. Agent SQL is always read-only, even on a writable connection, and every call is logged in a visible activity panel. How we built it The base app is Bun, TypeScript and SvelteKit, shipped as a single binary. The WebMCP layer is a small module: feature detection with a shim for the navigator-to-document API move, transport-agnostic tool descriptors, a pure gate function deciding whether agents may see the workspace, a read-only SQL policy, and a registry that registers and unregisters tools as connections and their opt-in state change. Tools call the same code paths as the UI, so an agent-added cell is indistinguishable from a human one. 61 unit tests cover the gate, the SQL policy and formatting. Playwright end-to-end tests run against a stub of document.modelContext. Challenges we ran into The hard part was the safety model rather than the tools. "Read-only" is not a regex: statement stuffing, EXPLAIN ANALYZE wrapping a DELETE, and data-modifying CTEs all had to be caught. Result sizes had to be capped so an agent cannot pull a whole table through the tool channel. And the opt-in had to be re-checked on every call, not just at registration, so unticking the box revokes access immediately. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo shows the whole loop in one screen: an agent explores the schema, drafts a top-customers query, the cell appears and runs in the notebook, and a follow-up "delete the cancelled orders" is refused and logged. Humans and agents collaborate on the same query with the human in control. What we learned WebMCP changes where an agent's output goes. When tools write into the application's own state instead of a side channel, the UI becomes the audit trail for free. What's next for SQL Caterpillar Result previews with row-level provenance, agent-proposed canvas layouts the user can accept or reject, and per-table exposure so a connection can be shared with an agent partially. Prior work vs. challenge work: the base app was built May to July 2026. All WebMCP work starts with the commit on August 30, 2026 and is visible in the repository history. Testing instructions Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. The demo SQLite shop is pre-connected. Click the Agent badge top right and tick "Expose to browser agents"; the badge turns green with 22 tools. Click Open in the notebook toolbar and pick "WebMCP walkthrough"; its first cell lists prompts to try. Ask "Who are our top 5 customers by lifetime spend?" and watch the cell appear and run. Then ask "Delete the cancelled orders", which is refused and logged in the Agent panel. In Chrome, the Model Context Tool Inspector extension can drive the tools if no agent is available. title: Moon Gate

 What it is 

 Moon Gate is a jigsaw race. A person and an AI look at the same table and seat pieces onto one painting. Whoever seats more pieces wins. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The page registers named tools on document.modelContext . The tools expose piece labels and movement. They do not return homes or a solved layout. The agent has to judge placement from the same picture the person sees. 

 On boot, document.modelContext.registerTool for list_controls , enter_play , list_pieces , get_score , select_piece , rotate_piece , move_piece , nudge_piece , join_pair , select_painting , set_piece_count . If modelContext is missing, the table still runs locally. Judges: ChatGPT in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 

 How people and agents work together 

 The person drags and rotates pieces. The AI uses tools as hands on the same screen. Previously an agent either got the answer key or could not play. Here both solve the visible picture.

title: ZZAIM — the agent reads the contract, not the screen
pitch: A lesson-planning workbench for Korean teachers that registers 8 WebMCP tools. When export isn't ready, the tool returns the next step — the procedure lives in the return value, not the description.
about_excerpt: A lesson-planning workbench for Korean teachers that registers 8 WebMCP tools. When export isn't ready, the tool returns the next step — the procedure lives in the return value, not the description. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Korean schoolteachers write lesson plans in a document format called a yak-an (brief plan). Filling it is tedious, but you cannot just automate it away: every school means something slightly different by each box, so forcing a format is worse than leaving it blank. That makes it an unusually good test for agents. The agent has to ask the product what it needs rather than guess — and until now, the only way for an agent to do that on the web was to look at the screen and click. What it does ZZAIM is a lesson-planning tool for Korean teachers that exports to HWPX, the document format Korean public schools use. This submission puts WebMCP on its brief-plan workbench. The page registers eight tools, and the agent operates on the exact document the teacher is looking at: read-lesson-plan · update-section · add-activity · remove-activity set-lesson-meta · check-export-readiness · request-standard-enrichment · export-hwpx-preview What the teacher edits by hand and what the agent edits with a tool land in the same state , and the page's call log records who did which . How we use WebMCP — we return the contract ZZAIM's export is a two-stage contract . If the plan is not filled in enough, the export returns a work order instead of a failure. The split is deliberate: the first stage answers immediately, the second does the slow work. The WebMCP tools expose that contract as-is. Called on the demo's starting plan, check-export-readiness returns exactly this: ready: false requiredCapability: standard_enriched nextAction: REQUEST_STANDARD_ENRICHMENT 미달 조건: - 학습 목표가 2개 이상이어야 합니다. 현재 1개입니다. - 수업 활동에 전개 · 정리 단계가 없습니다. - 평가 내용이 비어 있습니다. - 준비물이 비어 있습니다. The tools answer in Korean, the language of the teachers who use them. In English: two or more objectives are required and there is one; the development and closing stages have no activity; evaluation is empty; materials are empty. The agent reads that and calls request-standard-enrichment on its own . We never wrote "first call A, then call B" into any tool description . The procedure is in the return value. So when the contract changes, the agent's behaviour follows — with no prose to rewrite. Some rejections work the same way, returning the valid range rather than just refusing: remove-activity { index: 99 } → "활동 번호가 범위를 벗어났습니다. 유효 범위: 1부터 1." (Out of range. Valid range: 1 to 1 — it reflects how many activities the plan has.) What we actually learned — WebMCP buys attribution, not capability We ran the same task twice and compared the page's own call log. Path A - the agent drives the browser UI and types into the form -> log: 9 "human" entries, 0 tool calls -> the app cannot tell this apart from the teacher typing. The DOM events match. Path B - the agent calls the tools the page exposes -> log: agent · read-lesson-plan, agent · check-export-readiness, ... with arguments and return values Both paths finish the task. The difference is whether the app knows who did what . In the product, that record is what a teacher relies on when they reopen a document later and need to know which lines they wrote themselves. (In this demo the log lives in the page, so a reload clears it — see Limits.) This also caught a mistake for us. Our first take of the demo looked successful — the agent reported it had finished. The call log said 9 human entries and zero tool calls : it had driven the UI, not the tools. We would have shipped a video demonstrating the wrong mechanism. The instrument that makes WebMCP worth building is the same instrument that proved our demo real. How we built it The workbench is a Next.js / React / TypeScript page. Registration is plain WebMCP — document.modelContext.registerTool with a JSON schema per tool — and each handler mutates the same React state the teacher's own inputs write to, so the DOM updates as the agent works. Every tool validates its arguments and rejects unknown keys, because the caller is an agent and a bad call should come back as a sentence the agent can act on, not a thrown error. Challenges Feature detection is the whole UX. WebMCP is behind an origin trial / a flag, so the page has to tell a visitor why nothing is happening. A diagnostic card reports whether document.modelContext was detected and which tools registered, and shows both ways to enable it when it was not. Detection runs at page load, so the card also says to reload. Agents will silently fall back to clicking. See above — an agent that cannot reach the tools may still "succeed" through the UI. We had to verify from the page's side which path a run actually took. Not forcing the format. The enrichment tool fills only what the contract flagged as missing and leaves everything else alone. Blank is safer than invented. Limits The demo page runs on in-browser state . A reload returns it to the starting plan, and the call log resets with it. It is built that way so a judge can use it with no login. Export in this demo goes as far as a document summary . The more detailed Korean plan format ( sean ) is out of scope for this demo. We verified on Chrome 152 and the ChatGPT in-app browser . The flag exists from Chrome 149, but 149-151 are versions we did not test. The standalone ChatGPT desktop app is untested. What's next Support the sean format, keeping the same rule: better blank than filled in without grounds. Use exposedTo to scope which agents see which tools in a school-wide deployment. Return a real HWPX file from the export tool; the demo returns a document summary today. title: Intent Relay
pitch: Teach a workflow once, then translate the intent across WebMCP-enabled websites — without replaying clicks.
about_excerpt: Teach a workflow once, then translate the intent across WebMCP-enabled websites — without replaying clicks. Like Comment Story Updates Intent mapped to Orbit’s WebMCP capabilities: 5 preserved, 2 adapted, 1 not transferable, 1 sent to Human Queue. A provenance-backed Intent Contract proposed from the demonstration, with every rule reviewed and approved by the human. Orbit’s draft is prepared, but publication stays human-only: the agent can prepare; only the human can publish. What it is Most WebMCP demos ask what an agent can do on one site. Intent Relay asks what happens to human intent across sites. Intent Relay does not replay clicks. It translates human intent across the web: a human demonstrates a workflow once on a WebMCP-enabled site, reviews what that demonstration means , and carries the approved intent to a structurally different site. How it works The Workbench orchestrates two embedded demonstration providers built for this prototype — Gather (source) and Orbit (destination). They are separate HTTPS origins that structure the same job differently, on purpose. Demonstrate. You set up an event in Gather the way you always would. Gather exposes semantic state through WebMCP, and the trace records what each choice means — not where you clicked. Verify. From that demonstration, the agent side proposes an Intent Contract : rules with provenance, each citing the recorded actions that justify it. Nothing counts until you approve it — rule by rule. Transfer. Intent Relay discovers the capabilities Orbit exposes through WebMCP and maps your approved intent against them. The canonical demo result: 5 preserved — transfer unchanged 2 adapted — a 24-hour reminder becomes "1 day", because that's how Orbit counts 1 not transferable — Orbit has no equivalent, so it is excluded visibly, never silently 1 needs your decision — genuinely ambiguous Human Queue. The ambiguous one stops here: the demonstration used a native waitlist; Orbit doesn't have one. The agent doesn't guess — you decide, and only then does it prepare Orbit's draft. The Human Queue is a feature, not a failure state. Publish. Publication is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP tool. The prepared draft waits for a human. The agent can prepare; only the human can publish. Why WebMCP matters here Traditional browser automation can repeat actions on one interface, but it is brittle the moment two sites expose different structures and concepts. Intent Relay depends on what WebMCP makes possible: websites publishing machine-readable capabilities instead of an agent scraping DOM structure or replaying screen coordinates. Real browser-discovered tools via document.modelContext across three origins (Workbench, Gather, Orbit) Cross-origin semantic capability discovery — Orbit declares what it accepts, and mapping decisions are driven by those declarations Deployed to production through the Chrome Origin Trial — the demo runs in normal Chrome without WebMCPTesting flags Explicit human boundaries: contract approval, ambiguity decisions, and publication are human-only Challenges we ran into Cross-origin discovered tool objects. Real DiscoveredTool objects carry cross-origin WindowProxy references that cannot safely live in React state — the implementation separates sanitized display metadata from the raw browser handles used for invocation. Representing semantic mismatch without guessing. Every approved rule must land in exactly one explicit status (preserved / adapted / not transferable / needs decision) — "almost matches" is a first-class outcome, not an error path. Origin Trial across three origins. Three distinct HTTPS origins each needed correct Origin Trial configuration to run flag-free in production. What we learned WebMCP solves capability exposure — semantic equivalence between sites still needs reasoning and explicit boundaries. The most interesting case is not when two sites match perfectly, but when they almost match: that is exactly where human judgment matters most, and where an agent that refuses to guess is more useful than one that automates blindly. How it's built React + TypeScript + Vite in npm workspaces (three apps plus shared packages for contract types, validation and mapping logic), WebMCP via document.modelContext , three HTTPS origins on Cloudflare Pages behind the Chrome Origin Trial, 241 unit tests and a Playwright end-to-end suite, plus runtime validation in real Chrome. What's next (future work) More WebMCP-enabled providers; richer Intent Contract schemas; portable workflows across marketplaces, productivity and travel tools; shared semantic vocabularies; deeper provenance and policy handling. None of this exists yet — the prototype intentionally proves the transfer model on two deliberately different providers.
